How does that person walk?
He does not dare to run.
He does not dare to turn his head to look for cars.
Every step is tense.
He is not afraid because the things are heavy;
he is afraid
because he might drop them.
The fuller his grasp,
the less he dares to move.
The more he owns,
the more he fears losing.
Pilate was that man crossing the street with his arms full.
He was carrying his position,
carrying the people’s favor,
carrying Caesar’s trust,
carrying his own future.
So he did not dare to do what he knew was right.
We are often the same.
We think
that the more we grasp,
the more peaceful our hearts will be.
A little more money saved, and we feel at ease.
One more guarantee, and we feel relieved.
If the children would just listen to me more, I would not worry.
A little more influence in the church, and I would feel secure.
The result is exactly the opposite.
The more we grasp,
the tighter our hearts become.
Because anything that can be taken away
will make a person afraid.
Only the Lord who cannot be taken away
can give true peace.
2. The Lord’s Silence Is the Most Solemn Judgment
Verse 9:
Pilate went into the Praetorium again
and said to Jesus:
“Where are you from?”
This is a good question.
In fact it is the central question of the whole Gospel of John.
Where did Jesus come from?
Where is He going?
Who is He?
With this question,
Pilate had already come to the doorway.
But what comes next
is the most startling six words in this passage:
“But Jesus gave him no answer.”
The Lord was silent.
Before Caiaphas,
He had been silent.
Before Herod,
He had been silent.
Isaiah 53:7 had long ago prophesied:
“He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth.”
But the silence here
carries another layer of meaning.
Because before this,
the Lord had already said a great deal to Pilate.
In John 18:37,
the Lord told him Himself:
“For this reason I have been born, and for this reason I have come into the world, that I should testify to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.”
How did Pilate respond then?
He said one sentence:
What is truth?
And then he turned and walked out.
He asked a question
but did not wait for the answer.
He pushed the door open a crack,
and then shut it again with his own hand.
So now,
when he turned back and asked:
“Where are you from?”
the Lord did not answer.
Dear family,
I want to say this very carefully:
the Lord’s silence
is not because the Lord is unloving.
It is because people keep shutting the door.
When a person repeatedly refuses the light that has already shone in,
he slowly loses the ability to hear again.
It is not that God has taken back His voice;
it is that the person has covered his ears.
This is a very solemn principle in the Bible.
When the light shines in and we do not respond,
after a while
the light is no longer light,
but becomes judgment.
So the Lord’s silence
is itself a kind of judgment.
It is not punishment;
it is a mirror.
It lets Pilate, in that stillness,
hear the voice within his own heart.
Today we too must ask ourselves a question:
Is there something
the Lord has already told me very clearly,
yet I keep pretending not to hear?
Is there a relationship,
a habit,
an account,
an “I’m sorry” I should have said long ago,
that the Lord has reminded me of three times, five times,
and each time I said, “Let’s see later”?
Dear family,
as long as you can still hear the Lord’s voice,
that is grace.
As long as your heart can still be uneasy,
that is grace.
Please do not wait until one day
everything inside is quiet,
you feel nothing at all,
and only then discover that the most frightening thing is not being rebuked,
but being unable to hear.
3. “I Have Power”: This Sentence Is the Prototype of Humanity’s Fall
Verse 10:
Pilate was provoked.
He said:
“Are you not speaking to me?”
The tone of this sentence
is the tone of one who has been offended.
What power cannot bear
is being ignored.
You can curse it,
and it still has something to do.
Ignore it,
and it panics.
Then he spoke the heart of this whole passage:
“Don’t you know that I have power to release you, and have power to crucify you?”
I have power.
Please set these words in your heart
and read them slowly once.
I have power.
Brothers and sisters,
this is the prototype of humanity’s fall.
In Genesis chapter 3,
what did the serpent say to the woman?
“You will be like God, knowing good and evil.”
It meant:
you can decide for yourself what is right and what is wrong.
You do not need God to tell you.
You can sit down in that seat yourself.
From that day on,
humanity’s sickness has been the same sickness:
leaving one’s own place,
reaching out to grasp power that does not belong to us.
Wanting to take God’s place.
When Pilate said “I have power to release you, and have power to crucify you,”
what he meant was:
your life and death
are in my hands.
I am the one who decides.
But as we read on, we see
how empty this sentence was.
He said he had power to release,
yet he did not release.
He clearly found no guilt in Jesus,
he clearly wanted to let Him go,
he clearly knew it was out of envy,
and in the end he still handed the Lord over.
He had power,
but did not dare to use it.
So who was really in power?
It was those voices shouting outside.
It was the five words “friend of Caesar.”
It was his own fear for his future.
This is the truest condition of the one who grasps power:
he thinks he holds power,
but in fact he is ruled by what he fears.
If a person does not let God be Lord,
he does not thereby become his own master.
He only gets a fiercer master.
It may be other people’s opinions.
It may be sales figures.
It may be face that he cannot swallow.
It may be “what will others think.”
Pilate stood in the highest position,
yet he was the least free person that morning.
4. All Authority Is Borrowed, Entrusted, and Must Be Accounted For
Verse 11:
Jesus spoke.
The Lord’s silence is not a silence forever.
When Pilate lifted himself up to “I have power,”
the Lord spoke:
“You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above.”
“From above”
in the original is a very particular word,
meaning “from above” and “from the beginning.”
In John chapter 3,
when the Lord told Nicodemus, “Unless one is born anew, he cannot see the kingdom of God,”
He used the very same word.
New birth
is birth from above.
Authority
is given from above.
With this one sentence,
the Lord turned the whole scene around.
Pilate thought he was judging Jesus.
In fact the little authority in his hands
had been entrusted to him by Jesus’ Father.
The judgment seat he sat on
was lent to him by another.
The pen in his hand
was put there by another.
Romans 13:1 says:
“For there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God.”
All authority
is on loan.
It is entrusted.
It must be accounted for.
I think of something very ordinary.
We go to the library and borrow a book.
With the book in your hand,
it really is in your hand.
You can take it home,
put it on your desk,
and keep it all night without returning it.
But you know one thing very well in your heart:
this book is not yours.
One day you will return it.
When you return it,
the librarian will flip through it,
checking whether it has been torn,
whether it has been scribbled all over.
If someone borrowed a book
and signed his name all over it,
and even replaced the cover with his own photo,
what would we think was wrong with him?
Because he forgot the most basic thing:
the book is borrowed.
Dear family,
everything in our hands is borrowed.
Our health is borrowed.
Our time is borrowed.
Our position is borrowed.
Our authority as parents at home is borrowed.
Our service in the church is borrowed.
Even our children
are only entrusted into our hands by the Lord for a time.
Everything must be returned when due,
and accounted for.
A person who knows he is borrowing
uses things very carefully.
A person who thinks the things are his own
will misuse them.
Pilate’s tragedy
was that he forgot he was only borrowing.
But notice,
the Lord went on to say one more sentence:
“Therefore he who delivered me to you has greater sin.”
This sentence is very important.
The Lord did not say that, because “authority is given by God,”
Pilate bore no responsibility.
Nor did the Lord, because He was suffering,
simply say “it doesn’t matter.”
At the moment of greatest pain,
the Lord was still righteous,
still clear-minded.
He still distinguished the weight of guilt.
“He who delivered me to you”
refers to the religious leaders who brought the Lord before Pilate.
Why was their sin greater?
Because Pilate was a Gentile.
He had no law.
He had no prophets.
He did not know who this One was.
But the high priest and the council did.
They had Moses,
they had the prophets,
they had the temple,
they had the Scriptures.
They read the prophecies of the Messiah every day,
yet they bound the Messiah and sent Him to be crucified.
The more light a person has received,
the greater his responsibility.
Luke 12:48 says:
“To whomever much is given, of him will much be required; and to whom much was entrusted, of him more will be asked.”
This applies to us today
even more than to Pilate.
Because we have the whole Bible in our hands.
We have gatherings,
sermons,
hymns,
brothers and sisters.
We have heard far more teaching
than Pilate heard in a lifetime.
So we cannot say, “I didn’t know.”
To know and not to do
carries an even greater responsibility.
But I want to say,
this is not meant to frighten anyone.
This is the Lord’s honesty.
A Lord who, even when being utterly humiliated, is willing to tell you plainly what weighs more and what weighs less
is a Lord who truly loves you.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Pride Is Leaving One’s Place and Grasping Power; Humility Is Laying Down Power and Returning to One’s Place
This passage today
sets before our eyes
the most fundamental path in the 321 principles.
The 321 principles say:
Pride is leaving one’s place and grasping power,
leaving the human place, grasping God’s power,
wanting to take God’s place.
Humility is laying down power and returning to one’s place,
letting man be man and letting God be God.
Look at Pilate.
He left his place.
He was originally “one entrusted,”
yet he said he was “one who has power.”
He was originally only a passer-by sitting in that seat,
yet he thought the seat was his.
And the result?
The more he grasped,
the more afraid he became.
The more afraid he became,
the weaker he became.
The weaker he became,
the more he was led around by the crowd.
Pride provokes pride,
and both are hurt.
That day,
Pilate lost,
and the religious leaders lost too.
Now look at Jesus.
Who is He?
He is the Son of the One who “gives” authority.
He originally had all authority.
Yet that morning,
His hands were bound,
and He stood before a man who was borrowing His Father’s authority,
quiet and still.
He did not leave His place.
He completely obeyed the Father
and walked the road the Father had arranged for Him.
This is humility.
Humility is not self-belittling,
not feeling that one is worthless.
Humility is returning to the place where I should stand:
letting God be God,
letting man be man.
I am a man,
so I will be a man well.
God is God,
so I will let Him be God.
So,
“Let Jesus be King,” these words
are never a slogan.
They are very concrete.
They mean handing the decisions of my life
back to God, one by one.
Whether to change jobs,
leave it to Him to decide.
How to spend money,
leave it to Him to decide.
Whether to forgive that person,
leave it to Him to decide.
Which way my child’s road will go,
leave it to Him to decide.
Whether I will contend for that position in the church,
leave it to Him to decide.
As long as there is one corner where I still say “I’ll decide this myself,”
Jesus is not yet King in that corner.
Dear family,
each one of us
actually holds a little authority.
At home,
at work,
in the classroom,
in service.
It need not be large;
a little is enough to hurt someone,
and a little is also enough to help someone.
There is only one question:
do I treat it as mine,
or as something the Lord has lent me?
When I know it is borrowed,
I will be humble,
I will be careful,
I will use it to bless people,
not to press them down.
When I think it is mine,
I will be like Pilate,
saying “I have power”
while being scared to death.
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, power cannot give a person peace. The one who grasps the most is often the one with the least security in his heart.
Second, the Lord’s silence is a kind of judgment. It is not that the Lord is unloving; when people keep refusing the light, they lose the chance to hear again.
Third, “I have power” is the prototype of the fall. Leaving one’s place and grasping power does not make a person his own master; he only gets a fiercer master.
Fourth, all authority is given from above. It is borrowed, entrusted, and must be accounted for, so we should use it with care.
Fifth, the more light, the greater the responsibility. The more a person knows, the less he can say “I didn’t know,” because from the one entrusted with more, more is asked.
Let Us Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us see today the Lord Jesus standing before Pilate. Your Son was bound, yet He was the freest one there; the one who judged Him sat in a high seat, yet was afraid in his heart. Lord, we confess that there is a Pilate within us too, always wanting to grasp something so that we may feel secure, always wanting to make our own decisions, unwilling to hand over the steering wheel. Have mercy on us, take away the pride within us, and cause us to lay down the power that does not belong to us and return to the place where we should stand, letting God be God and man be man. When You speak to us, keep our hearts soft, and do not let us keep pushing away Your voice until we cannot hear it. Help us to treat all that is in our hands, health, time, responsibility, family, and service, as entrusted to us by You for a time, to use it faithfully and to give a good account. May Jesus truly be King in every corner of our lives and receive all the glory. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

2\. Is there something lately that the Lord has already said to you very clearly, yet you keep saying “we’ll see”? How are you willing to respond to Him today?

v: At this, Pilate was seeking to release him, but the Jews cried out, saying, “If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend! Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar!”
When Pilate therefore heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called “The Pavement”, but in Hebrew, “Gabbatha.”
Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, “Behold, your King!”
They cried out, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” Pilate said to them, “Shall I crucify your King?” The chief priests answered, “We have no king but Caesar!”
So then he delivered him to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus and led him away.
b: This is the final scene of the trial.
From chapter 18 until now,
Pilate has come in
and gone out again and again,
wanting to release Him,
yet never daring to release Him.
In today’s passage,
he finally made his decision.
He was not persuaded by the truth.
He was conquered by a threat.
These five short verses
record the most unjust verdict in human history.
They also reveal
the truest battle in every human heart.
1. What Knocked Pilate Down Was Not an Argument but a Threat
Verse 12:
The Jews cried out:
“If you release this man, you aren’t Caesar’s friend.”
Notice,
the moment those words came out,
the whole situation was turned over.
Earlier they accused Jesus of blasphemy,
and Pilate paid no attention.
They said Jesus was the King of the Jews,
and Pilate examined it
and found no guilt.
But this sentence was different.
This sentence was not about Jesus.
This sentence was about Pilate.
“Caesar’s friend”
was, at that time, an extremely weighty political title.
Once someone reported to Rome
that a certain governor had let go a man who called himself a king,
that would mean not only losing office;
it could mean losing his life.
And Pilate’s record was not clean to begin with.
His several harsh actions in Jerusalem in the past
had already been reported by the Jews.
He had a handle on him that others were holding.
So this sentence
struck right at his weak point.
Dear family,
we must see something very solemn:
\*\*Once a person has a handle on him in someone else’s hands, he cannot stand up for righteousness.\*\*
It is like a person
who has signed his IOU into someone else’s hands.
Ordinarily you notice nothing.
But one day,
that person takes out the IOU
and lays it gently on the table,
with no need to say a word.
And you know
that in this matter today,
you cannot act according to your conscience.
Pilate’s IOU
was in the hands of the Jews.
So he sat in the highest seat,
yet was the least free of all.
We too must ask ourselves:
Whose hands hold my IOU?
Is it some past I dare not bring into the light?
Is it some person I cannot afford to offend?
Is it the income I am so afraid of losing?
Is it the reputation I care so much about?
When that IOU is taken out,
can I still tell the truth?
2. He Sat on the Judgment Seat, but He Himself Was the One Being Judged
Verse 13:
Pilate brought Jesus out,
to the place called The Pavement,
which in Hebrew is Gabbatha,
and sat down on the judgment seat there.
“The Pavement”
was a large square paved with flagstones.
“Gabbatha” means
a raised place.
That was where the Roman governor formally pronounced sentence.
The moment he sat down there,
what he said had the force of law.
From a human point of view,
that was the highest seat in all Jerusalem.
That day,
the one sitting above was Pilate,
and the one standing below was Jesus.
But if we wipe our eyes a little clearer, we will see:
the one truly on trial
was not the One standing.
It was the one sitting.
In the previous passage Jesus had already said to him:
“You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above.”
The authority in Pilate’s hands
was given by God.
He used the authority God gave him
to judge the One who gave him that authority.
And the question he was truly being examined on was only one:
will you act according to the truth you know?
He knew Jesus was innocent.
Three times he said he found no guilt in Him.
His wife had also warned him.
He knew everything.
He simply did not dare.
So,
the most frightening thing before the judgment seat
is never “I didn’t know.”
It is “I knew, but I didn’t dare.”
\*\*To know and not to do is itself a verdict.\*\*
Brothers and sisters,
we too sit in judgment every day.
In the office,
at home,
at the moment when we must decide whether to tell the truth,
we too are sitting on a small judgment seat.
We think we are deciding that matter.
In fact that matter
is deciding what kind of people we are.
3. We Have No King but Caesar
Verse 15:
The chief priests answered:
“We have no king but Caesar!”
Family,
please stop at this sentence.
This sentence
is one of the saddest in the whole Bible.
The ones who said it were not Gentiles.
They were the chief priests of Israel.
Those who stood in the temple,
offering sacrifices to God for the people every day.
Their ancestors for generation after generation confessed:
Yahweh is our King.
Every year at the Passover they remembered
that God had delivered them from the hand of Pharaoh
so that they would no longer be slaves of men.
And yet on this day,
on the eve of the Passover,
they declared with their own mouths their loyalty to a foreign emperor.
In order to get rid of Jesus,
they were willing to sell anything.
In the time of Samuel,
Israel clamored for a king,
and God said to Samuel:
“They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me, that I should not be king over them.”
(1 Samuel 8:7)
Back then it was to set up Saul.
On this day,
what they wanted was Caesar.
Here is a very deep lesson:
\*\*If people will not have God as King, they will surely find something else to be king.\*\*
The throne in the heart
is never left empty.
A house,
if no one lives in it,
does not really stay empty.
Before long,
dust moves in,
mice move in,
and strangers move in too.
A house left empty
is not safe;
it is in danger.
The human heart is the same.
Send Jesus out,
and that seat will not be left blank.
Whatever sits down in it
may be power,
may be money,
may be reputation,
may be the look on someone’s face,
may be what other people think of me.
With our mouths we will not say “We have no king but Caesar.”
But every decision we make each day
is answering:
who exactly is sitting in that seat in my heart.
4. About the Sixth Hour, the Lamb of God Was Handed Over
Verse 14 says:
“Now it was the Preparation Day of the Passover, at about the sixth hour.”
John deliberately wrote down the time,
and there is a purpose in it.
On the Preparation Day of the Passover,
the whole city of Jerusalem was busy.
Every household was preparing unleavened bread,
preparing bitter herbs,
preparing the lamb that was to be slain.
And at the temple,
the priests were just about to begin slaughtering the Passover lambs.
At that very hour,
at the Pavement,
Pilate said:
“Behold, your King!”
The crowd cried out:
“Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!”
Verse 16:
“So then he delivered him to them to be crucified.”
When the lambs in the temple were being led out,
the Lamb of God was also being handed over.
At the very beginning of this book John the Baptist had said:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”
(John 1:29)
Here,
that word was fulfilled.
Family,
see one thing:
the people of that day thought
that it was the shouting of the Jews that decided the outcome,
that it was Pilate’s weakness that decided the outcome.
But with God,
this hour
had been set thousands of years before.
On that night in the land of Egypt,
when the lamb’s blood was put on the doorposts,
the destroying angel passed over.
That lamb
foreshadowed the One handed over today.
People thought they were dealing with a nuisance.
In fact God was accomplishing His salvation.
Human evil
did not block God’s plan.
Human evil
was instead used by God to fulfill His plan.
This is not to say evil bears no responsibility.
Pilate is responsible,
the chief priests are responsible,
and the crowd that cried “Away with him” is also responsible.
But above all this confusion,
there was One seated,
and He is God.
He had not lost control.
Not for a single minute.
5. We Too Often Hand the Lord Over Between Fearing Men and Reverencing God
Finally, let us be a little honest.
When we read about Pilate,
it is easy to shake our heads
and feel what a coward this man was.
But if we are willing to quiet down,
we will find:
the choice Pilate made,
we too often make.
We will not sit in judgment at the Pavement.
But in a meeting,
we know very well that what is being done is wrong,
yet we lower our heads and say nothing.
Among a group of friends,
when we could easily mention the Lord’s name,
we change the subject.
In a relationship,
for fear of losing the other person,
we give way step by step,
until we even set down our own faith.
We are afraid of losing our jobs,
afraid of being misunderstood,
afraid of being labeled,
afraid of an awkward atmosphere.
And so,
we hand the Lord over.
The way we hand Him over
is sometimes not denial,
but only silence.
Proverbs 29:25 says:
“The fear of man brings a snare, but whoever puts his trust in Yahweh will be exalted.”
This verse sets the two roads out very clearly.
Fearing people
does not bring peace;
it brings only a snare.
Because the compromise you make today to keep something
becomes tomorrow the rope that binds you.
The Lord Jesus also said:
“Don’t be afraid of those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.”
(Matthew 10:28)
Dear family,
we are not called to be heroes.
We are called to be honest people.
In the one matter you must face today,
ask the Lord for a little courage,
it need not be great,
just enough to say one true word.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Order of Relationships: First with God, Then with Self, Then with Others, Then with Things
The 321 principles often remind us of an order:
first build the relationship with God,
then deal with the relationship with self,
then deal with the relationship with others,
and only last the relationship with things.
This order cannot be reversed.
Once reversed,
a whole life falls into disorder.
Pilate’s order
was exactly upside down.
What he considered first
was his relationship with Caesar.
That was his power,
his future,
his position.
What he considered second
was his relationship with the Jews.
He feared the crowd would riot,
feared that a report of an uprising would be sent to Rome.
Only after that
did he think of the unease in his own heart.
He washed his hands,
wanting to feel a little better.
As for his relationship with God,
he put it last.
Indeed he never put it in at all.
A person who puts his relationship with people ahead of his relationship with God
will in the end sell out the truth.
It is not that he is especially wicked;
it is that that order
simply cannot hold.
The chief priests’ order
was also upside down.
What they cared about most was keeping the temple,
keeping their status,
keeping Rome’s tolerance of them.
To keep these “things,”
they would rather say:
“We have no king but Caesar.”
Family,
the lesson we must learn is this:
when my relationship with God stands firm first,
I do not have to live by other people’s faces.
I do not have to buy security with compromise.
Because my security
is not with Caesar;
it is with God.
A person who first aligns with God
is able to be honest with people.
A person who first lets Jesus be King
will not be led around by the thrones of men.
This is also the heart of the 321 principles:
let Jesus be King,
let Jesus receive all the glory.
There is only one throne in the heart.
When Jesus sits,
Caesar cannot sit.
When Caesar sits,
Jesus is handed over.
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, one who has a handle on him in another’s hands cannot stand for righteousness. True freedom is placing ourselves completely in God’s hands.
Second, every day we sit on a small judgment seat. The most frightening thing is not not knowing, but knowing and not daring to act.
Third, the throne in the heart is never left empty. If we do not let Jesus be King, something else will surely come up to be king.
Fourth, the Lamb of God being handed over at the Passover was set by God long ago. Human evil did not block God; it was used by Him to fulfill salvation.
Fifth, fearing people leads into a snare; trusting in God brings security. Ask the Lord for enough courage to say one true word.
Let Us Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, we come before You and see the scene at the Pavement, and our hearts are quiet and lit by Your light. Lord, we confess that there is a Pilate within us too: we know clearly what is right, yet for fear of losing, fear of being misunderstood, fear of paying a price, we choose silence. Forgive us, and also remove from our hands those handles that others hold, so that we may answer to You alone. Lord Jesus, thank You that in that hour You were willing to be handed over, to become the Passover Lamb, and to cover us with Your blood. Wash our fears clean with Your precious blood. Holy Spirit, help us to put our relationship with You first: to align with You first, then be reconciled with ourselves, then get along with others, and then deal with the matters before us. Sit on the throne in our hearts, and do not let any person or any thing take that seat. May we all our lives acknowledge only You as King, and give all the glory to You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.

v: He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”,
where they crucified him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle.
Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, “I am King of the Jews.” ’ ”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”
b: The trial was over.
Pilate handed Jesus over to them.
From this verse on,
John no longer records any arguing.
He records only a road,
and a hill.
It is remarkable.
When John writes about the cross,
he writes with great quietness.
No gory detail,
no description of the pain.
He simply says, plainly:
There they crucified Him.
Because what he wants us to see
is not how terrible the punishment was,
but who
the One being crucified really is.
1. He Went Out Carrying His Own Cross
Verse 17 says:
“He went out, bearing his own cross.”
Under Roman law at that time,
a man condemned to death
had to carry the crossbeam of his cross himself,
from the place of judgment,
through the streets of the city,
all the way to the place of execution.
That beam was heavy.
And the route was deliberately made roundabout,
so that the whole city would see:
this man has been condemned.
So that road
was not only physical torture,
it was the stripping away of dignity.
And Jesus walked out like that,
carrying His own cross.
Dear family,
notice these three words: “His own.”
The Lord once said to His disciples:
“He who doesn’t take his cross and follow after me isn’t worthy of me.”
(Matthew 10:38)
He also said:
“If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
(Luke 9:23)
The Lord did not say these words
while standing off to the side.
He carried it first Himself.
He did not ask us to walk a road He had not walked.
He did not ask us to carry a weight He had not carried.
He walked ahead of us.
He first laid the beam on His own shoulder.
We often misunderstand what “carrying the cross” means.
We think it means being unwell,
or trouble at work,
or having a hard-to-get-along-with person at home.
Those are burdens,
but they are not necessarily the cross.
The meaning of the cross is very simple:
the cross is for putting people to death.
A person carrying a cross
is a person walking toward death.
So to take up your own cross
is not to endure the troubles of life,
but to nail your own sovereignty to it.
It is to take “I want,”
“I think,”
“I believe,”
“I must have it my way,”
and bring them all to that place
and nail them there until they die.
With our own lives,
we often want only to fix them up a little.
Like an old machine that has been used for a long time,
making strange noises,
barely running,
breaking down every few days.
So we swap a part,
add a little oil,
give it a wipe,
hoping it will hold out a few more years.
But the cross is not maintenance.
The cross is scrapping.
It is admitting that this old one
cannot be fixed,
that the whole thing has to be handed over,
and a brand-new one put in its place.
Paul said:
“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
(Galatians 2:20)
First crucified together,
then living together.
First self-denial,
then Christ.
2. Jesus in the Middle
In verse 18,
John writes a sentence that seems quite ordinary:
“...and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus in the middle.”
One on each side.
Jesus in the middle.
In the eyes of the Romans,
these were simply three men condemned to death that day.
Jesus was placed in the middle
because He was considered the chief criminal,
the one who drew the most attention.
But in God’s eyes,
this position
had been foretold long before.
Isaiah 53:12 says:
“He was numbered with the transgressors.”
He was not placed in a clean place.
He was placed among sinners.
In fact,
this was the place He occupied all His life.
He was born in a manger.
He sat at table with tax collectors and sinners.
He let a sinful woman touch His feet.
He washed His disciples’ feet.
In the end,
He died between two robbers.
He never stood far off, pointing at people and saying,
You are not good enough.
He always walked in
and stood among the people.
Luke’s Gospel records
that the two men crucified with Him
reacted completely differently.
One mocked Him, saying:
“Aren’t you the Christ? Save yourself and us!”
The other rebuked his companion,
and then turned to Jesus and said:
“Jesus, remember me when you come into your Kingdom!”
Jesus answered him:
“Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”
Family,
look carefully at this.
These two men
were exactly the same distance from Jesus.
Equally near.
Equally able to see His face.
Equally able to hear every word He said.
Equally under the same punishment.
Yet one entered Paradise,
and the other did not.
The difference was not distance,
the difference was attitude.
It is like two people standing on the same platform.
The same train pulls in,
and the doors open right in front of them.
One lifts his foot and steps aboard.
The other stays where he is,
watching the doors close,
watching the train pull away.
He was not farther from the train,
he simply did not get on.
Dear family,
how many sermons you have heard,
how close you are to the church,
how many years you have spent in a faith environment,
none of these is the key.
A person’s distance from the cross does not matter;
a person’s attitude toward the cross is what matters.
3. Salvation Accomplished at Golgotha
Verse 17 says
that the place is called the Place of a Skull,
which in Hebrew is Golgotha.
“Golgotha” means
skull,
the head bone of a dead person.
Some say it is because the hill was shaped like a skull,
others say it is because it had long been a place of execution.
Whichever the reason,
the name itself says it all:
this was a place tied to death.
It was outside the city.
A place where people were thrown out.
Hebrews 13:12 says:
“Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside of the gate.”
Family,
take this to heart:
the greatest salvation in human history
was not accomplished in the temple.
It was not accomplished in the royal palace.
It was not accomplished in a majestic,
clean,
beautiful place.
It was accomplished in a place called “the Skull.”
It was accomplished outside the city,
in the ugliest,
most defiled place,
the place most like death.
This
is a great comfort to us today.
Because inside each of us
there is also a Golgotha of our own.
It is the place we least want anyone to see.
It is our failures,
our most shameful memories,
the corner we think God would never come near.
We always want to tidy ourselves up first,
and when we are a little better,
then come near Him.
But the gospel is exactly the opposite.
God does not wait until you have cleaned up that ground.
He walks straight onto that ground
and begins His work there.
He was born in a manger,
and gave His life at Golgotha.
He has never found any place of ours too dirty.
So today,
if you feel your condition is unbearable,
if you feel you have no face to show the Lord,
please remember Golgotha.
God’s greatest work
has always been accomplished in the place people considered least possible.
4. That Sign, a Proclamation to the Whole World
In verses 19 and 20,
something very special appears.
Pilate wrote a sign
and put it on the cross.
It read:
“Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.”
By Roman custom,
a sign was hung on the cross,
stating the man’s crime,
so that those passing by would know why he was crucified.
But what Pilate wrote
was not a charge.
It was a title.
And we know what was on Pilate’s mind.
Throughout the whole trial,
he was led along by the chief priests,
and in the end went against his own conscience and handed Jesus over.
He was angry inside.
So when he wrote this sign,
his intent was to mock the Jews:
Look,
here is your king.
The king you wanted
is exactly this kind.
Pilate was taking revenge.
But God used that sign.
Verse 20 says
that many of the Jews read this title,
because the place of execution was near the city,
and it was written in Hebrew,
Latin,
and Greek.
Family,
notice these three languages.
Hebrew
is the language of religion.
The language of the temple,
the law, and the prophets.
Latin,
the Roman language,
is the language of power.
The language of politics,
the army,
and the law.
Hellenistic writing,
that is, Greek,
is the language of culture.
The common language of the whole Mediterranean world at that time,
the language of thought,
philosophy,
and trade.
Religion,
power,
culture.
The three great realms of the human world at that time
were written on one sign at the same time,
all pointing to the same Jesus.
Pilate thought he was only humiliating a few chief priests.
But God, through his hand,
on the cross,
issued a proclamation to the whole world:
Jesus of Nazareth
is King.
Not only King of the Jews.
King of every language,
every people,
every realm.
Revelation says
that in the future those standing before the throne
will be from every nation,
every tribe,
every people,
every language,
a multitude no one can count.
What will be accomplished on that day
was already written beforehand
on the sign at Golgotha.
This is exactly the direction we have been speaking about:
building God’s system.
Not only inside the church.
It is to enter the realm of religion,
the realm of power,
the realm of culture.
It is to reach all nations and all peoples.
The gospel is not a comfort for a small circle.
The gospel is a proclamation to the whole world.
5. What I Have Written, I Have Written
In verses 21 and 22,
the chief priests protested immediately.
They said to Pilate:
“Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, I am King of the Jews.’”
See how much those few words mattered to them.
Because if the sign hung as it was,
it would amount to official Roman recognition
that this crucified man
was the King of the Jews.
So they wanted to add “he said.”
Just by adding those words,
it would turn from a proclamation
into the delusion of a madman.
But Pilate answered:
“What I have written, I have written.”
This sentence
in the original language is in the perfect tense.
It means:
what is written is written,
it is settled,
it will not be changed.
Brothers and sisters,
this was the one moment in Pilate’s whole life
when he stood his ground.
All night long he had been backing down.
When the truth was set before him,
he backed down.
He knew Jesus was innocent,
and he backed down.
He wanted to release Jesus,
but when the crowd shouted,
he backed down again.
He washed his hands,
thinking he could shift the blame,
when in fact it was the most complete retreat of all.
And the one time he finally stood firm
was over a sign.
It was to settle a grudge.
It was to get back at a few chief priests.
He did not know what he was doing.
He simply refused to give way.
But God used this very stubbornness of his
to nail the words “Jesus is King”
to the cross forever.
Proverbs 21:1 says:
“The king’s heart is in Yahweh’s hand like the watercourses. He turns it wherever he desires.”
Dear family,
this gives us great security.
God can use not only those who obey Him.
God can also use a weak man.
A man sulking over wounded pride.
A man who did not know Him at all.
A sign that was meant to humiliate people.
Nothing can hinder God’s purpose.
No one’s ill will
can rewrite what God has written.
What He has written,
He has written.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Take Up Your Own Cross, Deny Self and Follow the Lord
Today’s passage
walks us along this road of self-denial
from beginning to end.
The 321 principles say:
self-denial means for Jesus,
for others,
not for ourselves.
It means taking up your own cross
and denying self to follow the Lord.
And in this passage,
we see how the Lord Himself walked this road.
He went out carrying His own cross.
He was numbered with the transgressors.
He died outside the city at the place called the Skull.
He did not argue one word for Himself.
The chief priests argued over the words on the sign.
Pilate argued to save his own face.
The disciples hid.
Only the One who was truly King
said not one word for Himself.
Because there was no self in Him.
So let us distinguish once more:
carrying the cross
is not enduring the troubles of life.
It is not gritting your teeth
and getting through a difficult person
or a difficult situation.
That is endurance.
That is good,
but it is not yet the cross.
Carrying the cross
is nailing your own sovereignty to it.
It is, every day, in one small matter after another,
handing over “I want it my way.”
It is not arguing when you could argue,
because I am no longer the lord.
It is staying silent when you could explain,
because my reputation is not mine to manage.
It is letting go when you could hold on,
because the one sitting on that throne is not me.
Nailing it down like this day after day,
we will arrive at the place Paul spoke of:
no longer I,
but Christ lives in me.
Family,
this is not a slogan.
It is a road.
The Lord has already walked it.
He walks ahead of us carrying His own cross,
and today He turns back and says to you:
Come,
follow Me.
Life Response
This passage reminds us:
First, the Lord carried His own cross first. He did not ask us to walk a road He had not walked.
Second, a person’s distance from the cross does not matter; attitude does. The two robbers were equally near, yet their ends were completely different.
Third, salvation was accomplished at Golgotha. God’s greatest work is often accomplished in the place people consider the most unbearable.
Fourth, the sign was written in three languages. The gospel is to reach every realm, every people, all nations and all peoples.
Fifth, God can use anyone to accomplish His purpose. Even a sulking Pilate wrote a proclamation that will never be changed.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your Son Jesus Christ carried His own cross, walked out through the gate, and went to the place called Golgotha, where He gave His life for us. Lord, we often misunderstand what carrying the cross means, thinking it is only enduring the troubles of life; please enlighten us, so that we understand it means handing over our own sovereignty and nailing “I want it my way” to Your cross. Please remove the self within us, so that we do not argue when we could argue, are quiet when we could explain, and let go when we could hold on, because the One sitting on that throne is You, not me. Lord, we also have our own Golgotha within us, corners we least want anyone to see; thank You that You never reject us, and that You are at work right there. Please also carry Your gospel into our families, our workplaces, and every realm where we live, so that the words “Jesus of Nazareth is King” are proclaimed among all nations and all peoples. May we no longer live for ourselves, but may Christ live in us all our lives, and may all the glory go to You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
q: 1\. In your life right now, what is it that you keep holding in your hand and refuse to give up the right over? Are you willing to bring it to the cross today?
2\. Is there a “Golgotha” inside you, a place where you feel God would not come near? Are you willing to let the Lord begin working there today?

v: Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the coat. Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.

Then they said to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says, “They parted my garments among them. For my cloak they cast lots.” Therefore the soldiers did these things.
b: These two verses
read quite plainly.
No miracle.
No thunder.
No angel appearing.
Only four soldiers,
squatting at the foot of the cross,
dividing a pile of clothes.
But we must remember,
right above their heads,
the greatest event in human history was taking place.
The Son of God
was giving His life for all the people of the world.
The sky was about to go dark.
The veil in the temple was about to tear.
The problem of sin was about to be settled once for all.
And the people at the foot of the cross
kept their heads down,
dividing clothes.
John wrote this scene down so carefully,
not to keep a record.
It is because this scene
is a picture of all humanity in miniature.
1. Salvation Accomplished Overhead, Yet Human Eyes Fixed on a Little Something in Their Hands
Verse 23 begins:
“Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part.”
This was Roman custom.
The soldiers carrying out an execution
could take the belongings of the condemned man.
That was their “perk.”
So to these four soldiers,
that day was just another day on the job.
When the nailing was done,
they sat down to divide the goods.
Brothers and sisters,
imagine that picture.
The Savior of the world
was bleeding above their heads.
The door to eternal life
was opening above their heads.
And they kept their heads down,
intently tearing a robe into four pieces,
calculating who got the bigger share.
This is not scolding those four soldiers.
This is looking in a mirror.
We are often like this too.
God is doing something enormous in us,
and we only care about counting the small gains and losses in front of us.
God is carrying out His eternal plan,
and we are angry over a remark,
haggling over a sum of money,
upset over a position.
It is like being in a movie theater
where the most crucial scene of the whole film is playing on the screen,
while someone in the front row has his head down,
feeling under his seat for a coin he dropped.
When the film is over,
he has seen nothing.
He only got back a coin.
We are often that person.
The 321 principles say:
the focus is on Jesus,
not on self,
not on others,
not on circumstances.
Our focus determines what we see all our lives.
The same place,
the same moment,
the one who looks up sees salvation,
the one who looks down sees only a piece of clothing.
Dear family,
today we ask the Lord to help us lift up our heads.
Do not, at the foot of the cross of salvation,
care only about dividing up our own share.
2. He Lost Even His Last Garment, to Cover Our Nakedness with a Robe of Righteousness
“Took his garments and made four parts.”
When we read this sentence,
we need to pause.
What does it mean?
It means that the Lord Jesus,
at that moment,
had nothing left on Him.
He had never had a house.
No land.
No place to lay His head.
In the end,
even the few clothes on His body
were divided up by others.
He hung naked on the wood.
In the Jewish way of thinking,
nakedness was a great shame.
What He bore was not only physical pain,
but also the shame of being stripped of everything.
Second Corinthians 8:9 says:
“Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that you through his poverty might become rich.”
This verse
was fully cashed in at the foot of the cross.
And brothers and sisters,
why did He have to be stripped?
Because we were naked.
The first time people discovered they were naked
was after they sinned.
Adam and Eve sewed fig leaves together into coverings,
trying to hide themselves.
It could not hide them.
Genesis 3:21 says:
“Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.”
To have skins,
an animal had to be killed.
That was the first time in the Bible that blood was shed for people.
That was the first shadow.
At Golgotha,
the shadow became the reality.
The Lamb of God was stripped of His clothes
so that He could put a robe of righteousness on us.
Isaiah 61:10 says:
“He has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness.”
Galatians 3:27 says:
“For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.”
Because He was naked,
we have clothes to wear.
Because He was stripped,
we are covered.
Because He had nothing,
we lack nothing.
So today when we stand before God,
we do not stand on fig leaves we sewed ourselves.
Not on our own performance,
our own achievements,
our own efforts.
We stand on the robe of righteousness He prepared for us on the cross.
3. The Seamless Tunic Is the High Priest’s Robe, and Also a Call for Unity
The second half of verse 23 says:
“Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.”
Why did John write in such detail?
Because this garment was different.
The ordinary tunic of that time
was sewn together from two pieces of cloth.
But this one
was woven from top to bottom in one piece,
without a single seam.
In the Old Testament,
the inner robe worn by the high priest
was also woven,
not pieced together.
Here the Bible gently reminds us of something:
the One hanging on the cross
is not only a victim.
He is the High Priest.
He is offering a sacrifice.
And the sacrifice He offers
is Himself.
Ordinary priests offered sacrifices standing up.
This High Priest
was lifted up to offer Himself.
Ordinary priests offered bulls and sheep.
This High Priest offered His own body.
What a picture this is.
And this seamless tunic
has been used through the generations to remind the church of one thing.
The soldiers looked at the garment
and said:
“Let’s not tear it.”
Even four Roman soldiers who did not know God
could not bear to tear this garment.
Because they knew
that once it was torn,
all four would end up with a scrap of rag,
and no one would have anything whole.
Brothers and sisters,
here is a sentence that cuts deep:
\*\*What even soldiers could not bear to tear, the church often tears apart itself.\*\*
Outsiders could not bear to tear it,
but insiders often, over some small matter,
tear the body into several pieces.
Over a different way of doing things.
Over a word not well said.
Over who takes the lead, who partners.
Over how things are divided and how money is used.
Once it is torn,
everyone is left with only rags in their hands.
It is like a hand-knitted sweater.
It is warm,
and neat,
but it is made of a single thread.
If you just grab one end of the yarn
and pull hard,
the whole garment unravels all the way.
After it unravels,
it does not become two smaller sweaters.
It becomes a pile of yarn.
It can never be worn again.
The unity of the church is just like this.
It is not something that can still be used when split into pieces.
Once torn,
everyone is left with only yarn.
The Lord Jesus’ prayer in John 17:21 was:
“That they may all be one.”
Ephesians 4:3 says:
“Being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”
The words “being eager to keep” are weighty.
Unity does not happen naturally.
Unity has to be earnestly guarded.
4. Even the Soldiers’ Casual Casting of Lots Was Within God’s Prophecy
Verse 24 says:

“They said therefore among themselves, ‘Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it, to decide whose it will be,’ that the Scripture might be fulfilled, ‘They parted my garments among them. For my cloak, they cast lots.’ Therefore the soldiers did these things.”
This is the most astonishing sentence.
Because this sentence comes from Psalm 22:18.
It was written by David,
about a thousand years
before Jesus was crucified.
David had never seen a cross.
The punishment of crucifixion
did not yet exist in David’s time.
Yet he wrote:
“They divide my garments among them. For my clothing, they cast lots.”
The outer garments were divided.
The tunic was decided by lots.
Even that the two garments were handled differently
was written out clearly.
And those four soldiers
had no idea what they were doing.
They had never read the Psalms.
They did not know David.
They simply tossed it casually
to see who had good luck.
They thought it was a little gamble.
In fact it was a line God had written a thousand years earlier.
Brothers and sisters,
what do we want to see today?
God is in control down to the smallest detail.
He does not only govern the great events.
Even the toss in a soldier’s hand
was within His foreknowledge.
He does not only govern the cross.
Even who would get the garment at the foot of the cross
He had already accounted for.
The Lord Jesus said:
“Even the hairs of your head are all counted.”
(Luke 12:7)
The God who foretold even who would get the garment,
would He forget your difficulty today?
No.
The God who, on the most chaotic day,
still fulfilled His word without the slightest error,
would He fail in your matters?
No.
There is also something here for us to learn.
Those four soldiers were free.
No one forced them to cast lots.
They did it of their own will.
Yet what they did
fell exactly within God’s plan.
People are busy with their own calculations.
God accomplishes His purpose.
This is our reason to rest easy.
Not because all people are good,
but because God has never lost control.
The Light of the 321 Principles: People Matter More Than Things, Relationships More Than Possessions
Today’s passage
sets one thing bare before us.
At the foot of the cross,
there were two kinds of people.
One was the One being crucified.
He was giving.
Giving His clothes,
giving His dignity,
giving His life.
The other was the people at the foot of the cross.
They were taking.
Taking clothes,
taking benefits,
taking their own share.
One giving,
a crowd taking.
This is the sharpest contrast in the whole Bible.
The 321 principles keep reminding us:
people matter more than things.
Relationships matter more than possessions.
Do not hurt people for the sake of a task.
Do not damage relationships for the sake of things.
When we look back at those around us,
we find something very sad.
Many families
did not fall apart in hardship.
They fell apart when it came time to divide things.
After the parents passed away,
over how to divide the house,
how to count the savings,
brothers and sisters stopped speaking from then on.
Many coworker relationships
did not break in persecution.
They broke over “who is in charge, who decides, who gets it.”
Many churches
were not scattered by attacks from outside.
They tore themselves apart from within.
Brothers and sisters,
if things are lost,
you can have them again.
If a relationship is lost,
it often cannot be mended in a lifetime.
If a task is done badly,
you can start over.
If a person is hurt,
it will take a very long time before they come close to you again.
So we should learn from that seamless tunic.
Better not to tear.
Better to take a little less ourselves.
Better to let what is whole remain.
And a deeper level is this:
the reason we can let go
is that our focus is not on ourselves.
The 321 principles say:
the focus is on Jesus,
not on self,
not on others,
not on circumstances.
When my focus is on myself,
I will certainly fight for that share,
because I am afraid of losing out.
When my focus is on Jesus,
I can no longer fight.
Because I look up and see
Him on the cross,
without even His last garment.
Before that One,
what is there left for me to fight over?
Philippians 2:7 says
that He “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.”
The Lord was emptied of self.
We, though, are full of self.
When the cross deals with “self,”
we no longer need to take a little more
to prove our worth.
Those emptied of self can let go.
Those who can let go
can keep their relationships.
Life Response
This passage reminds us:

First, do not busy yourself at the foot of the cross of salvation with dividing things up. God is accomplishing something eternal; do not let your eyes stop at the small gains and losses in your hands.
Second, the Lord hung naked to cover us with a robe of righteousness. Our standing before God is not leaves we sewed ourselves, but the robe He prepared for us.
Third, what even soldiers could not bear to tear, the church must not tear apart itself. Unity does not happen naturally; unity must be earnestly guarded.
Fourth, God is in control down to the smallest detail. Even a casual casting of lots was within His prophecy, and He has not overlooked your difficulty today.
Fifth, people matter more than things, and relationships more than possessions. If things are lost you can have them again; when a relationship is wounded it often cannot be mended in a lifetime.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You. Today we stand at the foot of the cross and see the Lord Jesus giving everything for us, losing even the last garment on His body, hanging naked on the wood to cover our nakedness with Your robe of righteousness. Lord, forgive us. We are often like those four soldiers, keeping our heads down to calculate how much we can take even while You are accomplishing the greatest thing. Please lift up our heads, so that our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances. Teach us that people matter more than things and relationships more than possessions; let us no longer hurt a person over a task, nor damage a relationship over a little thing. Please keep Your church whole like the seamless tunic, so that even outsiders could not bear to tear it. Strengthen our hearts also, to know that You are in control down to the smallest detail, that You counted even the soldiers’ casting of lots, and that You will surely not forget our difficulties today. May all the glory go to You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
q: 1\. Is there a relationship of yours right now stuck on “one matter” or “one thing”? If people matter more than matters, and relationships more than things, what small step can you take first today?
2\. The Lord gave up even His last garment for you. When you think of this, can you still let go of what you are gripping so tightly right now?

v: But standing by Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.
b: On the cross,
the Lord Jesus spoke seven sayings in all.
Today’s passage
is one of them.
We might have thought
that in such agonizing pain,
a person could not possibly think of anyone else.
But the Lord did.
At the very moment He was bearing the sin-debt of all humanity,
He looked up and saw a mother.
And He saw a disciple.
Then
He placed the two of them
into one family.
This was the first spiritual family
born at the foot of the cross.
1. Those Standing by the Cross Were the Ones Who Loved to the End
In verse 25,
the Holy Spirit, through John,
took care to record a list of names:
“But there were standing by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.”
Notice this list.
The twelve disciples who had followed the Lord for three years
were, by this time, mostly gone.
One had sold the Lord.
One had denied the Lord.
The rest had scattered and hidden.
Those who remained at the scene
were mostly women.
In that age,
a woman’s word was not even accepted in court.
They could not rescue the Lord from the cross,
could not even argue one word on His behalf.
What they could do
was only one thing:
stand there.
Dear family,
this is a sentence we should remember all our lives:
\*\*Love does not necessarily make a person capable, but love makes a person stay.\*\*
We often think
that serving means being able to solve problems.
You need eloquence,
resources,
the ability to come up with solutions.
So when we meet someone who is suffering,
our first reaction is often:
“I can’t help anyway.”
“I don’t know what to say.”
And so we don’t go.
But think about it.
In a hospital,
the chair beside the sickbed.
The person sitting in that chair
cannot perform surgery,
cannot prescribe medicine.
He sits there all night,
and in fact does nothing.
Yet everyone who has been hospitalized knows:
whether someone is in that chair
makes an enormous difference.
When someone is sitting there,
the night is not so long.
The Lord is the same.
The Lord did not record who said which beautiful words.
What the Lord recorded was:
who stood nearby.
Today’s ministry is often like this too.
What is most precious is not how much we can do,
but whether we are willing
to stand there and keep company.
2. A Heart Pierced by the Sword Is the Price of Co-Laboring
Verse 26 says:
“Therefore when Jesus saw his mother... standing by.”
We often see only the pain on the cross.
But at the foot of the cross,
there was also a heart bleeding.
Thirty-three years earlier,
when Mary carried the infant Jesus into the temple,
an old man, Simeon, said a word to her:
“A sword will pierce through your own soul.”
(Luke 2:35)
At that time she probably did not understand.
A young mother,
holding her newborn child,
how could she imagine that thirty-three years later
she would stand at the place of execution
and watch this child be nailed to death.
But that day came.
Dear family,
we must say one thing honestly:
on the road of following God,
some suffering
is not punishment.
Mary was obedient.
She had said: “Be it to me according to your word.”
She had not taken a wrong road.
She had not offended God.
Yet her heart
was still pierced by the sword.
So please do not read your own life by a formula:
“I am in so much pain,
I must have done something wrong.”
Not necessarily.
Some suffering is discipline,
and we should receive it humbly.
But some suffering
comes because God has placed you in a position very close to His heart.
That is the price of co-laboring.
That is the weight of bearing together with the Lord.
A mother feels pain in bearing and raising children.
A spiritual parent,
in bringing a life to the Lord,
will feel pain in the same way.
That is not a sign of failure.
It is a sign of love.
3. In the Midst of Agony, the Lord Still Thought of the One Before Him
In verse 26,
Jesus said to His mother:
“Woman, behold, your son!”
First we need to understand
the Lord’s situation at that moment.
He had been scourged.
He had been crowned with thorns.
His hands and feet were pierced with nails.
He was accomplishing salvation for all humanity.
At such a moment,
anyone would have every reason to say:
“Don’t bother me now.”
But the Lord did not.
He lifted His head
and saw His mother.
What He thought of was:
after I am gone,
what will become of her in her old age?
Brothers and sisters,
please keep this scene in your heart.
While accomplishing the greatest thing of all,
the Lord did not overlook the need of the one before Him.
This is where we often fail.
When we get busy,
our eyes see only tasks.
We are busy with the church’s affairs,
but fail to see the person at home.
We can spend a whole week preparing a meeting,
yet cannot spare twenty minutes
to hear a wounded person finish speaking.
The 321 principles say it clearly:
people matter more than things,
relationships matter more than possessions.
Do not hurt people for the sake of a task,
do not damage relationships for the sake of things.
And the order is:
life first,
then relationships,
then ministry.
The Lord Jesus on the cross
lived out this order Himself.
He was doing the most important ministry in the world,
yet still dealt with a relationship first.
Because love has never been an abstract slogan.
\*\*Love is a concrete arrangement.\*\*
It does not end with saying, “I’ll pray for you.”
It really finds her a home.
It really makes sure she has food to eat, a place to live, someone to call on.
The Lord’s love
has always been a love that touches the ground.
4. “Behold, Your Son,” “Behold, Your Mother”: A New Family Born at the Cross
In verses 26 and 27,
the Lord spoke two sentences.
To His mother:
“Behold, your son!”
To the disciple:
“Behold, your mother!”
Put together, these two sentences
make a brand-new family.
We should notice:
it was not that Mary had no other sons.
The Bible records
that Jesus had several younger brothers.
But at that time,
His brothers did not yet believe in Him.
So the Lord did not entrust His mother to those closest by blood,
but to the one closest in faith.
What a momentous declaration this is.
The Lord, at the foot of the cross,
before the whole world, said:
beyond blood,
there is a deeper bond:
in Christ, we become one family.
Paul said:
“So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God.”
(Ephesians 2:19)
This is exactly the nature of the church.
The church is not a religious institution.
The church is not a club that meets once a week.
The church is a family.
I can use a modern illustration.
Think of donating blood.
A bag of blood is drawn from one person
and put into another person’s body.
The two are complete strangers,
with no blood relation,
and may never meet in their whole lives.
But from that day on,
the same blood
flows in both bodies.
Dear family,
our relationship is deeper than that.
Because what flows in us
is the precious blood the same Lord shed for us.
This is the “920” in the 321 principles:
everyone who has a relationship with us
is our 2.
Not a passerby,
not a member number,
but our 2.
And in this passage,
the Lord went a step further
and established the “3” relationship:
spiritual parents
and spiritual children.
John gained a mother.
Mary gained a son.
From then on,
John cared for her,
not out of duty,
but out of the Lord’s trust and love.
Brothers and sisters,
in the church,
is there an elder
you can call a “spiritual mother”?
Is there a young person
you are willing to be a spiritual parent to?
If not yet,
today you can begin to ask.
Psalm 68:6 says:
“God sets the lonely in families.”
This is God’s heart.
He never intended His children
to live alone.
5. True Obedience Has Action
The last sentence of verse 27 is short:
“From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.”
Notice the word “took.”
And notice the words “from that hour.”
Not after a few years.
Not after his situation was a little more stable.
From that very day.
John did not say:
“Lord, I will pray for her.”
John did not say:
“Let me settle myself first.”
The Lord entrusted,
and John took her in.
This is obedience.
\*\*The Lord entrusted, and I took her in.\*\*
Obedience is not a feeling,
obedience is an action.
Many times,
we are moved to tears in a meeting,
and say in our hearts:
“Lord, I am willing.”
Then we go home,
and life goes on as usual.
That is not obedience,
that is only being moved.
True obedience changes the budget,
and puts one more set of bowls and chopsticks on the table.
We must be very honest:
taking an elderly person into your own home to live
has a cost.
Life will be disrupted.
Freedom will lessen.
There will be added expense,
and added patience needed.
But John took her in,
because she was the one the Lord had given him.
Brothers and sisters,
the Lord also places certain people into our hands.
Perhaps an aging parent.
Perhaps a brother newly come to the Lord.
The Lord says:
“Behold, your mother.”
It means:
from now on,
she is your responsibility.
May we also be like John,
saying little,
and simply reaching out,
taking the one the Lord has entrusted
into our own lives.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The First Spiritual Family at the Foot of the Cross
Today’s passage
takes the “920” and “3” relationships in the 321 principles
and shows them most clearly.
The 920 says:
everyone who has a relationship with us
is our 2.
Live out the 0 of self-denial,
and bear the nine fruits of the Spirit.
At the foot of the cross,
the Lord Jesus made Mary and John
each other’s 2.
And not only 2,
but 3:
spiritual parent,
spiritual child.
But see something very important:
the Lord did this on the cross.
That is to say,
a spiritual family
comes from self-denial.
It does not come from getting along or talking things through.
It comes from “not for myself.”
If everyone thinks of their own convenience,
a family cannot be built.
John had to lay down his own space
in order to take in a mother.
Mary had to lay down her own grief
in order to receive a new son.
Emptied of self,
we can build God’s system.
So the order is very clear:
life first,
then relationships,
then ministry.
First there is the life of Christ in me,
then there are true spiritual relationships;
with true spiritual relationships,
there is ministry that can bear weight.
If there are only activities,
only programs,
only service schedules,
but no spiritual parents,
no spiritual children,
then what we have is an organization,
not a family.
From today on, may we
not only ask:
what do I do in the church?
May we also begin to ask:
which person has the Lord
placed in my hands?
Life Response
This passage reminds us:

First, love does not necessarily make a person capable, but love makes a person stay. Do not stay away because you cannot help; being willing to stand there and keep company is itself the most precious service.
Second, some suffering is not punishment but the price of co-laboring. Mary’s heart was pierced by the sword not because she took a wrong road, but because she was so close to the Lord’s heart.
Third, love is not a slogan, it is a concrete arrangement. While accomplishing salvation, the Lord still settled the need of the one before Him.
Fourth, in Christ we are one family. Beyond blood there is a deeper bond, and this is the very nature of the church.
Fifth, true obedience has action. The Lord entrusted, and John took her in; if being moved has no action, it is not yet obedience.
Let’s Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, we worship You. Thank You that the Lord Jesus, in the most painful moment on the cross, still looked up and saw a mother and a disciple, and placed them into one family. Lord, we admit that we are often too busy and put too much weight on tasks, overlooking the one beside us who needs to be seen. Please forgive us and give us the Lord’s way of seeing, so that we understand that people matter more than things and relationships more than possessions, and so that we live by the order of life first, then relationships, then ministry. Lord, when we meet a suffering family member, please give us courage, so that even when we cannot help, we are willing to stand beside them and keep company. Raise up among us true spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that the church is not only a place of meetings but a true family. And please let us be like John, responding immediately when we hear Your entrusting, and taking those You give us into our own lives. May all the glory go to You. We pray in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, amen.
