v: So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it.
Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of one hundred fifty-three great fish. Even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn.
Jesus said to them, “Come and eat breakfast!” None of the disciples dared inquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord.
Then Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise.
This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.
b: The disciples had toiled all night
and caught nothing.
As day was breaking,
the Lord stood on the shore.
They cast the net as the Lord said,
and the net was full.
Now
they had come ashore.
The first thing they saw when they landed
was not rebuke,
not an interrogation,
but a fire,
with fish on the fire,
and bread.
This passage is very short.
So short there is almost no doctrine to preach.
Only a breakfast.
But this breakfast
is one of the gentlest scenes in the whole Bible.
I. There was a fire of coals—the Lord brought Peter back to where he was hurt most deeply
Verse 9,
“So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there.”
The word “fire of coals”
appears only twice
in the whole New Testament.
Once here.
The other time
is John 18:18:
“Now the servants and the officers were standing there, having made a fire of coals, for it was cold. They were warming themselves. Peter was with them, standing and warming himself.”
That was the courtyard of the high priest.
That was the night Peter denied the Lord three times.
The fire of coals that night
lit up his face
and also exposed his weakness.
Since that night,
there was probably a place in Peter’s heart
he no longer dared to approach.
A fire.
A smell.
A kind of light.
Whenever he smelled that smoke again,
he would remember the words he had said:
“I don’t know Him.”
And now
the risen Lord,
at the seashore of Galilee,
with His own hands lit another fire of coals.
Family,
this is no coincidence.
The Lord did it on purpose.
With a fire of coals
He brought Peter back to the place where the wound was deepest.
Not to shame him.
Not to dig up old accounts.
But to heal him there.
It is like two people who once had a terrible quarrel at a certain restaurant,
and since then neither dares mention the name of that place.
One day
one of them books the very same table
and invites the other to another meal.
He does not mean to replay that quarrel.
He means to rewrite that memory
in the very same place.
God’s healing
is often like this.
It does not go around;
it goes back to the same place and starts over.
We always hope God will skip past the painful place.
But the Lord often takes us by the hand
and walks us back down that road.
Because a wound that has not been faced
does not heal by itself.
It only forms a scab
and keeps festering underneath.
The Lord is waiting for you beside the fire of coals,
not to settle accounts,
but to restore.
A few verses later,
the Lord will, beside this very fire of coals,
ask Peter three times:
“Do you love me?”
Three denials
covered by three affirmations of love.
The Lord’s healing
is never careless.
II. The risen Lord Himself lit the fire, grilled the fish, and prepared breakfast
Verse 9 also says
that on the coals “there was fish laid on it, and bread.”
Think about this picture.
The Lord who had just risen from the dead,
the Lord who conquered death,
conquered Hades,
conquered the power of Satan,
what is He doing at this moment?
He is lighting a fire.
He is grilling fish.
He is waiting for a group of failed disciples to come ashore for breakfast.
When we read the accounts of the resurrection,
we often expect to see visions of glory,
voices from heaven,
earth-shaking declarations.
But what John records
is a breakfast.
Verse 13 says:
“Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish likewise.”
He did not tell the disciples to help themselves.
He “took” it and gave it to them.
The Lord of the universe,
for a group who had run away,
who had denied Him,
who had given up,
bent down
and handed over a piece of bread.
This is the gentlest theology.
Family,
if you think the risen Lord is far from you,
look at this fire.
It was lit for those who are cold.
It was for those who are hungry.
It was prepared for those who had toiled all night
and gained nothing.
Peter had not yet confessed his sin.
He had not yet explained.
He had not yet spoken plainly.
Yet the Lord had already made breakfast.
Grace never waits until we are good enough to arrive.
Grace is the Lord moving first.
The 321 principles say:
Jesus is my example.
This example
is not only in the pulpit,
not only in the miracles.
It is also beside a fire of coals.
When we serve people,
we often first think about what doctrine to teach.
The Lord first gave people a hot meal.
First He cared for that person’s cold and hunger,
and only then spoke about that person’s weakness.
This is the Lord’s order.
III. “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught”—the Lord does not lack our fish
Verse 10,
Jesus said:
“Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”
This sentence is worth pausing over.
Because verse 9 already says
there was fish on the coals.
Breakfast was already prepared.
The Lord did not lack those few fish.
So why did He still ask the disciples to bring some?
Because the Lord wanted them to have a share.
He could easily have finished everything Himself
and let the disciples sit and wait.
But He said:
Of what you caught,
bring some.
Family,
this is the truth about serving.
It is not that God needs us.
It is that God gives us the opportunity.
God has never called us because He was short of hands.
When He made heaven and earth He did not look for helpers.
When He raised the dead He needed no one’s help.
He asked us to bring fish
because He wants us to have a part in His work.
Seeing this
will save us from two diseases.
The first disease is pride:
“This cannot be done without me; if I don’t do it, no one will.”
No.
The fish are already on the fire.
The second disease is feeling small:
“I am so weak; what are these few fish I caught worth?”
No again.
The Lord specifically asked for them.
What He wants is not the number of fish.
What He wants is you, willing to come over.
And notice who He called.
Whom did the Lord call?
That group who had fished all night,
caught nothing,
and had just been stunned by grace.
He did not wait for them to be in better shape before using them.
He gave them something to do on the spot.
Because having a share in the Lord’s work
is itself part of the healing.
IV. One hundred fifty-three fish, yet the net was not torn
Verse 11,
“Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of great fish, one hundred fifty-three; and even though there were so many, the net was not torn.”
The number one hundred fifty-three
has been explained in many ways by commentators through the ages.
Some say
that people then thought the known kinds of fish in the sea
numbered one hundred fifty-three,
so it represents all nations and peoples being found by the Lord.
Some say
that the fishermen really did count them one by one after landing,
so John wrote it down as it was.
We need not get stuck on the number.
But one thing is most certain:
the net was not torn.
So many fish,
yet the net was not torn.
By ordinary reason,
a catch like this
should long ago have burst the net.
But the Holy Spirit specifically had John write down this line:
the net was not torn.
Because this is a picture of the church.
The Lord’s net
has room for everyone He has found.
Room for one hundred fifty-three different kinds of fish.
Room for different temperaments,
different backgrounds,
different accents,
different pasts.
And it does not tear.
Brothers and sisters,
let us ask honestly:
why does the church today
so often have torn nets?
Most of the time it is not because there are too many people.
It is because there is too little love.
When a net tears,
it is not the fish’s problem;
it is the net’s problem.
We often say:
“This person is too hard to get along with.”
“That person’s thinking doesn’t fit mine.”
“He really is unbearable.”
But the Lord’s net has never complained that there are too many fish.
A church that cannot hold people
is not so because the people in it are too unusual;
it is because the fibers of the net are too brittle.
What makes the net brittle?
It is “self.”
I often think of the zipper on clothing.
The two rows of teeth of a zipper
each originally sit on their own side,
pointing different directions,
shaped in opposite ways.
But when the slider passes over,
they lock together tightly,
without a gap.
When does a zipper burst open?
Mostly not because the garment is too big,
but because a small corner of fabric got caught in the middle.
Just one little piece of extra material caught in between,
and the whole zipper comes apart.
It is the same among us.
Brothers and sisters are different to begin with.
Being different does not make us split.
What really gets caught in the middle
is that little piece of “me.”
My opinion.
My pride.
My grievance.
My rights.
That little piece of self that will not let go
is where the net tears.
V. No one dared ask, “Who are You?”
Verse 12,
“Jesus said to them, ‘Come and eat breakfast.’ None of the disciples dared inquire of him, ‘Who are you?’ knowing that it was the Lord.”
This sentence is written very truly.
They did not dare ask.
Why not?
On one hand,
it was reverence.
The One before them
was the One they had watched be crucified
and buried.
Now He stood by the fire grilling fish.
That shock
left them speechless.
On the other hand,
it was familiarity.
“Knowing that it was the Lord.”
They did not ask,
not because they did not know,
but because they knew too well.
That voice,
that movement,
that gesture of handing over the bread,
they had followed Him for three and a half years.
No need to ask.
They simply knew.
Family,
this is how it looks after a long time with the Lord.
The maturity of faith
is sometimes not more questions,
but fewer.
Not because of numbness,
but because of recognition.
A little child who hears footsteps in the dark
does not need to turn on the light
to know that Dad is home.
Because those footsteps
he has heard since he was small.
What we need is not more information about God,
but to know this God Himself more deeply.
Verse 14 says:
“This was now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples, after he had risen from the dead.”
The third time.
The Lord came again and again.
He did not appear once,
and leave when your response wasn’t right.
He came again.
Again.
He came even a third time.
If today you feel
that you have let the Lord down too many times,
and the Lord probably won’t come looking for you again—
look at this verse.
The Lord appeared to the disciples;
this was the third time.
He is still on His way.
Light from the 321 principles—only self-denial brings oneness; the net was not torn
Today’s passage
draws the road of “only self-denial brings oneness”
concretely with a fishing net.
Oneness is not everyone being the same.
In the net were one hundred fifty-three fish,
and each one was different.
Oneness is this:
so many different ones
held in the same net,
and the net did not tear.
So the key to oneness
has never been in other people;
it is in the fibers of the net.
It is in me.
It is in how much of that “self” is left inside me.
When there is self,
I measure people by my own ruler:
those like me,
I accept;
those unlike me,
I reject.
The net is stretched open, mesh by mesh.
When there is no self,
my heart becomes the Lord’s net:
whom the Lord gathers,
I gather;
whom the Lord loves,
I love.
The net holds.
The 321 principles have a sentence that says it very clearly:
everyone who has a relationship with us
is our 2.
Not only the ones I pick.
Whoever the Lord has placed beside me
is.
That hard-to-get-along-with co-worker
is my 2.
That elder whose thinking differs from mine
is my 2.
That brother who once hurt me
is also my 2.
As I live out the 0 of self-denial,
on each one of these 2s
I bear the nine fruits of the Holy Spirit.
Love,
joy,
peace,
patience,
kindness,
goodness,
faithfulness,
gentleness,
self-control.
Not one of these nine
can be borne by hiding away alone.
All of them can only grow among people.
Ephesians 4:3 says:
“being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.”
The words “being eager to keep” are important.
Oneness does not happen naturally.
Oneness is taking the knife to ourselves every day.
Removing that little piece of “self” that jams the zipper,
again and again.
Only then will the net not tear.
And when the net does not tear,
those the Lord has found can be kept.
This is building God’s system.
Our Response to Life
This passage reminds us:
First, the Lord will bring us back to where we were hurt most deeply. He does not come to settle accounts, but to heal us there.
Second, the risen Lord Himself prepared breakfast for us. Grace is always the Lord moving first; it does not wait until we are good enough.
Third, the Lord does not lack our fish, yet He wants us to have a share. Serving is not that God needs us; it is that God gives us the opportunity.
Fourth, the net was not torn. A church’s net tears not because there are too many people, but because there is too little love and too much self.
Fifth, knowing the Lord matters more than knowing things about the Lord. After a long time with the Lord, there is no need to ask; you simply know.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your Son Jesus Christ, who after the resurrection did not stay in glory but returned to the seashore of Galilee to light a fire, grill fish, and prepare breakfast for a group of failed disciples. Lord, many of us have a fire of coals in our hearts that we dare not approach again, a memory we do not want to recall. Take us by the hand and bring us back to that place, not to shame us, but to heal us. Remove also that little piece of “self” within us that jams things up, and let our hearts become Your net, able to hold everyone You have found, without disdain, without rejection, without bursting. Help us see everyone who has a relationship with us as the 2 You have entrusted to us, and let us live out the life of self-denial on them and bear the fruit of the Holy Spirit. May we know Your voice all our lives, so that without asking, we simply know it is the Lord. Give all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. Is there a “fire of coals you dare not approach again” in your heart? If the Lord invited you today to come back to that place for breakfast, would you be willing to go?
2\. Is there someone recently who is the place where your net is about to tear? What is that little piece of “self” caught in the middle?

v: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.
b: This is the warmest passage in the whole Gospel of John.
It is also the most painful.
Because the one the Lord is about to heal
is a man who denied Him three times.
There was a fire of coals by the sea.
Breakfast was finished.
Seven disciples were there.
The Lord did not take Peter aside to speak with him privately.
Nor did He wait until everyone had left.
Right there beside that fire of coals,
in front of his brothers,
one word at a time,
He lifted Peter up out of the ashes.
This passage tells us one thing:
the Lord does not only forgive people;
the Lord also restores them.
1. He called him “Simon, son of John”
At the very beginning of verse 15,
the Lord’s way of addressing him is striking.
He did not call him “Peter.”
He called him:
“Simon, son of John.”
This was his original name.
It was the name he had back when he was still fishing.
It was the name he had before he met the Lord.
We remember that three years earlier,
Andrew brought him to Jesus,
and the Lord looked at him and said:
“You are Simon the son of Jonah. You shall be called Cephas.”
(John 1:42)
Cephas, translated,
is Peter,
which means “a stone.”
That was the new name the Lord gave him.
That was the Lord’s heart for him.
But now,
the Lord sets the new name aside
and calls him again:
Simon, son of John.
Why?
Not to humiliate him.
It is because after those three denials,
there was one thing Peter knew better than anyone:
I am not a stone.
I am not a stone at all.
I am the Simon who trembled before a servant girl.
I am the Simon who stood by the fire of coals and said, “I am not.”
The Lord knew the words in his heart.
So the Lord called him by the true name he carried inside.
Dear family,
this is the first step of restoration.
Restoration does not begin with “I must pull myself together.”
Restoration begins with admitting who I really am.
Only when I admit I am not a stone
can the Lord make me into a stone again.
We often do the opposite.
After we fall,
we rush to patch ourselves up,
we rush to cover the breach,
we rush to keep others from seeing it.
We use a new name to cover over the old self.
We use titles,
we use ministry,
we use busyness,
to cover that Simon who has not yet been healed.
But the Lord does not do it that way.
The Lord first lifts the cover.
The Lord first calls out that true name.
Because God heals only the wounds He can see,
and He sees everything;
the question is,
are we willing to let ourselves see them too?
2. Three questions, reaching as deep as the three denials
In verses 15, 16, and 17,
the Lord asked three times.
Peter answered three times.
The Lord entrusted him three times.
This was no accident.
On that night,
Peter stood by the fire of coals
and said three times:
“I am not.”
Now,
beside another fire of coals,
the Lord gives him three chances to say:
“Lord, You know that I love You.”
Notice how the Lord goes about this.
First,
the Lord did not pretend it had never happened.
The Lord could have passed over it lightly,
so that everyone avoided the subject
and just moved on.
But that kind of reconciliation is false.
A wound that is never faced
is only a wound that has been buried.
A buried wound festers.
Second,
the Lord did not bring up old accounts either.
From beginning to end the Lord did not say a single word like:
“How could you do that to me that night?”
Not one word of blame.
Not one word of reopening the case.
Not one “I told you so.”
The Lord simply asked:
Do you love Me?
Brothers and sisters,
this is God’s way of healing.
There is a kind of fracture
that was not set properly at the time,
and so it healed crooked.
On the outside it looks mended,
it no longer hurts,
and the person can walk,
but the posture is bent.
For a doctor to truly heal it,
he must break that bone again
at the place where it first broke,
set it straight once more,
and join it back together.
That process hurts.
But it is the only way to walk straight.
What the Lord did for Peter
was exactly this.
He did not just put ointment on the surface.
He went down to the depth where Peter had fallen.
Three denials
met three questions.
Layer by layer,
He set that crooked bone straight again.
So know this:
if the Lord has been asking you about the same matter lately,
touching you at the very same place,
it is not harassment.
He is setting you straight.
3. “Do you love Me more than these?”
In the first question
there is a phrase the other two do not have:
“Do you love me more than these?”
What are “these”?
It may refer to the boat nearby,
the nets,
and those one hundred fifty-three fish,
the old trade he knew so well.
It may also refer to the brothers standing beside him.
Because Peter had once said:
“Even if all will be made to stumble because of you, I will never be made to stumble.”
(Matthew 26:33)
He had once been more certain than anyone else.
Now the Lord asks him:
Do you still dare to compare?
Whichever it is,
the point is the same:
what the Lord wants
is not his ability.
Not his experience.
Not his achievements.
Not how he measures up against others.
The Lord asks only one thing:
Do you love Me?
We need to hear this very clearly.
In our age,
it is far too easy to treat ministry as a job.
We look at gifts.
We look at eloquence.
We look at experience.
We look at the results produced.
We look at whether anyone follows.
But the Lord never asked Peter:
Can you preach?
How many people can you lead?
How much have you learned in three years?
What the Lord asked was:
Do you love Me?
Because the only qualification for ministry
is loving the Lord.
A person who is very capable but does not love the Lord
will find that his ministry in the end becomes a performance.
A person of limited ability who truly loves the Lord
will have a ministry full of life.
When the owner entrusts his sheep to someone,
he does not hand them to the best bookkeeper;
he hands them to the one who, hearing a sheep cry in the middle of the night,
is willing to get up.
4. The Lord stoops to the little you can give right now
In the original language of this passage
there is a deeply moving detail.
The first two times the Lord asks, “Do you love Me?”
He uses one word,
which means the highest,
the divine kind of love,
a love willing to lay down one’s life.
All three times Peter answers
with a different word,
which means the affection between friends,
a warm fondness,
“I truly count You my dearest friend.”
It is not that Peter did not love.
Peter simply no longer dared to boast.
Once he had said:
“I will lay down my life for you.”
In the end he did not do it.
So now he does not dare to use so great a word again.
He dares only to say:
Lord, I do have deep feeling for You,
You know it.
And then
the Lord did something.
When He asked the third time,
the Lord changed the word.
The Lord used Peter’s own word to ask him:
“Are you fond of Me?”
The Lord came down.
The Lord did not insist that Peter first give the level of love He had originally asked for.
The Lord stooped to the place where Peter could meet Him now.
It is like a grown-up speaking kindly to a little child:
he does not stand tall and toss words down,
he crouches down
so that his eyes
are level with the child’s eyes.
That is how the Lord crouched down
and asked Peter.
Dear family,
if today you feel
that your love for the Lord seems shallow,
that you dare not say you love Him enough to lay down your life,
that you can only say you have not left Him—
then honestly give Him that much.
The Lord will not despise it as too little.
The Lord will crouch down,
receive the little you can give now,
and then take you by the hand
all the way until you grow into the kind of love He meant to give you.
And at that very moment,
the Scripture says:
“Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, ‘Do you love me?’”
That grief
was not the grief of being condemned.
It was the grief of being found out.
It was the Lord’s hand pressing exactly on the most painful place.
Brothers and sisters,
to be questioned by the Lord at your sore spot
is grace.
When God pierces the heart,
it is never to knock a person down.
It is to drain the infection.
An infection that is never drained
forms a scab on the outside
while it keeps festering inside.
Paul said:
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation, a repentance which brings no regret; but the sorrow of the world works death.”
(2 Corinthians 7:10)
The sorrow of the world says:
I am finished.
Godly sorrow says:
I will go back to the Lord.
The psalm says:
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, God, you will not despise.”
(Psalm 51:17)
So,
when the Lord’s word pricks you,
do not run.
He is performing surgery,
not pronouncing your condemnation.
5. The proof of love for the Lord is shepherding the Lord’s sheep
Three questions
came with three commissions.
Feed My lambs.
Tend My sheep.
Feed My sheep.
There are lambs,
and there are grown sheep;
there is feeding,
and there is tending.
Feeding is giving food.
Tending is leading,
watching over,
protecting,
and healing.
The Lord placed the whole flock,
from the smallest to the largest,
into Peter’s hands, one after another.
There is a very important order here:
the Lord first asked, “Do you love Me?”
and only then said, “Feed My sheep.”
Love first,
work after.
Relationship first,
commission after.
And notice that the Lord says “My sheep.”
Not “your sheep.”
The sheep belong to the Lord.
The shepherd is only entrusted with them.
That is why Peter later wrote to the elders:
“Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising oversight, not under compulsion, but willingly.”
(1 Peter 5:2)
He had learned it.
So,
what is the proof of loving the Lord?
It is not a feeling.
It is not tears shed in a meeting.
It is not how beautifully one speaks.
The proof the Lord gives is very concrete:
go and care for the ones I love.
You say you love Me,
then go and feed those I gave My life for.
When you love a person,
you care for what he treasures.
If you love your friend,
and he leaves his child with you for an afternoon,
you do not brush the task off.
The Lord has handed us the sheep He bought with His own blood,
and that is the deepest trust He has in us.
So,
loving the Lord is never an emotion that stays inside the heart.
Loving the Lord will always go out,
and reach people.
Light from the 321 principles—the path of service: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God
Today’s passage
shows us the “path of service” of the 321 principles, acted out from beginning to end.
The path of service is five words:
Spirit—the Holy Spirit’s guidance.
Understanding—the Bible as our standard.
Life—living out the life of Jesus.
Service—letting Jesus be King.
God—letting Jesus be glorified.
We often get this wrong,
supposing that service begins with “Service.”
We see a need,
and we go and do it.
We have a gift,
and we step onto the stage.
But the order the Lord gave Peter by the sea was not like that.
The Lord first dealt with “Life.”
He first healed that fallen Simon
at the deepest place in his life.
He first set that crooked bone straight.
He first let him face himself honestly.
Then the Lord dealt with the “relationship.”
Do you love Me?
Do you love Me?
Do you love Me?
Three questions,
all of them about relationship.
Not ability,
not plans,
not strategy.
It was whether between you and Me
there is still something there.
Only when life was restored
and the relationship was restored
did the Lord speak the commission:
Feed My sheep.
This is exactly the order the 321 principles have always taught:
life first,
then relationships,
then ministry.
Change the concept and you change the life,
change the life and you change the way you live,
and only then is there true relationship and ministry.
Brothers and sisters,
this order cannot be reversed.
Ministry without life
is empty.
Ministry without relationship
is heavy.
That is no commission;
that is a burden.
If a person has not been healed by the Lord in his life,
then when he goes to serve,
he carries his own wounds to touch other people’s wounds.
If a person’s relationship with the Lord is cold,
then when he goes to serve,
sooner or later he will be held hostage by people’s opinions,
held hostage by results,
held hostage by his own “self.”
But a person whose life has been healed
and whose relationship has been restored,
when he goes to shepherd,
it is “life” flowing out.
He is not doing a job;
he is living out Jesus.
And the end of this road is “God”—
letting Jesus have all the glory.
Peter said it very plainly in the end:
“When the chief Shepherd is revealed, you will receive the crown of glory that doesn’t fade away.”
(1 Peter 5:4)
The Chief Shepherd is the Lord.
We are all just little shepherds.
The sheep are His.
The glory is His.
We are nothing,
only that Simon who once fell,
was lifted up again by the Lord,
and then was sent by Him to lift up others.
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, restoration begins with admitting who I really am. Only when I admit I am not a stone can the Lord make me into a stone again.
Second, the Lord heals you at the depth where you fell. He does not pretend it never happened, and He does not bring up old accounts; He simply sets you straight, layer by layer.
Third, the only qualification for ministry is loving the Lord. The Lord does not ask about your ability, experience, or results; He asks only whether you love Him.
Fourth, the Lord stoops to the little you can give now. You do not need to have great love first; just give Him honestly what you have now.
Fifth, the proof of loving the Lord is shepherding the Lord’s sheep. Loving the Lord is not a feeling; it is caring for the ones He loves.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for Your Son Jesus Christ, who by the fire of coals at the seaside did not give up on a man who denied Him three times. Lord, we confess that we too often deny You before others, through silence, through shrinking back, through fear of people. We also often rush to cover over our falls and refuse to let You see who we really are. Today, as You did with Peter, call us by our original names and bring to light, one by one, the places in us that have not yet been healed. Lord, we no longer dare to boast; all we can say is: You know all things, You know that we love You. Stoop to our weakness, receive this little love we can give now, and lead us all the way until we grow into the love You desire. And according to the order of life first, then relationship, then ministry, heal our lives first, then restore our relationship with You, and then entrust Your sheep into our hands with confidence. May we spend our whole lives as faithful little shepherds, giving all the glory to the Chief Shepherd. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. If the Lord called you by your original name today and asked, “Do you love Me?”, what is the place in you that you least want Him to touch?
2\. Who is the little lamb the Lord has placed beside you this week to feed? How do you plan to care for him in a concrete way?

v: Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”
b: This is near the end of the Gospel of John.
By the Sea of Tiberias,
beside the fire of coals,
the Lord had just asked Peter three times:
“Do you love me?”
He had just placed the flock in his hands three times.
Forgiveness had been given.
Restoration had been accomplished.
The commission had been spoken.
And then,
only then, the Lord spoke the two verses we read today.
He told Peter
how far the road ahead would go,
and how great the price would be.
These two verses are very short.
So short you can read them in a minute.
Yet they are the map of a whole lifetime.
It is also the stretch of road every follower of the Lord
will sooner or later have to walk into.
1. The “freedom” of fastening your own belt is really the smallest freedom
Verse 18.
The Lord first said:
“Most certainly I tell you.”
In the Gospel of John,
whenever this phrase appears,
the Lord is about to say something of great importance.
Then He said:
“When you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to.”
We first need to understand the picture in this sentence.
The Jews of that day wore long robes.
The robes were wide and long.
To walk,
to work,
to set out on a journey,
the first thing was to tie the belt around the waist
and gather up the robe.
“Fastening the belt”
meant “I am setting out.”
A young man
fastens his own belt,
decides for himself where to go,
and goes wherever he wants.
The Bible has a phrase for it:
“walked where you wanted to.”
When Peter heard this,
he must have thought at once of how he was as a young man.
If he wanted to fish, he fished.
If he wanted to draw a sword, he drew it.
If he wanted to say something, he said it.
If he wanted to jump into the water, he jumped.
How exhilarating that was.
How free that was.
Dear family,
this is not only a picture of Peter’s youth.
It is also a picture of every one of us as the old self.
Deciding for myself.
Arranging for myself.
Going to the places I want to go.
Fastening my own belt.
People call this freedom.
But let me say something plainly:
the freedom of fastening your own belt
is really the smallest freedom.
Because the range of that freedom
can never be larger than “myself.”
As far as I can think,
is as far as I can go.
My life is only as big
as what I can see.
I think I am choosing,
but in fact I am only going around in circles inside my limited imagination.
I think of a horse.
A wild horse
running on the grassland,
no reins,
no rider,
and it looks perfectly free.
But all its life it can only run around the same stretch of grass.
It does not know what lies on the other side of the mountain.
And it will never draw water
from the well to the field.
That same horse,
if it were harnessed
and willing to lower its head,
could leave the grassland,
climb the mountain,
cross the river,
and pull a whole cart of water
to irrigate an entire stretch of dry land.
The harnessed horse
looks as if it has lost its freedom,
but in fact it has entered into something it could never do in all its life.
The 321 principles say:
the old self’s life of self
must become the new self’s life of self-denial.
“Fastening your own belt”
is having self.
A person full of self is not a bad person.
A person full of self is often diligent, zealous, and sincere.
Peter was exactly that kind of person.
But people full of self share one limit:
their whole life
cannot be bigger than themselves.
2. Stretching out your hands, to be bound by another—obedience is handing over sovereignty
The Lord went on:
“But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you, and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
This sentence has three movements,
each deeper than the last.
The first movement: stretching out your hands.
Not clenching a fist.
Not grasping.
It is opening the hands
and reaching out.
The second movement: another will dress you.
Before, you fastened it yourself;
now someone else fastens it.
The belt is still the same belt,
but the one who fastens it has changed.
The third movement: carry you where you don’t want to go.
Before, it was “walked where you wanted to”;
now it is “don’t want to go.”
The direction is no longer decided by me.
Dear family,
this is the picture of obedience.
For a person who truly follows the Lord,
in the end,
sovereignty over his life must be handed over.
We often think
that believing in the Lord means asking Him to help us carry out our plans.
It is not so.
Believing in the Lord is placing my plans
in His hands.
From “Where do I want to go?”
to “Where do You want me to go?”
From “Lord, please bless my road”
to “Lord, Your road is my road.”
Here is a very important detail:
the text says “where you don’t want to go.”
The Lord did not say:
you will be very willing.
The Lord did not say:
by then you will find it very sweet.
The Lord said honestly:
that is a place you do not want to go.
Obedience does not mean there is no struggle.
Obedience is, even when unwilling,
still stretching out the hands.
In the Garden of Gethsemane,
the Lord Himself prayed in just this way:
“Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”
He too was unwilling.
He went anyway.
That is what obedience is.
Church history tells us very clearly
that Peter did later walk this road.
In Rome,
under Nero’s persecution, he was martyred.
The tradition of the early church agrees in recording
that when he was crucified,
he said he was not worthy to die in the same posture as the Lord,
and asked to be crucified upside down.
The words “stretch out your hands”
were fulfilled completely on the cross.
That Peter who as a young man wanted to draw a sword,
that Peter who jumped into the water the moment he grew anxious,
in the end opened both of his hands
and let others bind him.
In 2 Peter 1:14
he himself wrote this sentence:
“Knowing that the putting off of my tent comes swiftly, even as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.”
All his life he remembered this word by the sea.
I think of flying on a plane.
A person walking on the ground
is bound by no one.
He goes as fast as he likes,
and stops whenever he likes.
But when he is really going to fly,
the moment he boards the plane,
the first thing he does is fasten his seat belt.
Interesting, isn’t it:
the very moment he is about to fly highest
is the moment he is strapped in tightest.
The seat belt is not there to limit the flight.
The seat belt is there for the flight.
And where the plane flies to
is not decided by the person in the seat.
Our whole lives are like this.
To be bound
is not to have life made smaller.
It is that life is at last placed in the hands of a Lord
who knows the flight path.
3. Even death can glorify God—my days are in His hands
First half of verse 19:
“Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God.”
Notice these words:
by what kind of death he would glorify God.
We have always thought
that glorifying God is a matter of living.
I will serve well,
to glorify God.
I will bear witness well,
to glorify God.
I will do my work well,
to glorify God.
All of these are right.
But here the Lord tells us something deeper:
even death
can glorify God.
A person can glorify God not only with a whole life,
but also by the way he departs from this world.
Dear family,
let me slow down here.
This sentence is not meant to make us imagine a tragic scene.
When the Lord said this,
He was not trying to frighten Peter.
We can see this in the second half of verse 19:
as soon as the Lord had said it,
He immediately said to him:
“Follow me.”
The Lord was not telling him to be afraid;
the Lord was telling him to come and follow.
So what this sentence really brings
is not fear
but security.
Where does the security lie?
It lies in this:
my days are in His hands.
Psalm 31:15 says:
“My times are in your hand.”
How I live
is in His hand.
How long I live
is in His hand.
How I end
is also in His hand.
A person who knows his days are in God’s hand
no longer needs to fear tomorrow.
Romans 14:8 says:
“For if we live, we live to the Lord. Or if we die, we die to the Lord. If therefore we live or die, we are the Lord’s.”
Whether we live
or die,
we are the Lord’s.
What a great release this is.
Paul also said:
“Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death.”
(Philippians 1:20)
If a person can hand both life and death over to the Lord,
nothing in the world can threaten him anymore.
Most of us will not walk the road of martyrdom.
But every one of us
must face the aging of the body,
face the fading of strength,
face the day we must hand over the work in our hands,
face the parting from loved ones,
and face our own end.
Here the Lord tells us:
those days
can also glorify God.
An elderly person
who still trusts on a sickbed,
glorifies God.
A person who can no longer do much
and prays in secret for others,
glorifies God.
A person who has come to the end of the road
and still has peace on his face,
glorifies God.
Glorifying God has never depended on how much we can do.
It depends on whom we have entrusted ourselves to.
4. “Follow me”—a whole lifetime’s lesson is these two words
The end of verse 19:
“When he had said this, he said to him, ‘Follow me.’”
Every time I read this I am deeply moved.
Because the Lord could have said so much.
He could have said:
“Peter, you must try hard.”
He could have said:
“Peter, be careful, there is danger ahead.”
He could have said:
“Peter, don’t fall again.”
If it were us,
we would probably give a long list of cautions.
But the Lord said only two words:
Follow me.
No blame.
No bringing up old accounts.
Not one word like “Didn’t you say last time that you would lay down your life for me?”
Only:
Follow me.
Dear family,
the lesson of the Christian life
is these two words.
Not “You must become better.”
Not “You must become more capable.”
Not “You must beat someone.”
But: Follow me.
The meaning of following is very simple—
He goes ahead,
I come behind.
He decides the direction,
I am responsible to keep up.
I do not need to know the whole journey;
I only need to see His back.
Let us look back at one more thing,
and it is very important.
When did the Lord say these words?
It was after He had first forgiven Peter.
It was after He had first prepared breakfast for Peter.
It was after He had first asked three times, “Do you love me?”
and first entrusted the flock to him.
The Lord first restored,
and then revealed.
The Lord first gave grace,
and then gave the commission.
The Lord first let Peter know he was loved,
and then let Peter know the cost ahead.
When God gives revelation,
He always gives grace first.
This is how our Lord has always worked.
He never first piles the heavy load on us
and then tells us to find our own way.
He always feeds you first,
forgives you first,
raises you up first,
and then says:
Come with Me.
So when today we feel the road ahead is hard,
we must first turn back and confirm one thing:
the One who calls me to walk
is the One who first loved me,
first forgave me,
and first died and rose again for me.
There is one more thing worth noting.
In John 13:36,
Peter once asked the Lord:
“Lord, where are you going?”
The Lord answered:
“Where I go, you can’t follow now, but you will follow afterwards.”
Peter would not accept it then,
and said:
“I will lay down my life for you!”
And that very night he denied the Lord three times.
But today,
by the sea,
the Lord says:
“Follow me.”
“Afterwards” has come.
In those days Peter relied on himself to say he would lay down his life,
and failed.
Today Peter has been restored by the Lord,
entrusted by the Lord,
bound by the Lord,
and he truly walked that road to the end.
The very same road.
By self it cannot be walked.
With self-denial, it can be walked.
Light from the 321 principles—from self to self-denial; self-denial is not nothingness but entering the infinite
This passage today
has drawn the most central road of the 321 principles
as a picture.
When you were young,
you fastened your own belt
and walked where you wanted.
That is the old self’s life of self.
When you are old,
you stretch out your hands
and another binds you.
That is the new self’s life of self-denial.
The person full of self
makes himself king.
The person of self-denial
lets Jesus be King.
The person full of self asks:
Where do I want to go?
The person of self-denial asks:
Lord, where do You want me to go?
But listen carefully to one thing,
so that we do not misunderstand.
Self-denial is not nothingness.
Self-denial does not turn a person into an empty shell,
does not make a person lose himself,
lose his worth,
lose his life.
Self-denial is setting down that small,
limited “me”
that can only go around in circles around itself,
so as to enter into the infinite God.
Peter laid down the freedom of fastening his own belt.
What did he gain?
He gained three thousand people turning to the Lord from one sermon on the day of Pentecost.
He gained carrying the gospel into a Gentile household.
He gained two letters that still comfort suffering saints all over the world.
He gained a story that we are still reading two thousand years later.
That fisherman who only wanted to fish on the Sea of Galilee,
if all his life he had fastened his own belt and walked where he wished,
his life would have been only one lake.
When he stretched out his hands
and let the Lord bind him,
his life entered eternity.
Self-denial is not nothingness.
Self-denial is entering the infinite and living out the infinite.
So the Lord Jesus said:
“If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
(Matthew 16:24)
Deny himself,
and then follow.
The order cannot be reversed.
Because a person who does not deny himself
is in fact still following himself.
Paul walked this road to the very end
and wrote the words:
“It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”
(Galatians 2:20)
\*\*This is a life from fastening one’s own belt to being bound by the Lord.\*\*
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, the freedom of fastening your own belt is the smallest freedom. I can go only as far as I can think; my whole life is no bigger than myself.
Second, obedience is stretching out your hands and letting the Lord decide the direction. Obedience does not mean no struggle; obedience is still stretching out the hands even when unwilling.
Third, even death can glorify God. Because my days are in His hands, whether I live or die I am always the Lord’s.
Fourth, the Lord’s final commission is only two words: Follow me. It is not that you must try harder; it is that He walks ahead and I follow behind.
Fifth, when God gives revelation, He always gives grace first. The Lord first forgives, first restores, first entrusts, and only then tells us the cost ahead.
Pray Together

v: Then Peter, turning around, saw a disciple following. This was the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one who had also leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper and asked, “Lord, who is going to betray you?”
Peter seeing him, said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”
Jesus said to him, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.”

This saying therefore went out among the brothers, that this disciple wouldn’t die. Yet Jesus didn’t say to him that he wouldn’t die, but, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?”
b: This is the last conversation in the Gospel of John.
The Lord had just, by the Sea of Tiberias,
asked Peter three times:
“Do you love me?”
and three times placed the charge to shepherd the flock in his hands.
Then the Lord said:
“Follow me.”
What a glorious moment that was.
The failed one had been restored.
The fallen one had been sent out again.
But in the very next second,
Peter did something every one of us does.
He turned around
and looked at someone else.
1. Just entrusted with a charge, and already looking at someone else
The first words of verse 20
are only a few:
“Peter turned around.”
Those few words
capture the true state of the human heart.
The Lord’s words were still in his ears,
the warmth had not yet faded,
and Peter had already turned around.
He saw John following behind.
The Bible takes care to remind us
who John was:
the one who, at supper,
leaned against Jesus’ chest.
In other words,
in Peter’s mind,
John had always been “the one closest to the Lord.”
So a voice began to speak inside Peter:
What about me?
Compared with him,
what am I, really?
Dear family,
notice the order here.
It was not that he compared after he fell.
He compared after he received grace.
It was not that he felt uneasy when he was rebuked.
He felt uneasy when he was entrusted.
The time we are most prone to comparing
is often not at our lowest point,
but at the very moment the Lord has just lifted our head.
Because the “self” is still there.
As soon as the “self” is built up,
its first act is to look for an object
to prove whether it measures up.
The 321 principles say:
having self is the root of the fall of humanity.
This turn of Peter’s head
was very natural,
and also very dangerous.
2. “What about this man?”—comparison is the killer of joy
Verse 21.
Peter opened his mouth and asked:
“Lord, what about this man?”
On the surface,
this sounds like a caring question.
But we must remember what came before.
The Lord had just told Peter in verse 18:
when you are old,
you will stretch out your hands,
and another will dress you
and carry you where you don’t want to go.
The Lord had already made clear
that Peter would glorify God through martyrdom.
After hearing his own road,
Peter’s first reaction was:
What about him?
Will he end up like this too?
Or will he have it easier?
Comparison is the killer of joy.
As soon as a person starts using someone else’s road
to measure his own road,
gratitude vanishes on the spot.
The joy of receiving a charge
is replaced by “Why me?”
We are the same today.
Serving in the same way,
some have a road that is long and smooth,
and some have a road that is short and hard.
Loving the Lord in the same way,
some are strong and healthy to eighty,
and some are bedridden at forty.
Equally faithful,
some are noticed,
and some live their whole lives unknown.
If we keep looking to the side,
our hearts will never be at peace.
I often think of tailoring.
A garment that truly fits
is measured by the master across a person’s shoulders,
waist,
and length,
inch by inch.
On you it fits just right.
But if you envy someone else’s garment
and insist on swapping,
it will be either too tight
or too loose.
It is not that the garment is bad;
it was simply never measured for you.
John later lived a long life
and on the island of Patmos wrote Revelation.
Peter walked the road of martyrdom.
Two garments,
both measured by the Lord’s own hands.
Neither one is second-rate.
3. “What is that to you?”—the Lord’s words are a great release
Verse 22.
The Lord’s answer is so direct it almost seems to spare no feelings:
“If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?”
Reading this,
we may feel embarrassed for Peter.
But this sentence
is in fact the greatest release the Lord gave Peter.
“What is that to you” means:
this is not your load.
John’s road,
I will be responsible for it Myself.
You do not need to worry over him,
nor use him as a measuring stick.
Dear family,
how much of the weariness inside us
comes from carrying a weight that was never ours?
We grow anxious over other people’s growth.
We worry over other people’s choices.
We compare ourselves with other people’s gifts.
In the end,
our own lessons go undone,
while our minds are filled with other people’s lessons.
Paul said:
“But let each man examine his own work... For each man will bear his own burden.”
(Galatians 6:4–5)
He also said:
“Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls.”
(Romans 14:4)
There is only one Master.
He knows each servant’s strength,
knows how far each one can go,
and knows when it is time to stop.
I am not someone else’s master,
and someone else is not my measuring stick.
When I truly believe “What is that to you?”,
I am free.
I do not have to be responsible for anyone else’s lessons,
nor use anyone else’s report card
to decide my joy today.
4. “Follow me”—the Lord pulls the focus back to the same place, twice
Notice one thing.
In just a few verses,
the Lord said “Follow me” twice.
Once in verse 19.
Once again in verse 22.
What came in between?
Peter turning to look at someone else.
The Lord did not argue with him about John’s future.
The Lord did not explain,
nor did He compare.
The Lord simply said the same sentence
once more.
This is how the Lord leads people.
He does not go around in circles with us.
Again and again He pulls our eyes
back to the same focus.
Not that person.
Me.
The most central road of the 321 principles
is fully revealed here:
the focus is on Jesus,
not on self,
not on others,
not on circumstances.
Focus on self,
and you become proud or feel inferior.
Focus on others,
and you become envious or judgmental.
Focus on circumstances,
and you become fearful or complaining.
Only when the focus is on Jesus
does the heart find peace.
And the act of “following”
itself decides the direction of the eyes.
A follower
is one who walks behind.
If you want to follow,
your eyes can only fix on the One ahead.
The moment you start looking left and right,
your steps fall into disorder.
Peter’s problem was not that he did not love the Lord.
He truly loved the Lord.
He truly was willing to follow.
He had only forgotten for a moment where he was standing.
The disciple’s place
is behind the Lord,
not beside other people.
5. A saying distorted in the telling—do not replace the Lord’s words with other people’s words
Verse 23.
The Bible records something very true to life:
“This saying therefore went out among the brothers, that that disciple wouldn’t die.”
What the Lord had clearly said was:
“If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?”
That was a hypothetical.
But as it was passed along,
the hypothetical became an assertion.
A question became a prophecy.
Finally it became a rumor:
that disciple will not die.
When John wrote his Gospel,
he was already old.
He still had to come forward himself to clarify once more:
“Yet Jesus didn’t say to him that he wouldn’t die.”
Dear family,
think about it.
Even among the apostles,
a word the Lord Himself had spoken
could be distorted in the telling,
how much more so among us today.
It is like the telephone game we played as children.
The first person whispers a complete sentence into an ear;
by the fifth person,
the meaning is still there.
By the fifteenth person,
it is unrecognizable.
No one means to lie.
Each person just “passes on what he heard.”
But with every retelling,
a little context is lost
and a little guesswork is added.
In the end,
everyone is talking about a word the Lord never said.
So here are two very practical reminders.
First,
do not pass on what you have not verified.
When you hear something about a brother or sister,
pause first.
Did I hear it with my own ears?
Do I know the context?
If I pass it on,
will it help someone,
or hurt someone?
The 321 principles say:
people matter more than things,
relationships matter more than possessions.
Do not hurt people for the sake of a matter.
Many broken relationships
are not caused by anyone doing evil;
they are caused by someone saying one word too many.
Second,
do not replace the Lord’s words with other people’s words.
The saying that went around among the brothers
sounded very spiritual,
and those who heard it took it very seriously,
but it was not what the Lord said.
We too easily do the same today:
we hear a message passed on by someone,
a testimony,
a so-called “God told me,”
and take it as what the Lord said to me.
The Lord’s standard is only one,
the Bible.
The 321 principles say:
the Bible is my standard.
Whatever cannot return to the Lord’s own words
should be gently set down.
Light from the 321 principles—focus on Jesus, not on self, not on others, not on circumstances
This passage today
is the most direct source of this principle.
Peter’s one sentence, “What about this man?”
exposed all three wrong focuses.
He looked at himself:
why is my road so hard?
He looked at others:
what makes him different from me?
He looked at circumstances:
what will happen in the future?
The Lord’s answer was a single sentence:
Follow me.
Not “Don’t think too much.”
Not “Think positively.”
But “You follow Me.”
What the Lord gave was not a doctrine,
but a direction.
And this is exactly what the 321 principles say:
rely on the Spirit with the heart,
not on yourself with the head.
The person who uses the head
keeps calculating:
how others are doing,
how I am doing,
how the future will go.
In the end of all that calculating,
only worry is left.
The person who uses the heart
is sure of only one thing:
the Lord is ahead,
and I follow.
When the heart stays on the focus,
peace follows.
Because joy has never come from comparing;
joy comes from following.
The one who compares
has eyes that are always turning.
The one who follows
has eyes with only one direction.
That direction
is Jesus.
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, the time we are most prone to comparing is after receiving grace. As soon as the Lord entrusts us with a charge, the “self” wants to find someone to measure against.
Second, comparison is the killer of joy. Looking at other people’s roads makes me lose gratitude for the road the Lord has measured for me.
Third, “What is that to you?” is a release from the Lord. I do not have to be responsible for anyone else’s lessons, nor use anyone else as a ruler to measure myself.
Fourth, the disciple’s place is behind the Lord, not beside other people. The moment we start looking left and right, our steps fall into disorder.
Fifth, do not pass on what you have not verified, and do not replace the Lord’s words with other people’s words. The Bible is my only standard.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for shining through today’s passage on the truest condition inside us. Lord, we confess that as soon as we receive a charge we often turn around to look at others; we measure our gifts by other people’s gifts and our road by other people’s roads, and as a result we lose both gratitude and joy. Forgive us. Thank You for the words You spoke to Peter, “What is that to you? Follow me,” and for saying the same to us. Draw our eyes back from ourselves, from others, and from circumstances, to fix them on You alone. Help us walk in peace the road You have tailored for us, without envy, without complaint, without comparison. Guard our tongues too, that we would not pass on what has not been verified, nor hurt a person over a matter, but in all things return to Your Word as our standard. May we follow You to the very end, giving all the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. Is there someone lately whom you often find yourself comparing with? If the Lord said to you today, “What is that to you? Follow me,” what would you need to lay down?
2\. Among the words you heard and passed on this week, is there one you never actually verified? How will you deal with it?

v: This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.
There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.
b: We have come to the last two verses of the Gospel of John.
From “In the beginning was the Word,”
all the way through the wedding at Cana,
the conversation by Jacob’s well,
the paralyzed man by the pool of Bethesda,
the tomb of Lazarus,
the foot-washing in the upper room,
the dark night at Gethsemane,
the cross at Golgotha,
the morning at the empty tomb,
until the fire of coals by the Sea of Tiberias.
Now,
the writer is about to lay down his pen.
He did not write a splendid conclusion.
He wrote only two quiet sentences.
One was:
My testimony is true.
The other was:
what I have written
is in fact far from enough.
These two sentences
are his way of saying goodbye to us.
1. All his life he called himself by only one name: the disciple whom the Lord loved
Verse 24
begins by saying:
“This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things.”
Notice these words:
this is the disciple.
Right up to the last verse of the whole book,
the author still does not write his own name.
In the whole Gospel of John,
from chapter one to chapter twenty-one,
the name “John”
never once appears for himself.
He calls himself only:
“the disciple whom Jesus loved.”
In chapter thirteen he called himself this.
In chapter nineteen, under the cross, he called himself this.
In chapter twenty, running to the empty tomb, he called himself this.
In chapter twenty-one, when he recognized the Lord from the boat,
he still called himself this.
And at the very end,
he still says only:
this is the disciple.
Dear family,
I ask you to pause here.
What kind of person is this?
He was the son of Zebedee.
He was one of the three disciples closest to Jesus.
He had been up the Mount of Transfiguration.
He had entered Jairus’ house.
At the Last Supper,
he leaned close against Jesus’ chest.
He was the one to whom the Lord entrusted His mother from the cross.
He was the first to run to the empty tomb.
He was the first to recognize the Lord by the sea.
By human reckoning,
he had so many titles that could be printed on a business card.
But he wrote not one of them.
He wrote only:
the disciple whom Jesus loved.
We often think
this is humility.
It is not.
It is a kind of knowing.
It is what a person found
when, having grown old and looking back over his whole life,
he found his truest self.
I think of something.
In a family,
if there is one person who especially loves photography,
it is often like this:
dozens of photo albums in the house,
every photo taken by him,
every smile captured by him,
yet if you flip through all the albums,
you can hardly find him in them.
He spent his whole life behind the lens.
Because what he cared about
was not whether he was in the picture,
but whether the people he loved were well preserved.
John is that one standing behind the lens.
He spent the strength of a lifetime
to let us see clearly the face of Jesus.
He himself
stepped back behind the lens.
This is exactly what the 321 principles keep saying:
the old self’s life of self
always wants to put itself in the picture.
Wants to be seen.
Wants to be remembered.
Wants to leave its own name
in other people’s stories.
The new self’s life of self-denial
is content to step back,
and it is enough that the Lord is seen.
And at a deeper level:
when a person no longer knows himself by his titles,
he finds the most solid identity instead.
Because titles expire.
Positions are handed over.
Abilities decline.
Fame is forgotten.
But being “loved by the Lord”
does not expire.
Dear family,
if someone asks you today:
Who are you?
How will you answer?
You may name your job,
your status,
your post of service in the church,
whose father you are,
whose mother,
whose child.
All of these are true.
But all of these change.
Only one answer never changes:
I am the one whom the Lord loves.
This was John’s self-understanding for a lifetime.
I hope
it will become your and my self-understanding for a lifetime too.
2. “His testimony is true”—faith stands on facts, not on ideas
The second half of verse 24:
“and we know that his witness is true.”
This sentence uses a very important word:
testimony.
Testimony is not opinion.
Testimony is not impression.
Testimony is not inference.
Testimony is:
I was there.
I saw.
I heard.
I tell exactly
what I saw.
Under the Jewish law,
testimony was a most serious matter.
The law required
that testimony be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses.
False testimony was a capital offense.
For a person to stand up and say “I testify”
was to stake his own life on it.
When John wrote this book,
he was already a very old man.
Most of the apostles of his generation
had already been martyred for the Lord.
The things he had seen with his own eyes
were already sixty years in the past.
Yet he still said:
I testify.
And the people of the church together said:
we know that his testimony is true.
Dear family,
this is something very distinctive about the Christian faith.
Christianity is not a philosophy.
Philosophy is someone sitting down to think,
thinking out a system of ideas,
and then asking others to accept it.
Christianity did not come about like that.
Christianity is a group of people
who, because they saw,
because they heard,
because they touched,
could not help but speak.
In Acts 4:20,
Peter and John said to the council:
“For we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.”
Not “we dare not keep silent.”
“We cannot keep silent.”
John opens his letter the same way:
“That which was from the beginning, that which we have heard, that which we have seen with our eyes, that which we saw, and our hands touched, concerning the Word of life.”
(1 John 1:1)
Heard,
seen,
looked upon,
touched.
Four verbs,
each more concrete than the last.
Our faith
is not built on a beautiful idea.
It is built on something that really happened.
A man who really died
really rose again.
If this were false,
our faith would be in vain.
But if this is true,
then there is nothing in the world
more worthy of a lifetime’s response.
This is exactly the second foundation of 321:
the Bible is my standard.
The reason a standard can be a standard
is that it is reliable.
It is reliable
because it stands on facts.
If the Bible were only the religious feelings of a few people,
then I could listen when I was in a good mood
and ignore it when I was in a bad mood.
But if the Bible is a company of witnesses
who testified with their lives to what they saw,
then it becomes a lamp to my feet
and a light on my path for a lifetime.
Dear family,
there is one more thing worth thinking about.
John is the one who “wrote these things,”
and also the one who “testifies.”
In him, these two are one and the same.
He was not writing someone else’s story.
He was writing down
what he himself had experienced.
It is the same for us today.
You and I do not need to become theologians.
But you and I can all become witnesses.
You do not need to be able to explain everything.
You only need to say honestly:
I used to be that kind of person,
the Lord did this in me,
and now I am this kind of person.
The blind man said it best:
one thing I know,
that though I was blind,
now I see.
That is testimony.
And testimony
cannot be refuted by anyone.
3. “The world itself could not contain”—what is written is limited, the Lord’s works are limitless
Verse 25,
the last verse of the whole book:
“There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.”
Reading this sentence,
it is like an old man laying down his pen,
lifting his head,
and drawing a long breath.
He is not saying:
I have finally finished.
He is saying:
I could never finish.
What I have written
is not even a ten-thousandth of it.
I often wonder,
when John wrote this verse,
what rose up in his heart?
Perhaps those mornings that were never written down.
The mornings when the Lord prayed on the mountain.
Perhaps those roads that were never written down.
From Galilee to Jerusalem,
the words the Lord spoke all along the way.
Perhaps those people with no names,
touched by the Lord,
given a single look by the Lord,
and changed for life.
Three and a half years,
more than a thousand sunrises and sunsets,
and John chose only a few things to write down.
Because he had already stated his purpose.
John 20:31:
“But these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing you may have life in his name.”
He did not intend to write a biography.
He meant to lead people to life.
So,
is what the Bible records
enough?
Yes.
Enough for us to be saved.
Enough for us to know Him.
Enough for us to walk in the light all our lives.
I think of a map.
A map,
however detailed,
cannot possibly draw in every tree,
every stone,
every little stream on a piece of land.
If it really tried to draw them all,
the map would have to be as big as the land,
and then no one could unfold it.
But this is not a defect of the map.
This is precisely the grace of the map.
Because the purpose of a map
is never to replace the land,
but to bring you into the land.
Is the map enough to bring you home?
Yes.
Is the land far larger than the map?
Yes.
The Bible is just like this.
What it records
is enough to bring you into the Lord’s presence.
And the Lord’s riches
are far greater than what is recorded.
Dear family,
this verse hides one great comfort.
If the things the Lord did
are too many for the world to contain,
it means this:
the Lord’s work has never stopped.
He worked in the age of the apostles.
He worked through the years when the church was persecuted in every generation.
He worked on the ships where missionaries crossed the seas.
He worked in war,
in famine,
in prison.
He worked in the generation of our grandparents.
Today,
in your life and mine,
He is still working.
That book
has never been closed.
4. Your life is the book still being written
I want to push the previous point one step further.
If the things the Lord did can never be fully written,
then today,
where does He go on writing?
The answer is:
in you and me.
2 Corinthians 3:3 says:
“being made it clear that you are a letter of Christ, served by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tablets of stone, but in tablets that are hearts of flesh.”
You are a letter.
You are a letter the Lord wrote with His own hand.
Not written with ink,
but written with the Holy Spirit.
Not written on paper,
but written on the heart.
And the One who writes
has not yet put down His pen.
Dear family,
I want you to think very concretely about one thing today.
That step of obedience you took today,
that thing you were not very willing to do
but did anyway according to the Lord’s word,
that is a page the Lord wrote in you.
That time you forgave today,
that person you had thought about for so long,
had been stirred up about for so long,
and finally decided to let go,
that is a page the Lord wrote in you.
That time you stood firm today,
in a place where no one saw,
in a place where you could have compromised but did not,
that is a page the Lord wrote in you.
These things
will not make the news.
They will not be written into any book.
Perhaps even those closest to you do not know.
But they have been written down.
Written in heaven.
We often think
that the Lord’s great works are all in the Bible,
all long, long ago,
all in other people.
That is not so.
The newest page the Lord is writing today
is written on an ordinary person.
Written on a mother who rises in the morning
and prays quietly in the kitchen.
Written on a brother in the workplace
who decides to tell the truth.
Written on a sister who has cared for a sick family member
and has already cared for ten years.
Written on a person who often feels useless
yet still opens the Bible every day.
The 321 principles say:
accompany every person to become an overcomer.
Why accompany “every person”?
Because in God’s eyes,
no one’s page is dispensable.
Every person’s life
is a chapter the Lord is still writing.
Your chapter
has not been finished.
So do not draw conclusions about yourself too early.
Do not say:
this is all I will ever be.
Do not say:
I have no chance anymore.
On the night Peter denied the Lord three times,
if the Gospel of John had stopped at chapter eighteen,
Peter would forever be the failure.
But the Lord did not stop writing.
The Lord wrote all the way to chapter twenty-one,
to the fire of coals by the sea,
to the three “Do you love me?”s,
and restored Peter completely.
The Lord has not put down His pen
in you either.
5. Looking back at this book: from “In the beginning was the Word” to a breakfast on the shore
Dear family,
we have walked through the Gospel of John together.
Before we lay this book down,
let us look back once together.
This book began like this:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
(John 1:1)
How grand.
No time,
no beginning,
no created thing,
only the God who is, who was, and who ever will be.
And this book ended like this:
a fire of coals.
A few fish.
A single sentence, “Come and eat breakfast.”
A failed fisherman
sitting on the sand,
asked by the Lord, one sentence at a time:
Do you love Me?
Do you see it?
From a grandeur before the creation of the world,
all the way down into a single person’s heart.
From “the Word was God”
down to “Come and eat breakfast.”
Dear family,
this is the shape of the gospel.
God’s great history
unfolds for the sake of a person’s small story.
He created heaven and earth,
He established time,
He sent His Son,
He made the Word become flesh,
He went to the cross,
He rose from the dead—
all of this grandeur,
where does it finally land?
It lands on a man who once fell
being raised up again.
It lands on one sentence:
Follow Me.
Let us look once more at the framework of the whole book.
The Gospel of John first tells “who He is.”
I am the bread of life.
I am the light of the world.
I am the door of the sheep.
I am the good shepherd.
In me is the resurrection and the life.
I am the way, the truth, and the life.
I am the true vine.
One sentence at a time,
He reveals Himself.
Then the Gospel of John tells “what He did for us.”
The cross.
That word, “It is finished.”
The empty tomb.
That morning when He said “Mary.”
Those hands shown to Thomas.
Finally,
the Gospel of John tells “how He wants us to follow.”
Feed My sheep.
Follow Me.
Who He is.
What He did for us.
How He wants us to follow.
These three steps
are the order of faith for every one of us.
They cannot be reversed.
Only after knowing who He is
will we understand how great what He did is.
Only after understanding how great what He did is
will we be willing to follow.
If we skip the first two steps
and talk directly about following,
it becomes a heavy burden.
But if we truly know who He is
and truly receive what He did,
then following is not a burden;
it is a response.
Light from the 321 principles—one purpose: building God’s system
Dear family,
on this last day of the Gospel of John,
I want to bring the whole picture of 321
to a close once more, here.
What John did with his whole life
was one thing:
to place Jesus, whole, into the hands of those who come after.
This is exactly the one purpose of 321:
building God’s system.
What is God’s system?
It is not a set of regulations.
It is not an organization.
It is a group of people
filled with the Lord’s life,
who then pass that life on to the next group.
This is what John did.
What he saw,
he wrote down
and handed on to us.
And this system
stands on three foundations.
The first foundation: Jesus is my example.
The whole Gospel of John
sets this Example whole before our eyes.
How He loved people,
how He spoke the truth,
how He washed the disciples’ feet,
how on the last night He still comforted others,
how on the cross He still cared for His mother,
how after the resurrection
the first thing He did was prepare breakfast for His failed disciple.
An example is not a theory.
An example is a life that has been lived.
The second foundation: the Bible is my standard.
Today’s passage speaks of exactly this.
“His testimony is true.”
The book in our hands
is not legend;
it is testimony.
That is why it can be the standard.
The third foundation: the Holy Spirit is my guide.
In John chapters fourteen to sixteen,
the Lord promised again and again that the Comforter would come,
to guide us into all the truth.
The written word has an ending,
but the Spirit’s guidance does not stop.
Using the word already written,
He guides us day by day along roads we have not yet walked.
And these three foundations
bring forth two cores.
The first core: let Jesus be King.
That sentence by the sea, “Follow me,”
is letting Jesus be King.
Kingship is not a slogan.
Kingship means:
He decides, I obey.
He leads the way, I follow.
The second core: let Jesus have all the glory.
This is how John wrote the whole book.
He did not write his own name.
He cast every ray of light on Jesus.
He stepped back behind the lens.
Three foundations,
two cores,
one purpose.
And where does this purpose end?
In accompanying every person to become an overcomer,
in building God’s system,
in entering the great revival of the last days,
in welcoming the Lord Jesus’ return.
The Gospel of John is finished.
But that book that “the world itself could not contain”
is still being written.
It will be written until the day the Lord returns.
On that day,
everything that was never written down
will be revealed.
Everything done in secret
will be rewarded.
Every tear shed in silence
will be wiped away.
Our Response in Life
This passage reminds us:
First, the best identity is not a title, but “the one whom the Lord loves.” John never wrote his own name all his life, claiming only one identity.
Second, faith stands on testimony, and testimony stands on facts. What we believe is not a set of ideas, but something that really happened.
Third, what the Bible records is enough for us to be saved, yet the Lord’s works are far greater than what is recorded. A map is enough to bring you home, yet the land is far vaster than the map.
Fourth, your life is the book still being written. Today’s act of obedience, act of forgiveness, and standing firm are each a page the Lord has written.
Fifth, God’s great history unfolds for the sake of a person’s small story. From “In the beginning was the Word,” all the way down to a breakfast on the shore.
Pray Together

Dear Heavenly Father, we have walked through the Gospel of John together with You. Thank You that through John’s pen You have set the face of Your Son before our eyes, page by page. Lord, we see that writer who never wrote his own name all his life, claiming only one identity—the disciple You loved. Let our hearts rest in this identity too, no longer defining ourselves by other people’s opinions or by our own achievements. Thank You that Your Word is true and trustworthy, the standard for our whole lives; thank You that Your works are too many for the world to contain, and that even to this day they have not stopped. In each one of us, go on writing the page You want to write; let every act of obedience, every act of forgiveness, every time of standing firm become a witness to Your glory. Cause us to accompany one another in Your system and be overcomers together, until the day You return. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, Amen.
q: 1\. If someone asked you today, “Who are you?”, apart from all your titles and roles, could you say with a settled heart, “I am the one whom the Lord loves”? What is holding you back?
2\. This week, what page does the Lord want to write in the book of your life? Is it an act of obedience, an act of forgiveness, or a time of standing firm? Are you willing to let Him keep writing?

v: The first book I wrote, Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began both to do and to teach,
until the day in which he was received up, after he had given commandment through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
To these he also showed himself alive after he suffered, by many proofs, appearing to them over a period of forty days, and speaking about God’s Kingdom.
Being assembled together with them, he commanded them, “Don’t depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which you heard from me.
For John indeed baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”
b: In the last devotion, John laid down his pen and said that what he had written fell far short, for the things the Lord did were more than the world itself could hold. The moment the pen was set down, we almost thought the story was over.

It was not. Another writer immediately took it up. Luke’s very first sentence tells us that the earlier book recorded only “all that Jesus began both to do and to teach.” The Gospels are not the ending but the prologue; the cross and the empty tomb are not a full stop but a starting line.
I. “I wrote the first book”—The Four Gospels Were Only the “Beginning”
Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke; that was the “first book.” He says it recorded what Jesus “began” to do and to teach.

This word “began” is crucial. If the first book was the beginning, then this book is the continuation—and the subject of the continuation is still Jesus. The book of Acts is often called “the Acts of the Apostles,” but it is even more “the acts of the risen Lord, continuing through the Holy Spirit.” It is He who stood up and preached through Peter, He who sent Philip into the desert, and He who shone His light on Saul on the road to Damascus.
• The Lord has not retired: His ascension was not a resignation but a change in the way He works—from being bodily among the disciples to being, by the Spirit, within them.
