Peter said to them, “Repent, and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
For the promise is to you, and to your children, and to all who are far off, even as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.”
With many other words he testified, and exhorted them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation!”
Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.
b: In the last devotion, Peter’s sermon stopped at one declaration: “this Jesus whom you crucified, God has made both Lord and Christ.” At that point Peter did not add another word.

What happened next was not done by Peter; it was done by that sentence. Those who had cried out “Crucify him!” before Pilate fifty days earlier were very likely this same crowd; today they discovered that the One they had nailed up with their own hands was the Lord God had appointed. This passage records everything that happened after one true word fell into human hearts.
I. “They were cut to the heart”—The First Sign of Truth Entering a Person

“Cut to the heart” is a painful word in the original, meaning to be pierced through, stabbed, as if a sharp blade had gone in. It was not the stirring of having heard a good sermon; it was the pain of being struck at the vital point.

Peter did not comfort them; he laid the fact straight out: you crucified, and God has made Him Lord. That sentence left no way of retreat, and all their excuses fell before it. So they asked, “Brothers, what shall we do?”

Notice the direction of the question. They did not ask “How do you explain this?” or “By what authority do you say this?” They asked “What shall we do?” The first sign of truth entering a person is that the question changes from “What does this mean?” to “What shall I do?”
• Being cut to the heart is grace: without pain people will not turn back; God lets people hurt first so that they may be healed.
• The direction of listening: those who hear the word and still critique the speaker have the word still outside; those who hear and begin to ask “What shall I do?” have the word already within.
II. “Repent”—Not a Change of Mood, but a Turn Around
The first word of Peter’s answer was “repent.” In the original this means “a change of mind,” not merely feeling remorse, but the whole person’s direction turning around.

Anyone who drives understands the difference. When you take a wrong road, the navigation does not say, “Please adjust your mood and keep going”; it says, “Make a U-turn.” Remorse is sitting sadly on the wrong road; repentance is turning the car around. The people were already cut to the heart, but Peter said that was not enough: you must turn.

“Each of you” must not be skipped either. Three thousand were cut to the heart together, but repentance has no group ticket; each person must turn for himself. Change starts with me, and no one can turn around for me. And “be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” is the public declaration of this turning: fifty days earlier they had publicly rejected Him; today they publicly joined themselves to His name.
• Remorse and repentance are different: one is grieving on the wrong road, the other is turning the car around.
• Each one turns for himself: three thousand were cut to the heart together, yet they repent one by one.
III. “For the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit”—First Unloaded, Then Filled
In the second half of verse 38, Peter named two gifts that follow repentance: forgiveness of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

The order matters. First the forgiveness of sins, then the Holy Spirit. God first takes the sin off, then puts Himself in. This is also the entrance of “the Holy Spirit is my guide”—the Spirit is not a prize for the spiritual elite but a promise to everyone who repents.

Verse 39 widens the scope still more: the promise is for you, for your children, and for all who are far off. “Those far off” was an unfamiliar phrase in Jewish ears; it referred to the Gentiles (Eph. 2:13, “you who once were far off are made near in the blood of Christ”). Peter himself probably did not yet grasp how far that went; only when he entered Cornelius’ house in chapter 10 did he truly understand.

The last line is the key: “as many as the Lord our God will call to himself.” However wide the promise, the subject is still God—He is the One who calls. Salvation, from beginning to end, is God’s initiative, and people only respond.
• Unload first, then load: forgiveness first, the Spirit after; a vessel that has not been emptied cannot hold Him.
• The promise reaches farther than we think: those God calls far exceed the circle we draw.
IV. “Save yourselves from this crooked generation”—Not Moving Away, but No Longer Being Shaped by It
Verse 40 says Peter “testified with many other words, and exhorted them,” and Luke keeps only a one-line summary: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.”

The word “crooked” shares its root with the medical term for scoliosis—a bone that should be straight grown bent. Peter was using Moses’ words (Deut. 32:5, “a perverse and crooked generation”). A generation is crooked not because there are no good people in it, but because the whole generation’s shape is bent: centered on self, measuring everything by the self.

“Save yourselves” does not mean “move away.” After their baptism, not one of the three thousand left Jerusalem to live as a hermit; they lived in the same city and did the same work. To be saved from it means no longer being shaped by this generation—no longer measuring yourself by its ruler, no longer living on its applause.

The old self’s life of self is a miniature of this crooked generation: everything centered on me. To be saved from this generation is really to be saved from the bent self within; in daily life it looks like this: when someone else is promoted and I am not, I can still be truly glad for him.
• Crooked is a shape, not a place: the problem is not where you live but what shapes you.
• Deliverance begins inside: the generation’s bend is first straightened within me.
V. “That day there were added about three thousand souls”—“Added,” Not “Recruited”
Verse 41: “Those who received his word were baptized.” There was only one condition: receiving. Not everyone who heard was baptized, but those who received.

Then Luke records the number: from the hundred and twenty in the upper room to about three thousand added in one day. But notice the verb—“added.” Peter did not recruit them; they were added; verse 47 will make the subject clear: “The Lord added to them day by day those who were being saved.”

This is just what building God’s system looks like. It is not people designing an organizational structure and then recruiting to fill it; it is a group who let Jesus be King, to whom God adds people. The people’s responsibility is to speak the truth and bear witness; the adding is the Lord’s.
• Receive, then be baptized: many heard; those who received went in.
• The adding is the Lord’s work: we are responsible for faithfulness; the numbers belong to the Lord.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Being Cut to the Heart Is the Starting Point of Self-Denial
These five verses carry a clear thread: cut to the heart, repentance, forgiveness, the Spirit, saved from the generation, added by the Lord.

The starting point is being cut to the heart. One true word comes in and pierces the self within that has been defending itself all along. The old self’s greatest skill is explaining itself, and at the moment of being cut to the heart, the explaining stops. When a person no longer speaks for himself but asks only, “What shall I do?”, the throne in his heart has already begun to loosen.

Repentance, in the end, is returning to one’s proper place: letting God be God and man be man. Pride is leaving one’s place and wanting to take God’s; repentance is admitting I have put myself in the wrong place and giving that seat back. In daily life it looks like this: when someone points out your mistake, you no longer first think, “Who is he to say that?” but first ask, “Lord, is this true?”

Self-denial is not loss but entering the limitless—the three thousand laid down self and received forgiveness of sins and the Spirit of God, and were brought into a system the Lord Himself added to. What they lost was a crooked generation; what they gained was the kingdom of God.
a: Let the Word Pierce You
Hearing a sermon is not critiquing the speaker but asking, “What shall I do?”
Turn Around, Not Just Regret
Grieving on the wrong road does no good; each must turn his own car around.
Empty First, Then Receive
Forgiveness first, the Spirit after; let the Lord unload you first, and you can be filled with Him.
Deliverance Is Not Moving House
Don’t be shaped by the crooked generation; first straighten the self within.
Be Faithful Without Claiming Credit
We are responsible for speaking truth; the adding we leave to the Lord.
q: The last time you heard a sermon or read Scripture, was your reaction “Was that well said?” or “What shall I do?” Is there a word that has already cut you to the heart, yet you have never turned the car around?

The ruler of a “crooked generation” is centered on self. Is there something today for which you still use that ruler to measure yourself or others? Are you willing to let the Lord first straighten that stretch inside you?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that one true word can pierce a heart. Thank You for not letting us live comfortably in self-defense, but cutting us to the heart with Your word, making us stop and ask, “What shall we do?” We confess that we often feel remorse without repenting, grieving on the wrong road yet unwilling to turn the car around.
Lord Jesus, cut us to the heart again today. Pierce the self within us that is always explaining itself, so that each of us returns to our place, letting You be God and us be human. Forgive our sins, and fill these emptied vessels with Your Spirit; save us from this crooked generation, and let us no longer measure ourselves by its ruler. And add to Your church those whom You call, so that we need only be faithful in witness, and the numbers and the glory belong to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God, and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.
b: In the last devotion, three thousand were baptized in one day and added by the Lord to the disciples. The number is astonishing, but numbers are not what Luke wants to emphasize. In the next six verses he records how those three thousand lived after their baptism.

If verse 41 is the birth, verses 42 to 47 are the daily life of this new life. Luke does not record how many meetings they held or what rules they drew up; he records a few small things a group of people did every day—listening to the teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, prayer, sharing, eating, praising. The first church had no building and no institutions, yet it had life.
I. “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching”—First Set the Standard, Then Everything Else

Verse 42 lists four things, the first of which is the apostles’ teaching. “Continued steadfastly” is a word with strength in it in the original, meaning to hold on without letting go and devote oneself wholeheartedly; the same word is used in chapter 1 to describe the disciples “continuing with one accord in prayer” (Acts 1:14).

Most of the three thousand were Jews who had come from many places for the feast, and what they knew of Jesus may have been only Peter’s one sermon. So the first thing was to sit down and listen to the apostles tell what Jesus did and taught—this is the content that was later written into the four Gospels. From the start the church put listening to the teaching first, not because there was nothing else to do, but because zeal without a standard goes astray.

Among the three foundations, “the Bible is my standard” is exactly this one. The flames and tongues of Pentecost were stunning, but Luke takes care to tell us that after the stir, what they did every day was hold on to the teaching. Experience ebbs; the standard does not.
• Zeal needs a track: experience without teaching is like water without a riverbed, flowing for a while and then dispersing.
• Steadfastness is not once: the word means holding on, every day.
II. “The fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers”—Putting Lives Together

The last three things in verse 42: fellowship, breaking bread, and prayers. The original word for “fellowship” means “sharing in common, holding in common”—not just being together, but putting lives together.

Breaking bread was at once remembering the Lord’s supper and truly eating together (verse 46 says “breaking bread at home” and “took their food”). “Prayers” is plural in the original, referring to set times of prayer—at the opening of chapter 3, Peter and John went up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.

A piece of coal in the fire keeps burning; take it out and set it aside alone, and before long it goes cold. It isn’t that the coal itself is bad; it has left the fire. The Christian life was never designed to burn alone. “People matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things”—in the early church this looked like spending most of their time together listening to the teaching, eating together, and praying together.
• Fellowship is holding in common: not a handshake at a meeting, but handing over a part of your life.
• A coal away from the fire goes cold: don’t overestimate how long you can burn alone.
III. “Fear came on every soul”—Reverence Is the Air in the System
Verse 43: “Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.” The “fear” here is not terror but reverence—the trembling awareness that God is truly here.

The wonders and signs were not for excitement; God Himself was confirming the word the apostles preached; and the people’s response was not excited onlooking but reverence. In God’s system the air should be reverence, not excitement. With reverence, people dare not carry on their own business within it; without reverence, even many miracles are just performance.
• Reverence is protection: knowing that God is truly present, the self dares not run wild.
• Miracles point to God: not to the one who performs them, nor to those who watch.
IV. “Had all things common”—Relationships Matter More Than Things
Verses 44 and 45: all who believed were together and had all things in common; and they sold their possessions and goods and distributed them to all, according to each one’s need.

Let it be clear first: this was not a system. The verbs in the original are continuous—“kept selling,” not a one-time liquidation and confiscation; and the case of Ananias in chapter 5 shows that property remained each person’s own (Acts 5:4, “While it remained, didn’t it remain your own?”). It was voluntary, done when a need was seen. Many of the three thousand were from out of town, staying in Jerusalem to hear the teaching, with food and lodging a problem, so those who owned property sold it to provide.

What we see here is a group who put “things” after “people.” The old self’s life of self first grasps its own things—my money, my land, my rights. These people’s hands loosened. Self-denial here looks simple: when a brother has a need, I bring out what I have, and I don’t keep a record of it.
• Not a system but a life: no one required it of them; they were willing themselves.
• The sign of an open hand: things take their place behind people.
V. “Continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home”—Temple and Home

Verses 46 and 47 are the summary picture of this passage. “Daily”—not only on the Sabbath; “with one accord”—literally one mind; “in the temple”—public worship and witness; “at home”—private bread-breaking and meals.

“With gladness and singleness of heart” took their food—the word “singleness” in the original means “simple, without stones,” originally describing a level field with no stones in it. When they ate, there were no stones in their hearts—no scheming, no comparing, no guardedness. Then “praising God and having favor with all the people”; outsiders saw them and found them lovable.
The last line is the key to the whole passage: “The Lord added to them day by day those who were being saved.” People are responsible for living such a life; the adding is the Lord’s doing.
• Both temple and home: public gatherings without private fellowship are empty; a small circle without public witness is closed.
• The Lord adds: church growth is not a method but what God does among people emptied of self.
The Light of the 321 Principles: What God’s System Looks Like
These six verses are the earliest and clearest picture of “building God’s system.”

A system is not an organizational structure. Luke records no rules, titles, or departments; he records four things they held on to—teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, prayers—and the life of a group of people day by day in the temple and at home. God’s system is a realm formed by people who let Jesus be King; with Jesus as King, here it looks like this: the standard is in His word, possessions are yielded to those in need, and there are no stones in the heart.

And the order is clear: first life, then relationships, then ministry. They first received forgiveness and the Spirit, then fellowship with one another and bread-breaking at home, and then miracles, witness, and addition followed naturally. Today we often reverse it: do ministry first, strain to maintain relationships for the sake of ministry, and finally discover life has long been empty. Self-denial brings unity; the three thousand were of one accord not because their personalities were alike, but because each had laid down the self.
a: Hold On to the Teaching
Experience ebbs; returning daily to God’s word keeps you steady.
Put Lives Together
Don’t overestimate how long you can burn alone; return to the fire.
Hold Reverence
Knowing God is truly present, we dare not do our own thing in His house.
Let Things Come After People
When a brother has a need, can my hand loosen?
Leave No Stones in the Heart
When eating with family and brothers and sisters, remove scheming and comparing.
q: Teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, prayer—of these four, which one is your grip loosest on right now? What made you loosen your hand?
Is there something you would hesitate to bring out when a brother or sister is in need? Behind that hesitation, what is your self guarding?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us see what the first church looked like—no building, no institutions, yet real life. Thank You that Your system has never been held up by structure, but formed by people who laid down self and let Jesus be King.
Lord, we confess that we often reverse the order: busy with ministry first, then straining at relationships, and finally finding life empty. Bring us back to the beginning, to hold on to Your word every day, to put our lives together with our brothers and sisters, to hold reverence in Your house, and to let things take their place behind people. Remove the stones from our hearts, so that when we eat together it is with gladness and simplicity. And according to Your promise, add to Your church day by day those who are being saved, and all the glory be Yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Peter and John were going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour.

A certain man who was lame from his mother’s womb was being carried, whom they laid daily at the door of the temple which is called Beautiful, to ask gifts for the needy of those who entered into the temple.
Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive gifts for the needy.
Peter, fastening his eyes on him, with John, said, “Look at us.”
He listened to them, expecting to receive something from them.
But Peter said, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!”
He took him by the right hand and raised him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength.
Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God.
All the people saw him walking and praising God.
They recognized him, that it was he who used to sit begging for gifts for the needy at the Beautiful Gate of the temple. They were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
b: In the last devotion, Luke set before us the daily life of the first church: day by day in the temple and at home, with the Lord adding to them those being saved. At the opening of chapter 3, the camera moves from a great crowd to two people—Peter and John—and a man who had never stood up.

This is the first miracle recorded in detail in Acts. Chapter 2 says “many wonders and signs were done through the apostles,” and Luke does not list them one by one; he picks only this one to describe in detail. For this one is not only a healing; it brings out Peter’s second sermon, the Sanhedrin’s first persecution, and the first storm of the Jerusalem church. And the story begins with just two people going to pray.
I. “Peter and John were going up into the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour”—The Miracle Happens on an Ordinary Road

“The ninth hour” is three in the afternoon, the time of the evening sacrifice at the temple, and one of the three daily times of prayer for the Jews (Ps. 55:17, “Evening, morning, and at noon, I will cry out in distress”). Pentecost had passed and the Holy Spirit had come, yet Peter and John still went up to the temple at the set hour to pray, as was the Jewish custom.

They were not going to perform a miracle; they were going to pray. This matters. The miracle was not an item on their schedule; it happened within their obedient routine. A person who expects God only in special meetings but goes his own way in the ordinary three o’clock of every day will probably miss most of what God wants to do.
• Ordinary obedience is the road of miracles: miracles are not on the schedule, but they are on the road of obedience.
• Two went together: Peter and John went together; the Spirit’s leading often comes to those who walk together, not those who go it alone.
II. “Lame from his mother’s womb, carried daily”—The Most Beautiful Gate, the Man Who Could Not Move

Verse 2 introduces this man: lame from birth, and chapter 4 tells us he was more than forty years old (Acts 4:22). For more than forty years his routine had been to be carried, set down, hold out his hand, and be carried away.

He was set at the “Beautiful gate.” This gate is generally thought to be the Nicanor Gate leading to the Court of the Women, made of Corinthian bronze and more splendid than gold-plated gates. At the most beautiful gate of the temple sat a man who could least move. This contrast was deliberately kept by Luke: outward beauty cannot hide the inward lack.

Verse 3 says that seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he “asked to receive gifts for the needy.” His hope was just that big—a few coins. It was not that he did not try hard enough; he had never seen any other possibility. For more than forty years, he had learned to ask only for what he could get.
• The Beautiful Gate and the lame man: however splendid the system on the outside, if the people within cannot stand, it is still lacking.
• Hope too small: when people grow used to lack, even what they ask for shrinks.
III. “Look at us!”—First Lift Your Head, Then the Rest

Verses 4 and 5 contain a very fine movement. “Fastening his eyes” is a word of intent gazing in the original; Luke later uses the same word of Stephen “gazing into heaven” (Acts 7:55). Peter and John looked intently at him, and then Peter said, “Look at us!”

A beggar usually does not look at faces, only at hands; he is used to keeping his head down, waiting for money to fall in. Peter wanted him first to lift his head. Verse 5 says, “He listened to them, expecting to receive something from them”—he lifted his head, but his expectation was still money.

Our prayers are often like this too. Head down, asking the Lord for a handout, hoping to get something, yet our eyes do not truly look at Him. The Lord wants us to lift our heads first—first with God, then with self, then with people, then with matters. If the order of relationships is reversed, at most we receive a few coins.
• Look first, then ask: lifting your head to look at the Lord matters more than stretching out your hand.
• Aim the expectation right: he hoped for money, and God had prepared legs; what we hope for is often too small as well.
IV. “Silver and gold have I none, but what I have, I give you”—The One with an Empty Pocket Gives the Most Precious Thing
Verse 6 is the heart of the passage. Peter said: Silver and gold have I none, but what I have, I give you—in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk.

Peter’s pocket was empty, but he had a name. “Jesus Christ of Nazareth”—Nazareth was a small, despised place, yet this name is on the throne. Peter did not say “I tell you to rise”; he said, “In the name of … rise up.” The power was not in Peter but in that name.

A little child asks his father for a piece of candy. The father does not give candy but picks him up, takes him home, and sits him down to a hot meal. The child wanted candy, the father gave a meal; the child asked for the moment, the father gave for a lifetime. What the man asked for was a handout; what God gave him was a pair of legs.

In verse 7, Peter “took him by the right hand, and raised him up.” He did not just stand at a distance and declare; he reached out and pulled. Then Luke used a doctor’s technical words: “his feet and ankle bones received strength”—medical terms, with which Luke tells us this was no psychological effect; the bones were truly made whole.
• Without silver and gold you can still give: the most precious things were never in the pocket.
• The name is on the throne: the power is not in the one who delivers it, but in that name.
• Declaration plus a hand: Peter spoke and also pulled; faith is not only talk without action.
V. “Walking, leaping, and praising God”—He Entered the Temple for the First Time

The verbs in verse 8 come in a rush: leaping up, stood, walked, entered the temple, walking, leaping, praising God. A man who had not stood for more than forty years did not make his first move carefully testing; he leaped. This fulfilled Isaiah’s words: “Then the lame man will leap like a deer” (Isa. 35:6).

Note “entered with them into the temple.” This man had sat at the temple gate for more than forty years but had never gone in—he sat outside, only one step from God’s house, but that step he could not cross. Today he not only stood up, he went in. The purpose of healing was not that he could walk, but that he could worship.

In verses 9 and 10, all the people saw him and “recognized him, that it was he who sat for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple.” This line is important: they recognized him. The miracle did not happen to a stranger, but to a man everyone saw every day and walked past every day. Of real change, the most powerful witnesses are those who have always known you.
• Healing is for worship: God makes people stand so that they may go into the temple.
• Astonish those who know you: the most powerful testimony is old acquaintances seeing that you have changed.
The Light of the 321 Principles: No Silver or Gold, but the Name

“Silver and gold have I none”—this line is harder and harder to say in the church today. We have silver and gold, venues, resources, methods, yet we often lack that name that makes people rise up and walk. It is not that the name lacks power; we place our focus on what we have, not on Him.

The focus is on Jesus—not on self, not on others, not on circumstances. Peter’s focus was not on himself for a moment: he did not say “I command you,” he said “in the name of Jesus Christ”; he did not look at his empty pocket, he looked to the Lord seated on the throne. This is what self-denial looks like in ministry—not that you bring out what you have, but that you let Him bring out what He has.

And the man lame from birth lets us see ourselves, too. The old self’s life of self is like him sitting at the Beautiful Gate: outwardly seeming very near to God, yet never truly going in; asking only for the little he could get, not daring to hope for all God wants to give. Self-denial is not having nothing but entering the limitless—he laid down the hope of a few coins and received a pair of legs, a temple, and a life able to praise God.
a: Obey on the Ordinary Road
Miracles are not in special meetings but in the obedience of every three o’clock.
Admit Your Lameness
However near to God’s house outwardly, honestly face the places within that cannot stand.
Lift Your Head Before Your Hand
When praying, first look at the Lord, not only at His hand.
Give That Name
No silver or gold is fine; what matters is whether I have that name on my lips.
Go into the Temple to Worship
Healing is not just for walking, but for praising God.
q: In your recent prayers, have you been asking for a handout with your head down, or looking up to the Lord? Could what you hope for be much smaller than what God has prepared?

“Silver and gold have I none, but what I have, I give you.” If silver, gold, methods, and resources were all taken away, what would you still have to give? Does that name on your lips still carry power?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Your miracles are not on the schedule but on the road of obedience. Thank You for letting two people with empty pockets walk into the temple carrying Your Son’s name, and make a man who had not stood in more than forty years leap up and praise You.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we are often like the man sitting at the Beautiful Gate: only one step from Your house, yet never truly going in; asking only for the little we can get, not daring to hope for all You want to give. Make us lift our heads to look at You, not only at Your hand. Remove our dependence on silver, gold, resources, and methods, and bring our focus back to Your name, for power was never in us but only in You. Make us stand up and go into the temple, walking and leaping and praising You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: As the lame man who was healed held on to Peter and John, all the people ran together to them in the porch that is called Solomon’s, greatly wondering.
When Peter saw it, he responded to the people, “You men of Israel, why do you marvel at this man? Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified his Servant Jesus, whom you delivered up, and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had determined to release him.
But you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you,
and killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead, to which we are witnesses.
By faith in his name, his name has made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.
b: In the last devotion, the man lame from birth walked and leaped into the temple, and the people recognized him and were filled with wonder. The story did not stop there. Verse 11 says he “held on to Peter and John,” and all the people ran together to look.

This is the most dangerous moment for a person in ministry—everyone’s eyes are on you, the one just healed is holding your hand, and all think you are remarkable. Peter stood in this place and opened his mouth. His first words were not to explain the miracle but to turn the crowd’s eyes away from himself.
I. “Why do you fasten your eyes on us?”—Turn the Eyes Away from Yourself

The place in verse 11 is “Solomon’s porch,” a long colonnade on the east side of the temple, where the Lord Jesus had once taught (John 10:23) and where the early church would often gather (Acts 5:12). The people ran there and “fastened their eyes” on Peter and John—in the last devotion Peter fastened his eyes on the lame man; in this one the crowd fastened their eyes on Peter.

Peter’s reaction was two “whys”: Why do you marvel at this? Why do you fasten your eyes on us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made this man walk? “Power” and “godliness” are the two things people most easily credit to themselves—one is gifting, the other spiritual reputation. Peter pushed both away.

A pipe carries water to a home; if the pipe thought the water was its own, that would be the most absurd thing. The pipe’s worth lies in its being empty and open, water flowing through it, not staying in it. Peter knew he was a pipe, so his first act was to point to the source.
• The most dangerous moment for glory: not when you fail, but when you succeed and everyone is watching you.
• The pipe is not the water: power and godliness flow through; they are not mine.
II. “Has glorified his servant Jesus”—What the God of Our Fathers Has Done

In verse 13, Peter drew the people’s eyes to “the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers.” This is the name by which God introduced Himself to Moses in the burning bush (Exod. 3:6), and not one listener was unfamiliar with it. What Peter meant was: this is not a new religion; this is what the God of your fathers has done.

What did He do? “Has glorified his servant Jesus.” The word “servant” is exactly the word used in the Greek Old Testament for “the Lord’s servant” in Isaiah—“Behold, my servant will prosper. He will be exalted and lifted up, and will be very high” (Isa. 52:13). The suffering, despised One who bore everyone’s iniquity—God has glorified Him.

This is “letting Jesus receive all the glory” among the two core principles. It was not Peter’s power that made the man walk; God glorified Jesus, and that glorified name made the man walk. The glory has only one direction: toward Jesus.
• Not a new religion: the God of the fathers, fulfilling what He spoke from ancient times.
• The Servant glorified: the One who denied Himself to the end is the One God has exalted.
III. “But you … denied him”—Three Heavy Contrasts

From the second half of verse 13 to verse 14, Peter pointed straight at the audience with “you,” three times in a row: you delivered him up to Pilate; when Pilate had determined to release him, you denied him in Pilate’s presence; you denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer to be granted to you.

The contrasts here cut deep. The Gentile governor wanted to release; God’s chosen people wanted to kill. What they denied was “the Holy and Righteous One,” and what they wanted was a murderer—Barabbas. Peter did not say “they,” he said “you,” and he did not avoid the fact that among these very people were likely some who had shouted “Crucify him!” that very morning.

Peter dared speak this way not because he himself was blameless. On that same night, beside a charcoal fire, he had denied the Lord three times. He was not accusing from a height; he was a man who had once denied the Lord, speaking to a group who had denied the Lord. The truth must be told, but the one who tells it has no sense of superiority in his heart, because he knows he too is within that “you.”
• Contrast is for seeing clearly: exchanging the Holy and Righteous One for a murderer shows how absurd human choices can be.
• The qualification for speaking truth: not that I have no fault, but that I have been forgiven.
IV. “You killed the Prince of life, whom God raised from the dead”—The Most Absurd Sentence

Verse 15 is the sharpest line of this sermon: “You killed the Prince of life.” “Prince of life” in the original means “originator of life, captain of life, the One who blazes the trail,” and the same word is used in Hebrews to call Jesus “the author of their salvation” (Heb. 2:10) and “the author and perfecter of faith” (Heb. 12:2).

People killed the source of life—a self-contradictory sentence to the extreme. Like sawing off the very branch one is standing on. But the second half turns everything over: “whom God raised from the dead.” Man’s verdict was death; God’s verdict was life; the climax of the last sermon, “whom you crucified, God has made,” appears again here: whom you killed, God raised.
Then Peter added: “of which we are witnesses.” They were not speaking a theory; they were speaking of something they had seen with their own eyes and were prepared to guarantee with their lives.
• People killed the Prince of life: this is the extreme of all pride—wanting to remove the One from whom life comes.
• God’s verdict overturns man’s: even our deepest wrongs include none that God cannot turn around.
V. “By faith in his name”—Even Faith Is Given by Him

Verse 16 closes this passage and brings the sermon back to the lame man: “By faith in his name has his name made this man strong, whom you see and know. Yes, the faith which is through him has given him this perfect soundness in the presence of you all.”

In this verse “name” appears twice and “faith” appears twice. What made the man strong was the name, not Peter; and the faith that enabled one to trust that name was “the faith which is through him.” Peter did not keep even faith for himself—faith is not Peter’s ability but a gift from the Lord. This is self-denial at its furthest: not only is the power not mine, even the believing is not mine.
“Perfect soundness” means “whole, without defect” in the original, the word the Old Testament uses of sacrificial animals “without blemish.” A man born lacking was restored to wholeness by that name.
• The name heals, and faith too is His gift: from beginning to end, nothing is mine.
• Perfect soundness: what He does is not merely making usable, but restoring to wholeness.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Let Jesus Receive All the Glory
From beginning to end these six verses do one thing: take the glory away from Peter and place it on Jesus.

Peter pushed away “power,” pushed away “godliness,” and finally pushed away even “faith”—“the faith which is through him.” The old self’s life of self most wants to keep for itself these three: I can do it, I am spiritual enough, I believe enough. Peter kept none of them. Letting Jesus receive all the glory looks like this in daily life: when others praise you, the first thought in your heart is truly “The Lord did this,” rather than saying “glory to the Lord” with the mouth while quietly keeping it in the heart.

And “You killed the Prince of life” shines a clear light on the true face of pride: pride is wanting to remove the One from whom life comes so that I can be lord. But God raised Him up; human pride is defeated and God’s glory stands. Humility triumphs over pride, and self-denial triumphs over Satan; in this sermon it looks like this: a man who once denied the Lord three times stands today in Solomon’s porch and keeps not a bit of the credit for himself.
a: Turn the Crowd’s Eyes Away
When praised, immediately lead the eyes to the Lord.
Be an Open Pipe
Power and godliness flow through; they do not stay in me.
Speak Truth Without Superiority
I too was once within the “you,” only I was forgiven.
Believe God Can Overturn
However heavy man’s verdict, God’s resurrection can overturn it.
Give Even Faith to Him
Don’t say “I believed enough”; say only “He gave the faith.”
q: The last time someone praised your service or character, what was the first thought in your heart? In that thought, did the glory truly go to the Lord, or did you quietly keep some for yourself?

Peter dared to tell the crowd “You killed the Prince of life” because he knew he too had once denied the Lord. When you need to speak truth to someone, do you stand on a height, or in the position of “I was once like that”?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that You are the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of our fathers, and the God who is still at work today. Thank You for glorifying Your servant Jesus, making the One people denied and killed the Prince of life.
Lord Jesus, we confess that when we are praised, we often say with our mouths “glory to You” while quietly keeping it in our hearts. Remove from us the three things we want to keep for ourselves—my power, my godliness, my faith—so that, like Peter, we keep none of them and are only an open pipe. Help us also to remember that we too were once within the “you” who denied You, so that when we speak truth there is no superiority, only grace. May You receive all the glory, and may Your name in us make people completely whole. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: “Now, brothers, I know that you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers.
But the things which God announced by the mouth of all his prophets, that Christ should suffer, he thus fulfilled.
“Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord,
and that he may send Christ Jesus, who was ordained for you before,
whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke long ago by the mouth of his holy prophets.
b: In the last devotion, Peter said without holding back, “You killed the Prince of life.” If the sermon had stopped there, the crowd would have been left only with despair—what road is left for those who killed the Lord of life?

But Peter’s words turned, and he called out “Brothers.” One sentence earlier it was “You killed”; this sentence was already “Brothers.” These five verses are a road from condemnation to hope: from “ignorance,” to “repent,” to “blotted out,” to “times of refreshing,” to “restoration of all things.” Peter led a group of people who had killed to face the ending God had prepared since the creation of the world.
I. “I know that you did it in ignorance”—A “Brother” After the Condemnation
Verse 17: Peter said, “Now, brothers, I know that you did it in ignorance, as also did your rulers.”

This reminds us of the Lord’s prayer on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Peter had heard those words from a distance back then, and today he made them part of his own sermon. As the Lord left a door open for those who nailed Him, Peter likewise left a door open for these people.

“Ignorance” is not the same as innocence. If ignorance meant innocence, Peter would not have needed to call them to repent in verse 19. “Ignorance” means: this was not the hard heart of sinning knowingly to the end, so there is still a turning point. Under the Old Testament law, there was a sin offering for unintentional sin but none for sin committed defiantly (Num. 15:27–31); Peter was placing them on the side where a way of atonement still remained.

In dealing with others’ offenses, we often do only half: either condemn without leaving a door, or leave a door without condemning. Peter did both—first “you killed,” then “Brothers, you did it in ignorance.” Truth is spoken all the way, and the door is opened all the way.
• Name it first, then leave the door: truth is not discounted, and grace is not discounted.
• Ignorance is not an excuse but a turning point: it does not excuse, but it leaves a road open.
II. “God foretold by the mouth of all his prophets that his Christ should suffer”—Human Evil Fulfilled God’s Plan
Verse 18: “But the things which God announced by the mouth of all his prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled.”

“The Christ should suffer”—that the Messiah would suffer sounded almost contradictory to Jews of that day. The Messiah they hoped for was a triumphant king, not a suffering servant. But the prophets had long said: “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of suffering and acquainted with grief” (Isa. 53:3). The people did not know what they were doing, but God knew; their evil fulfilled God’s word exactly, step by step.

This is entirely consistent with Peter’s tone when speaking of Judas in chapter 1: human evil has never for a moment exceeded God’s control, and God’s sovereignty has never cancelled human responsibility. “You killed” is true, and “God foretold” is true; both stand at once.
• God’s plan does not depend on human goodness: even humanity’s deepest evil God can make accomplish His purpose.
• Suffering was the plan, not an accident: the cross was not a remedy after failure but a decision from the creation of the world.
III. “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out”—Wiped Away, Not Covered Over
The first half of verse 19 is the core action of this passage: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out.”

“Repent” is a turning of the mind, as the previous sermon already said; here “turn again” is added, meaning “turn back, return” in the original, the body’s direction swinging around to walk toward God. Repentance is turning inside; turning again is turning outside; together, the whole person turns around.

“Blotted out” is a very vivid word. Ink on ancient papyrus had no acid and did not bite into the paper; a damp sponge could wipe the writing clean, and the sheet could then be written on again. God says, “I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake; and I will not remember your sins” (Isa. 43:25), using exactly this idea.

This is quite different from how we deal with our own offenses. We are used to “covering”—pasting a new sheet over, so that it cannot be seen from outside, though the writing beneath is still there and will show again when the sheet is lifted. God does not cover; God wipes away. A whiteboard full of writing, once wiped clean, does not merely “look clean”; it is truly clean and can be written on again.
• The whole person turns: repentance is turning inside, turning again is turning outside.
• Wiped away, not covered: God’s forgiveness wipes the writing off; it does not paste a sheet over it.
IV. “Times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord”—A Breath of Air
The second half of verse 19 and verse 20: “that there may come times of refreshing from the face of the Lord, and that he may send Christ Jesus, who was ordained for you before.”

“Refreshing” in the original means “cooling, a breathing space, recovery of strength,” like someone who has walked a long way under a scorching sun finally stepping into shade. Repentance brings not only the blotting out of sin but also a relieved ease—no more propping up, no more covering, no more defending yourself.

And this refreshing comes “from the face of the Lord”; it is not produced by adjusting one’s own mood. Verse 20 pushes the view further into the future: the Lord will send the Christ. This is the first clear mention of the Lord’s return in Acts. The refreshing received by those who repent is partly today and fully in the future.
• Refreshing comes from the Lord’s presence: not self-relaxation, but the Lord Himself giving people room to breathe.
• Part today, the whole in the future: the day of the Lord’s return is the completion of refreshing.
V. “Heaven must receive him until the times of restoration of all things”—He Has Not Gone Far; He Is Waiting
Verse 21: “whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke of by the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old.”

“Heaven must receive him”—after the Lord’s ascension, heaven would keep Him for a time, not because He did not want to come back but because the time had not yet come. “Restoration of all things” in the original means “restoration to the original state, return to the proper place”—all that is broken, deformed, and strayed returned to the form in which God first made it.

This is the direction of the whole Bible. From creation, God through the prophets has been saying the same thing: this world will be returned to its proper place. And the center of this is the Christ; He is kept in heaven for the coming of that day, and for our days in between, to repent and turn, and be prepared to welcome Him.
• Heaven keeps Him, not heaven rejects Him: He is waiting, waiting for all things to return to their proper place.
• Restoration is return to one’s place: not a return to past excitement, but to what God first intended.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Repenting and Turning Is Returning to Our Proper Place

A thread runs through these five verses: repenting and turning is the starting point, restoration of all things is the end; and the two terms point the same direction in the original—“turn back” and “return to the original state.” An individual’s repentance is a miniature of the restoration of all things.

Pride is leaving one’s place and wanting to take God’s; humility is returning to one’s place, letting God be God and man be man. The restoration of all things is the whole creation returning to its place; my own repentance and turning is my own person returning to my place. In daily life it looks simple: I no longer decide for God what is good for me, I no longer cover for myself the writing God has already seen, I hand back the pen and let Him wipe it away and write anew.

People of self fear nothing so much as “blotting out”—for it means admitting they wrote it wrong. So they would rather paste a sheet over it, propping up, covering, defending, with not a day of refreshing. Those emptied of self are willing to let God wipe it clean, and they are the ones who first get to breathe. God gives grace to the humble and resists the proud—the times of refreshing come from the Lord’s presence to those willing to hand over the sheet they wrote wrong.

And the end of it all is the Lord’s return. Building God’s system is precisely accompanying each person, in these days of “heaven must receive him,” to return to their place and become overcomers, to welcome the day of the restoration of all things.
a: Name It and Leave the Door
Speaking truth to others is not discounted, and opening the door of grace is not discounted.
Trust That God Is in Control
My deepest wrongs have not exceeded His plan.
Let God Wipe It Away, Don’t Cover It Yourself
Hand over the sheet you wrote wrong; stop pasting another over it.
Receive Refreshing
Stop propping up and covering; let the Lord Himself give you room to breathe.
Live for That Day
Heaven keeps Him for the restoration of all things; my repentance today is a rehearsal of that day.
q: Is there a “sheet you wrote wrong” in your life that you have kept covering with another sheet, never letting God truly wipe it away? Today, are you willing to hand it over?
“Refreshing” is no longer propping up, covering, or defending. What is the one thing you are most tired from propping up right now? Behind that “propping up,” what are you guarding for yourself?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that after we killed the Prince of life, You still had Your servant call us “brothers.” Thank You for leaving a door open for us, and thank You that our deepest evil lies within Your plan from the creation of the world, and none of it made Your purpose fail.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we are used to covering the words we wrote wrong with a sheet, propping up and covering, yet without a single day of true refreshing. Today make us repent and turn, the whole person turning around to walk toward You; blot out our sins with Your precious blood—not cover them, but truly wipe them away. Let times of refreshing come to us from Your presence, so that we can breathe, and let us know that You are waiting in heaven for the time of the restoration of all things. Make us return to our place in these days of waiting, become overcomers, and prepare to welcome Your return. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: For Moses indeed said to the fathers, ‘The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him in all things whatever he says to you.
It will be that every soul that will not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.’
Yes, and all the prophets from Samuel and those who followed after, as many as have spoken, they also told of these days.
You are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘All the families of the earth will be blessed through your offspring.’
God, having raised up his servant Jesus, sent him to you first to bless you, in turning away every one of you from your wickedness.”
b: In the last devotion, Peter said, “whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things, which God spoke of by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old.” Having mentioned the prophets, Peter invited them to the stage one by one: Moses, Samuel, all the prophets, and finally back to Abraham.

The last five verses of this sermon are a quick tour from Genesis to the age of the kings, with only one purpose—to prove that this Jesus of Nazareth before them is the One to whom the whole Bible has been pointing. And the final sentence of the sermon lands in an unexpected place: the blessing God gave you is to turn each of you from your wickedness.
I. “A prophet like me”—The One to Whom Moses Himself Pointed

In verse 22, Peter quoted Moses: “The Lord God will raise up a prophet for you from among your brothers, like me. You shall listen to everything he says to you.” This is the promise of Deuteronomy 18 (Deut. 18:15); the Jews had waited more than a thousand years, always asking who that “prophet like Moses” was. When the people in John’s Gospel asked John the Baptist, “Are you the prophet?” (John 1:21), they were asking about this One.

Why “like Moses”? Moses led the people out of Egypt—a deliverer; Moses stood between God and the people on Mount Sinai—a mediator; Moses brought down God’s law—a covenant-maker; Moses spoke with God face to face (Deut. 34:10). Jesus lacks none of the four, and each is greater: He leads people out not of Egypt but of sin; He establishes not a covenant on stone tablets but a new covenant in blood.

And Moses’ command was only one sentence: “You shall listen to everything he says to you.” Of the three foundations, “Jesus is my example and the Bible is my standard” come together here as one thing—what that Prophet says is what I am to obey.
• Moses points to Him: even the giver of the law said that the One to listen to is the One coming after.
• Obedience is the only command: not to study Him, discuss Him, or admire Him, but to obey Him.
II. “Every soul that will not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people”—Obedience Is Not Optional
Verse 23 continues the quotation: “It will be that every soul that will not listen to that prophet will be utterly destroyed from among the people.”

This is a heavy sentence. “Destroyed from among the people” was the most severe penalty in the Old Testament—not bodily execution, but being cut off from God’s people, struck from the register. By placing this line here, Peter was telling this crowd: whether you are God’s people is judged not by bloodline but by whether you listen to that Prophet.

Today we often treat “obedience” as an advanced option in faith—believe first, obey when we have strength to spare. Yet neither Moses nor Peter divided it that way. Not to listen is not to be among the people. Obeying the Lord looks like this in daily life: in the moment His word conflicts with my own wish, I choose His.
• Obedience determines identity: whether one is God’s people is seen in whether one listens.
• There is no advanced option: obedience is not the second stage of faith but faith itself.
III. “All the prophets from Samuel and those who followed after … also told of these days”—One Baton After Another
Verse 24: “Yes, and all the prophets from Samuel and those who followed after, as many as have spoken, also told of these days.”

Why count from Samuel? Because Samuel was the beginning of the age of the prophets (1 Sam. 3:20, “All Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of Yahweh”), and he also anointed David, opening the royal line that leads to the Messiah. After Samuel, not one prophet spoke of anything else—what they spoke of were “these days.”

In a relay race the baton passes from Moses’ hand to Samuel, Samuel to Nathan, then to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Malachi; none of the runners reached the finish line, but each ran in the same direction. To whom was the baton finally handed? Peter said: these very days—this Jesus before your eyes. The whole Old Testament is not a pile of books each saying its own thing but a relay run toward one Person.

The reason “the Bible is my standard” can serve as a standard is precisely that from beginning to end it has only one center. If you read the Bible and do not find Jesus, you have not yet found its direction.
• All the prophets in one direction: from Samuel to Malachi, the baton is passed toward the same Person.
• Read the Bible until you reach Him: the center of Scripture is a Person, not a pile of rules.
IV. “You are the descendants of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with your fathers”—Your Name Is on the Covenant

In verse 25, Peter turned back to them: “You are the descendants of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘All the families of the earth will be blessed through your offspring.’”

This is God’s promise to Abraham (Gen. 12:3; 22:18), the root of the whole Bible. Paul later pointed out that “offspring” is singular in the original: “He doesn’t say, ‘To descendants,’ as of many, but as of one, ‘To your offspring,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16). All the families will be blessed through this One.

Peter told the listeners: you are heirs of this covenant, your names are on it. But notice—the covenant they inherit speaks of “all the families.” This covenant was never meant for one people alone; from the start it had the whole earth as its object. The “all who are far off” of chapter 2 appears again here.

An inheritance notice arrives at the house with your name on it. That your name is on it is a fact, but without signing for it the estate just sits there. Peter said your names are on the covenant; the question is whether you will sign for it before that Descendant.
• Your name is on the covenant: inheriting the promise is a fact, but signing for it you must do yourself.
• A covenant for all families: God had the whole earth in mind from the beginning; our circle is always smaller than His.
V. “Blessing you, in turning every one of you from your wickedness”—The Content of the Blessing Is Turning
Verse 26 is the last sentence of the whole sermon: “God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you, in turning away every one of you from your iniquities.”

“Sent him to you first”—“first” the Jews, and then all the families; this is the order of God’s salvation (Rom. 1:16, “to the Jew first, and also to the Greek”). The very people who killed the Lord of life were the ones to whom God “first” sent His Son to bless. The order of grace always reaches the least deserving first.

But what is the content of this “blessing”? Not wealth, not peace, not success—it is “turning away every one of you from your iniquities.” This is the most unexpected and most profound line of the whole sermon. When we ask for blessing, we mostly ask for things outside; the blessing God gives is turning a person out of sin. Turning is itself the blessing; leaving wickedness is itself the blessing.
“Every one of you” appears again, as in chapter 2. The blessing comes to a group, but turning must come one by one.
• First to the least deserving: those who killed the Lord are those to whom God first sent His Son to bless.
• Turning is the blessing: not that you are blessed after turning, but turning itself is the blessing.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Blessing Is Leaving Self

Peter’s second sermon ends here—in fact it was interrupted; at the beginning of chapter 4, the priests and the captain of the temple came. But what he had to say was already said: the whole Bible points to this One; He is the Prophet to be obeyed; your names are on the covenant; and the blessing He gives you is to turn you from your wickedness.

“Turn from wickedness,” in 321 terms, is leaving the life of self. The root of wickedness is pride, and the root of pride is self—wanting to be one’s own master, to bless oneself, to define what is good. The blessing God gives does not add things to this life of self but turns a person out of it. Self-denial here looks like this: no longer asking “What’s in it for me?” but asking “What did He say, and will I obey?”

From Moses to all the prophets, the direction passed from baton to baton finally lands on one Person; and that Person came to turn each of us. Change begins with me, not with others, not with circumstances. No longer I, but Christ—this is not about losing something; it is the blessing God gave Abraham in the beginning finally coming upon me.
a: Obey That Prophet
When His word conflicts with my wish, choose His.
Don’t Treat Obedience as Optional
Obedience is not an advanced stage of faith but faith itself.
Read Until You Reach Jesus
The whole Bible is a relay run toward one Person; don’t stop at the rules.
Sign for Your Name
Your name is on the covenant, but you must personally receive it before Him.
Ask for the Right Blessing
Don’t ask for something added outside; ask to be turned within and leave wickedness.
q: The last time the Lord’s word conflicted with your own wish, which side did you choose? What does that choice say about whether obedience in your life is an option or a foundation?

The blessing God gives you is “turning you from your wickedness.” The blessing you are asking for right now—does it turn you inward, or add on the outside? If everything outside were taken away, would you still feel blessed?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that from Moses to Samuel to all the prophets, You passed the promise down baton by baton, with no baton dropped on the ground, and in the end all of it landed on Your servant Jesus. Thank You that the covenant You made with Abraham had all the families of the earth in mind from the beginning, and had us in mind too.
Lord Jesus, You are the Prophet of whom Moses spoke; everything You say, we are to obey. We confess that we often treat obedience as an option, studying, discussing, and admiring Your word, yet choosing ourselves in the moment it conflicts with our own wish. Forgive us. You were sent to us first, and the blessing You want to give is to turn us from our wickedness—give us this blessing today; turn us out of the life of self, so that we no longer ask “What’s in it for me?” but only “What did You say?” May each of us turn, and may You live within us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: As they spoke to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came to them,
being upset because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
They laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day, for it was now evening.
But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to be about five thousand.
b: In the last devotion, Peter’s sermon stopped at “turning away every one of you from your iniquities.” When those words fell, Luke did not write “Peter finished,” but “As they spoke to the people”—the words were still being spoken when the men arrived.

The sermon in Solomon’s porch was interrupted. The first persecution in church history did not come years later; it came not long after Pentecost, in the temple, on the afternoon a lame man had just leaped up and walked. But the last word of these four short verses is not “arrested” but “five thousand.” Luke wants us to see: people were seized, but the word was not seized.
I. “The priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came to them”—Who Came
Verse 1 first names those who came, one by one: the priests, the captain of the temple, the Sadducees.

The priests were those on duty in the temple that day. The captain of the temple, second only to the high priest in the Jewish system, commanded the temple guard and kept order within the temple precincts—with so many gathered in Solomon’s porch, his coming was part of his duty. The Sadducees were the aristocratic party that held the temple and the high priesthood, few in number and great in power. Luke tells us later that this party “say that there is no resurrection” (Acts 23:8)—they accepted only the five books of Moses and believed in no angel, no spirit, and no resurrection of the dead.

So these three kinds of people happen to represent three things: the daily operation of religion, the order of religion, and the power of religion. They were not Gentiles, not Roman soldiers; they were people inside the temple. In the church’s first persecution, the persecutors were “our own.”
• Persecution often comes from within: those who obstruct God’s work are often not unbelievers but those with positions in religion.

• Duty and power can cover the eyes: the captain keeping order was not wrong, nor were the Sadducees guarding doctrine, but all of it together turned an afternoon that had just seen a miracle into a scene of arrest.
II. “Being upset because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead”—Truth Touched What They Held On To
Verse 2 explains why they came: “being upset because they taught the people and proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.”

“Upset” in the original means “worn through, ground sore,” an anger stirred from within, not a slight displeasure. What made them so uncomfortable? Two things. First, “taught the people”—these two had no rabbinic training yet taught people in the temple; this was overstepping. Second, “proclaimed in Jesus the resurrection from the dead”—the Sadducees’ whole theological position was that there is no resurrection, and now someone was pointing to a man they had sent to the cross with their own hands and saying He had risen from the dead.

This is the core of the problem. If the resurrection is true, the Sadducees’ whole system of faith would have to be rewritten, and their condemning Jesus to death would have to be retried. When truth touched what they held on to, they were upset.

We are the same. As we read God’s word, sometimes suddenly there is a stab of discomfort, and that discomfort is often not because the passage is hard to understand but because it touched something I am clinging to—a position, a habit, a judgment I thought was right. The most typical reaction of the life of self is this very upset: not to check whether it is true but first to feel offended. Humility here looks like this: when that discomfort comes, don’t rush to push it away; first ask: Lord, what are You touching in me?
• Being upset is a signal: truth has touched something I refuse to let go of.
• Don’t push away the facts to protect a position: what the Sadducees pushed away was not Peter but the risen Lord.
III. “They laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day”—Work Interrupted, Sovereignty Not Changed Hands
Verse 3: “They laid hands on them, and put them in custody until the next day, for it was now evening.”

Peter and John had gone up to the temple at the hour of prayer, which is three in the afternoon (Acts 3:1). Healing, onlookers, and a sermon had carried on until it was late. By Jewish custom, no cases were tried after sunset, so the two were put in custody overnight to await the Sanhedrin’s session the next day.

This was the apostles’ first time in prison. From a human viewpoint everything had been interrupted: the sermon halfway through, five thousand still listening, and suddenly the speakers were taken away. The most crucial scene was playing on stage, and the curtain was suddenly pulled down. But we must remember: the curtain was in their hands, but the script was not. The script is in the Author’s hands, and the Author had long since written the next day, chapter three, chapter four, all the way to Rome.

Luke later records that the Lord had told the disciples: “When they bring you before the synagogues, the rulers, and the authorities, don’t be anxious how or what you will answer, or what you will say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you must say” (Luke 12:11–12). This night was the eve of that word being fulfilled. Being held until the next day was not a delay but a preparation.
• Interrupted is not finished: the sermon was interrupted; God’s work was not.
• Prison is also on His itinerary: the Lord had said long before that this day would come, and promised the words for that day.
IV. “But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men grew to be about five thousand”—The Men Were Taken Away; the Seed Stayed in the Ground
The word “But” at the start of verse 4 is the turn of these four verses and Luke’s emphasis: “But many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of the men grew to be about five thousand.”

“Men” in the original refers specifically to adult males, and by the reckoning of the time, women and children were not yet counted. About three thousand had been added at Pentecost (Acts 2:41), and now the men alone came to five thousand. Peter’s second sermon was not finished; he was seized halfway through, yet more believed than the first time.

A farmer is sowing in the field and is dragged away halfway. But it is the farmer who is taken, not the seed—the seed has already fallen into the soil, and that night the farmer is in prison while the seed in the ground sprouts all the same. Paul later said it very clearly: “I suffer hardship in the gospel, even to the point of chains as a criminal. But God’s word isn’t bound” (2 Tim. 2:9). The word does not need the preacher present to work; the word works by itself.

This is a great release for us. We often think that for something to succeed, I must carry it through; if I am blocked, misunderstood, or removed, it is over. But this verse says: not so. The focus is on Jesus, not on self—even if the preacher is put in prison, the Lord’s word goes on, and goes even farther than when he was present.
• The word is not bound: people can be seized; the word cannot.
• Don’t think too highly of yourself: when I am absent, the Lord’s work goes on; this is liberating, not demeaning.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Focus Is Jesus, Not Circumstances

Two lines run in parallel in these four verses: one is the human line—the priests, the captain, and the Sadducees came, were upset, laid hands, and took them away; the other is God’s line—the word went out, people heard, believed, five thousand.

If you look only at the first line, it is bad news: the church had just begun and its leaders were seized. If you look at the second line, it is a great harvest. Which line is true? Both are true; the question is where the focus is placed.

In a life of self, the focus naturally falls on self and circumstances: What if I am arrested? Why are they treating me this way? What will happen next? The world seen through this focus is always dangerous, unfair, and upsetting. In a life emptied of self, the focus is on Jesus—Is He reigning? Is His word moving? If He reigns and His word moves, then whether I am in prison or at home tonight is not the first thing. This is not indifference, but the right order: first with God, then self, then people, then matters.

The Sadducees were upset for their own position, the apostles were taken for the Lord’s word, and five thousand believed for the word they heard. The same afternoon, three kinds of people, three focuses. Today, where is our focus?
a: See the Source of Persecution
Obstruction often comes from those with positions; don’t assume someone is right just because he is “from inside.”
Read the Signal of Being Upset
When God’s word makes you uncomfortable, first ask, “What are You touching in me?” rather than first protecting yourself.
Trust That the Script Is in His Hands
When work is interrupted and positions taken away, sovereignty has not changed hands.
Be at Ease Letting the Word Run
Even in your absence, God’s word is not bound; don’t think too highly of yourself.
Turn the Focus Back to Jesus
Today the question is not “What do I do?” but “Is He reigning? Is His word moving?”
q: In your most recent reading of Scripture or hearing of a sermon, was there a sentence that suddenly made you uncomfortable? Was that discomfort because you didn’t understand, or because it touched something you hold on to?
Is there something in your hands that is being “interrupted” or “held until the next day”? If you believe the word is not bound, what anxiety can you lay down today, turning your focus back to Jesus?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that on the afternoon of the church’s first persecution, Your word did not stop. People laid hands on Your servants, but could not lay hold of Your word; the sermon was interrupted halfway, yet the believers grew to five thousand. Thank You for letting us see that Your work has never depended on whether people are present, but only on whether You are reigning.
Lord, we confess that we are often like the Sadducees, upset the moment truth touches what we are clinging to, preferring to protect our own position rather than admit the facts. Forgive us, and help us in that uncomfortable moment to quiet down first and ask what You are touching in us. Move our focus off ourselves and our circumstances and set it back on You—when work is interrupted and positions are taken away, let us still believe the script is in Your hands and Your word is not bound. May You reign in our hearts, and may Your word go on in us, and through us, all the same. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: In the morning, their rulers, elders, and scribes were gathered together in Jerusalem.
Annas the high priest was there, with Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and as many as were relatives of the high priest.
When they had stood Peter and John in the middle of them, they inquired, “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?”
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “You rulers of the people, and elders of Israel,
if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,

may it be known to you all, and to all the people of Israel, that in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, this man stands here before you whole in him.
He is ‘the stone which was regarded as worthless by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner.’
There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved!”
b: In the last devotion, Peter and John were held for a night and the sermon was interrupted, but the believers grew to five thousand. In this devotion, day has dawned.

The next day, the most powerful people in all Jerusalem gathered and called two Galilean fishermen into their midst. A few weeks earlier, this same group, in this same place, had had Jesus standing in the middle. That night, Peter in the outer courtyard had said to a servant girl, “I don’t know him.” Today he stood inside.
I. “Rulers, elders, and scribes … Annas and Caiaphas”—The Same People, the Same Place

Verses 5 and 6 name those in the judgment seat. Rulers, elders, and scribes—these three together formed the highest council of the Jews, the Sanhedrin, seventy-one in all, presided over by the high priest. Luke names a few more: Annas, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and the relatives of the high priest.

Annas was high priest from AD 6 to 15 and was later deposed by the Romans, but five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas successively took that seat, and actual power remained in his hands. Caiaphas was the high priest then in office, the one who had tried Jesus and said, “It is advantageous for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish” (John 11:50). “The relatives of the high priest”—these words tell us something: this was not only a religious council; it was a family, and the temple’s power and interests lay in this family’s hands.

Jesus had been condemned to death before these very people. Now they sat in the same seats and watched two men who had followed Jesus brought in to stand in the middle. From a human viewpoint, it was the most unfavorable scene: the judges had already taken their position, and the accused were fishermen without even rabbinic training.
• The scene is recognizable: the same people who condemned Jesus to death a few weeks earlier, in the same place.
• Power takes root: Annas was deposed, yet power did not leave his house. What people grasp is not released just because the name changes.
II. “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?”—They Asked Not Whether It Was True, but By What Right
In verse 7, the Sanhedrin asked: “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?”

Notice what they did not ask. They did not ask, “Is that man really healed?”—the man was over forty, had lain at the Beautiful Gate all his life, and the whole city knew him; this they dared not question. What they asked was “By what authority?”: what power, whose name. “Name” in Jewish usage represents authority and identity; in whose name means by whose authority. The Sanhedrin’s meaning was: without our authorization, by what right do you act and teach in the temple?

This is a question about authority, not about truth. When a person can no longer deny the facts but still refuses to accept them, he turns to asking, “What qualifies you?” This is the most practiced move of the life of self—whether the matter is true or false is not important; what matters is whether control is in my hands.
• When the facts cannot be denied, people turn to asking qualifications: this is a way to protect a position, not a way to seek truth.
• “Name” is authority: they asked the right question, only they did not expect the answer.
III. “Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit”—The Promise of That Night, Fulfilled at This Moment
Verse 8 is only one sentence, yet it is the pivot of the passage: “Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them.”

“Filled” is passive in the original, which means this was not Peter screwing up his courage; the Holy Spirit came upon him. The Lord had promised: “When they bring you before the synagogues, the rulers, and the authorities, don’t be anxious how or what you will answer, or what you will say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you must say” (Luke 12:11–12). “In that very hour”—not the night before, not three days ahead, but the moment of standing there and opening the mouth.
