This is exactly the most practical form of “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” That night in custody Peter probably could not have written a script, and he did not need to. It was not that he had prepared so well by himself, but that he had handed himself to the Lord who promised to speak at that hour. Use the heart and rely on the Spirit, not the head relying on self—those who use the head spend the whole night thinking, “Tomorrow what will they ask, how will I answer, what if I answer wrong?”, and the more they think, the more anxious they get; those who use the heart know that at the moment of speaking tomorrow, Someone will be there.

The Peter who denied the Lord three times by the charcoal fire now stood before the high priest and spoke at once. What changed in between was not that Peter had become brave but that the Holy Spirit had come.
• Being filled is passive: not screwed up by people, but the Lord coming upon them.
• “In that very hour”: what the Lord gives is the words for that moment, not worry in advance.
IV. “By the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, this man stands here before you healed”—Turning the Question Around in the Answer

In verses 9 and 10, Peter opened with a sharp remark: “if we are examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man”—you held us overnight because someone did a good deed? He then answered directly the question of “in whose name,” and more fully than they expected: “in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead, this man stands here before you whole.”

There are three layers in this sentence. First, “Jesus Christ of Nazareth”—that very One, whom you know. Second, “whom you crucified”—Peter did not go around it but pointed directly at those sitting before him: you crucified. Third, “whom God raised from the dead”—the verdict you passed, God overturned.

There is one more detail: the word “healed” is the same word in the original as “saved” in verse 12. When Peter said this man was “healed,” he was already saying this man was “saved”—the lame leg being made well was only the visible half, with another half within.

Peter stood in the dock but spoke like one making a declaration. He did not defend himself with a single word; all his words pointed to Jesus. This is what letting Jesus have all the glory looks like in an interrogation: asked by what right, I speak of Him; when someone wants to credit me, I point to Him.
• No going around, no covering: you crucified Him, and God raised Him.
• Healed means saved: outward healing points to inward salvation.
V. “The stone which was rejected by you, the builders … there is no other salvation”—Only One Key

In verses 11 and 12, Peter closed by quoting Psalm 118: “He is the stone which was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 118:22). Jesus Himself had quoted this verse—just a few weeks earlier in the temple, to these same people (Matt. 21:42). Peter now took it back and added one word: “you” builders. The builders were you, and those who rejected the stone were you, yet God has made that stone the most important of the whole building—the head of the corner, the one that determines the direction and stability of the whole house.
Then verse 12, the peak of the whole defense: “There is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven that is given among men, by which we must be saved.”

They asked “in whose name,” and Peter’s answer was: not only this name, but only this name. “Under heaven among men”—a place with no exceptions; “that is given”—this name is given by God, not chosen by people; “no other salvation”—there is no second road.

If a door is fitted with only one key, trying a hundred other keys is in vain, not because the door is unreasonable but because the lock was made that way. This verse sounds harsh to today’s generation, but it is not proud; it is humble—Peter did not say “our name,” he said “the name that is given.” That man cannot save man is man’s place; that only the One whom God has given can save is God’s place. Letting God be God and man be man is verse 12.
• The rejected became the foundation: human judgment and God’s judgment are often exactly opposite.
• Only one name: not chosen by people but given by God; acknowledging it is not pride but returning to one’s place.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Standing in the Dock, Letting Jesus Be King
In this passage two “thrones” confront each other.

One is the seat of the Sanhedrin—Annas, Caiaphas, the relatives of the high priest sat on it and asked “By what right?” What they held was authority, what they protected was their seat, and even a fact like the resurrection set before them they would not look at. Pride is just like this: leaving one’s place, grasping power, wanting to take God’s place to decide who is qualified and whose name counts.

The other throne is the name on Peter’s lips. Peter stood in the dock with no seat, no learning, no authorization, yet every word he spoke said: the true King is not you but the One you rejected; the true name is not yours but the one God has given. He himself was not in his words—not “we healed him” but “by this name”; not “we have power” but “filled with the Holy Spirit.”

Letting Jesus be King looks like this in this scene: when asked “By what right?”, don’t prove yourself, only point to Him. This man who once protected himself by denying the Lord beside the charcoal fire now before the high priest laid himself completely down, leaving only that name. The difference in between is not courage but self-denial—no longer I, but Christ.
a: Recognize the Scene
Where power has taken root, people do not let go because of facts; don’t be surprised, and don’t be afraid.
Discern the Question
Is the other asking “Is it true?” or “By what right?” The latter is a question to protect a seat; don’t be led by it.
Hand That Moment to the Spirit
Don’t spend the whole night calculating with your head how to answer tomorrow; “in that very hour” He will give the words.
Don’t Defend Yourself
When asked by what right, speak of Him, not of yourself.
Acknowledge Only One Name
Not my name, my methods, my qualifications, but the One whom God has given.
q: When someone questions you with “By what right?”, is your first reaction to prove yourself or to point to Jesus? Recall the most recent time: how many times did “I” appear in your words and how many times “He”?

“There is salvation in no one else.” In your life, is there an area where you are still trying other keys on the door—relying on your own methods, on people, on circumstances, rather than truly on this one name alone?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that Peter, who denied You beside the charcoal fire, stood before the high priest today, filled with the Holy Spirit, and spoke Your Son’s name at once. Thank You that Your promise is “in that very hour,” not making us worry beforehand, but asking us only to hand over our mouths to You at that moment.
Lord Jesus, You are the stone rejected by the builders, now the head of the corner; there is no salvation in anyone else. We confess that we are often like the Sanhedrin: the facts are set before us, yet we only ask “By what right?”, to protect our own seat. We also confess that when we are asked, we are often quick to prove ourselves and rarely point to You. Forgive us, bring us down from our own thrones, and return us to our place—letting You be God and us be human. May every time we open our mouths not be to defend ourselves but to let Your name be heard; may You truly be King in our hearts and receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.
Seeing the man who was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it.
But when they had commanded them to go aside out of the council, they conferred among themselves,
saying, “What shall we do to these men? Because indeed a notable miracle has been done through them, as can be plainly seen by all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we can’t deny it.
But so that this spreads no further among the people, let’s threaten them, that from now on they don’t speak to anyone in this name.”
They called them, and commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus.
But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves,
for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.”
When they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people; for everyone glorified God for that which was done.
For the man on whom this miracle of healing was performed was more than forty years old.
b: In the last devotion, Peter stood in the midst of the Sanhedrin and turned his defense into a declaration: “There is salvation in no one else.” When he had finished, it was the judges’ turn to react.

Luke writes this passage very vividly: first the Sanhedrin’s astonishment, then a closed-door meeting, then a ban, then the two fishermen’s reply, and finally release. From beginning to end, those holding power were at a loss at every step, while those without power were at ease at every step. Who is reigning is plain to see.
I. “Seeing the boldness of Peter and John … they recognized that they had been with Jesus”—People Can Tell Whom You Have Been With
In verse 13, the Sanhedrin saw two things and then reached a conclusion.

The first thing they saw was “boldness.” This word in the original means “speaking openly and fearlessly,” a public, uncovered way of speaking, and it became one of the key words of Acts. The second thing they saw was that these were “unlearned and ignorant men”—“unlearned” means without formal rabbinic training, and “ignorant” means ordinary people with no office or status. Together these made them “marvel”: how could such men speak like this?

Then came the conclusion: “they recognized that they had been with Jesus.” They remembered; these two had once followed that Nazarene. And that Nazarene was also one of whom it was asked, “How does this man know letters, having never been educated?” (John 7:15), and also one who stood fearless before these very people. As the master spoke, so the disciples spoke.

“Jesus is my example”—in the end it is not we who say so ourselves; it is others who see it. A person who has been with Jesus shows it in his way of speaking, his posture before authority, his ease when questioned. When people see us, can they recognize whom we have been with?
• Boldness is not temperament but the trace of following: whom you have been with, you speak like.
• You can be recognized without learning: what is recognized is not credentials but the likeness of the Lord within.
II. “Seeing the man who was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it”—A Living Proof Stands
Verse 14: “Seeing the man who was healed standing with them, they could say nothing against it.”

There is a detail here easy to miss: that man was “standing with them.” The man who had lain at the Beautiful Gate all his life now stood alongside the apostles—on the legs he had never stood on in over forty years. He did not say a word, and Luke does not record anything he said, yet standing there, he left the Sanhedrin with “nothing to say against it.” Verse 22 adds: “the man was more than forty years old on whom this miracle of healing was performed.” Over forty—the length of years he had lain at the Beautiful Gate meant the whole city knew him; no one could say he had not been lame before, nor that he was still lame now.

The most powerful witness is often not spoken but stood. A life changed by the Lord, standing there, is proof that cannot be answered. We often want to refute others in argument, but what matters most is not that our arguments win but that our lives stand up. Change begins with me—if I have really been touched by Him inside, when people see it, they will have nothing to say against it.
• Witness stands: no need to speak; standing there is the proof.
• First let your life stand: arguments can be refuted; a changed life cannot.
III. “We cannot deny it … let us threaten them”—Knowing It Is True, Yet Choosing to Suppress It

Verses 15 to 18 are the Sanhedrin’s closed-door meeting. Luke does not say how he came to know what was said inside—perhaps a member of the Sanhedrin who later believed told him—but he recorded the contents of that meeting as they were, and the contents are astonishingly honest.

“That indeed a notable miracle has been done through them is evident to all who dwell in Jerusalem, and we can’t deny it.” This was the Sanhedrin’s own admission: the miracle was real, obvious, known to the whole city, and we cannot deny it. And then? One would expect the next words to be “So let us investigate what is going on.” But what they said was: “But so that it spreads no further among the people, let’s threaten them, that they no longer speak to anyone in this name.”

Admit the facts, then suppress the facts. This is the most terrifying place in the whole passage. It was not that they did not know; they knew, and then decided not to let others know. The smoke alarm in the house sounds, and their method is not to find where the fire is but to take down the alarm. Why? Because finding the fire would disturb their whole house, while taking down the alarm takes one reach of the hand.

This is the life of self at its extreme: the truth is set before me, but because it threatens my seat, my system, my vested interests, I choose to suppress it. This does not happen only in the Sanhedrin. Every time I know what the Lord wants me to do but pretend not to hear because the cost is too great, every time I know I am wrong but keep arguing because admitting it would be too embarrassing, I am doing the same thing—cannot deny it, yet must threaten.
• Admitting is not accepting: the Sanhedrin admitted the miracle but did not accept the One to whom the miracle pointed.
• Taking down the alarm is not putting out the fire: suppress the truth and the truth does not vanish; I am only closer to the fire.
IV. “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God … we cannot help but speak”—This Is Not Courage but Being Full Within

In verses 19 and 20, Peter and John’s reply became the motto of the church in every age when facing authority: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.”

Look first at verse 19. They did not say “We will not listen to you”; they turned the question back to the Sanhedrin: judge for yourselves which is right before God. This is a measured firmness—not despising authority, not exalting self, only putting God back in the highest place. “The Bible is my standard” means just this: human commands are not weightless, but when they conflict with God’s word, I know which side to stand on, and I can stand there calmly, without anger.

Now look at “we cannot help but speak” in verse 20. These words are not “we have decided to speak” but “we have no way not to speak.” When a pot of water boils, the lid jumps by itself; not because the lid is brave, but because the pot is full. Peter and John’s boldness was not something they screwed up—something had filled them: they had seen the risen Lord, heard His words, and had just been filled with the Holy Spirit. When full, it overflows; and what overflows cannot be held down by a ban.
We often ask for boldness when what we should ask for is fullness. If inside is empty, even great courage will not last long; if inside is full, no courage is needed, and it comes out naturally.
• Measured firmness: not despising people, not exalting self, only putting God highest.
• Cannot help speaking because full: rather than asking for boldness, ask to be filled with Him within.
V. “Finding no way to punish them … all men glorified God”—Power Spent, Glory to God
Verse 21: “When they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people.”

The most powerful group in all Jerusalem “found no way.” They had judicial authority, the temple guard, and Rome’s tacit permission, yet the facts before them were too plain and the people’s reaction too clear; they could not find a single reason to lay a hand on them. Power had run to its end, and what was left was only “threatened them”—speaking more fiercely, and then letting them go.

And the reason Luke writes all this is in the last line of verse 21: “because all men glorified God for that which was done.” Not glory given to Peter, not glory given to the Sanhedrin, but to God. A lame man rising and walking, a group of fishermen standing fearless before the Sanhedrin, a trial that could find no charge—the whole thing, from beginning to end, had only one result: God received the glory.

This is the second of the two core principles: letting Jesus receive all the glory. When Peter and John walked out of the Sanhedrin, no one said, “How impressive those two are”; people said, “How great God is.” This is the best ending to any ministry. Giving thanks in everything looks like this here: after being held a night, tried, and threatened, those who walked out were thinking not “How much wrong have I suffered” but “He has received the glory.”
• Power has an end: however great human power, it “finds no way” when it meets God’s work.
• To whom the glory goes shows who is reigning: when it was all over, the crowd praised God.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Those Who Have Been with Jesus Cannot Be Silenced by a Ban
In this passage the contrast between the Sanhedrin and the apostles is extremely sharp.

The Sanhedrin had learning, status, and power, yet was trapped by what it grasped: knowing it was true, it could not admit it; wanting to punish, it found no way; it could only threaten, and threats did no good. The life of self ends up like this—the more it grasps in hand, the less it can do, because every decision must first protect the self.

The apostles had no learning, no status, no power, yet were fearless, unanswerable, and could not help speaking. Their freedom was not won from outside but came from within: they had been with Jesus, seen, heard, and been filled. Those emptied of self have nothing to protect, so nothing can bind them. This is why self-denial is not having nothing but entering the limitless—the Sanhedrin took away their freedom, time, and safety, but could not take the One within them.

And the final outcome of it all was that all men glorified God. Those who have been with Jesus speak like Him, stand firm, cannot be suppressed, and finally all the glory goes to Him. This is the road: from Jesus as my example all the way to letting Jesus receive all the glory.
a: Let People Recognize Whom You’ve Been With
Not through learning or status, but through the way you speak and your ease before authority.
Let Your Life Stand First
Don’t rush to win in argument; a changed life is itself unanswerable.
Don’t Be One Who Takes Down the Alarm
If you know it is true, don’t suppress it to protect yourself.
Ask for Fullness, Not Only Boldness
When filled with Him within, you naturally cannot help speaking.
Give the Glory to Him
After being wronged, think “He has received the glory,” not “how much I suffered.”
q: If someone observed your speech and reactions for a whole day, could he recognize that you have been with Jesus? From what would he recognize it? From what would he fail to?
Is there something you know is true yet keep suppressing because the cost is too great? The Sanhedrin “could not deny it, but must threaten”—are you doing the same thing right now?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that two unlearned, ordinary men stood before the Sanhedrin, and people recognized that they had been with Jesus. Thank You that the man over forty stood there on legs he had never stood on, leaving the most powerful men in Jerusalem with nothing to say. Thank You that the end of it all was that all men glorified You.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we are often like the Sanhedrin, knowing Your word is true, yet pretending not to hear because the cost is too great, even finding ways to suppress it. Forgive us. Fill us within, not holding on by courage but so full that we cannot help but speak. Make our lives stand, so that when people see us they recognize that we have been with You; when human commands collide with Your word, let us stand calmly on Your side, not angry, not despising, only putting You highest. May all the glory go to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: Being let go, they came to their own company and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them.
When they heard it, they lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said, “O Lord, you are God, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them;
who by the mouth of your servant, David, said, ‘Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing?
The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take council together, against the Lord, and against his Christ.’
“For truly, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, were gathered together against your holy servant, Jesus, whom you anointed,
to do whatever your hand and your council foreordained to happen.
Now, Lord, look at their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness,
while you stretch out your hand to heal; and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.”
When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.
b: In the last devotion, the Sanhedrin threatened them and let Peter and John go. Having walked out of the Sanhedrin’s door, where did the two go?

This devotion tells us: they went back to their own people. Then the whole community did one thing—prayed. This is one of the most completely recorded prayers of the early church, and from beginning to end there is not one line asking for peace for themselves, yet when the prayer was finished, the place was shaken and all were filled with the Holy Spirit. What they asked for was exactly what they received.
I. “They went to their own company”—The First Thing for Those Released Is to Go Home
Verse 23: “Being let go, they came to their own company, and reported all that the chief priests and the elders had said to them.”

“Their own company” in the original means “their own people”—the group that belonged to them, their family. After being held a night, tried, and threatened, the two did not go home to rest separately, did not first go to find a lawyer to plan a response, and did not immediately rush back to the temple to keep preaching—they first returned to the brothers and sisters and told them all that had happened.

This order is worth noting. People matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things—first life, then relationships, then ministry. Peter and John had just gone through the first trial in church history, and the first thing they did was not to handle the matter but to return to people. They knew what lay ahead was not the matter of two people but the matter of the whole community; and a community that is not first together cannot pray with one accord.

When we meet difficulty, our first move is often to find a way by ourselves. But the Lord put us in one body so that when difficulty comes, we first return to the brothers and sisters, lay the matter open, and bring it together before God.
• Return to people first: when trouble comes, the first move is back to the community, not carrying it alone.
• Lay it open: “reported all”—no covering, no shrinking it; only by telling can you pray together.
II. “Lord, you are God, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them”—First See How Great God Is, Then How Small the Trouble Is

In verse 24, they “lifted up their voice to God with one accord.” The first line of the prayer was not “Lord, the Sanhedrin has threatened us” but “Lord, you are God, who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them.”

The “Lord” here is a special word in the original, meaning “master, absolute owner,” the word a servant uses for his master, rarely used of God in the whole New Testament. The moment they opened their mouths they put God in the absolute position of sovereign: You made heaven, earth, and sea; the Sanhedrin is Your creation, Annas and Caiaphas are Your creation, and the very room where we were tried is Your creation.

Anyone who has looked at the stars through a telescope knows the lens must first be aimed and focused to see clearly. Prayer is the same—first aim the focus on how great God is, and the trouble naturally shows its true size in the lens. Those who use the heart and rely on the Spirit begin prayer from God; those who use the head and rely on self begin prayer from the problem, and the more they speak, the larger it grows and the more anxious they become. The focus is on Jesus, not on circumstances—the most direct exercise of this is the first sentence of prayer.
• The first sentence decides the focus: begin from God, and the trouble shrinks; begin from the trouble, and God is crowded small.
• Call Him Sovereign: all that opposes us is in the hand of the One who made heaven and earth.
III. “Truly, in this city … to do whatever your hand and your counsel foreordained to happen”—Look at What Is Before You Within Scripture
In verses 25 to 28, they quoted Psalm 2 and then set the present situation beside it.

Psalm 2 says: “Why do the nations rage, and the peoples plot a vain thing? The kings of the earth take a stand, and the rulers take counsel together, against Yahweh, and against his Anointed” (Ps. 2:1–2). They went on: this is exactly what we have seen—Herod (the king of Judea), Pontius Pilate (the Roman governor), the Gentiles (the Roman soldiers), and the people of Israel (their own people): the four powers had indeed gathered in this city against Your anointed Jesus. What the psalmist wrote a thousand years earlier they had seen with their own eyes a few weeks before.

But verse 28 states the deepest layer: all this was “to do whatever your hand and your counsel foreordained to happen.” Kings and rulers gathered to oppose God, yet what they accomplished was what God had long decided—the cross. Human opposition became part of God’s plan.

This is what “the Bible is my standard” looks like in persecution. They did not first ask “What should we do?”; they first asked “What does Scripture say?” When what is before us is placed within Scripture, it is no longer a sudden, out-of-control accident but something written in it long ago. Since the four powers that attacked Jesus all accomplished God’s foreordained plan, how far beyond God’s hand can the Sanhedrin that threatens us today go?
• First ask what Scripture says: not first “What do I do?” but first find what is written in God’s word.
• Opposition accomplished the foreordained: even the crucifixion was in His counsel; today’s troubles are no exception.
IV. “Look at their threats … grant to your servants to speak your word with all boldness”—They Did Not Ask for the Persecution to Stop
Verses 29 and 30 are the real petition of this prayer and its most surprising part.

They said, “Now, Lord, look at their threats”—and then what did they ask? Not “Lord, make the Sanhedrin withdraw the ban,” not “Lord, keep us safe,” not “Lord, punish them.” They asked two things: grant to Your servants to speak Your word with all boldness, and stretch out Your hand to heal and to do signs and wonders.

In other words, what they asked was not “let there be no more trouble” but “in the trouble, let us go on doing what the Lord wants us to do.” The ban forbade “speaking in this name,” so they asked to “speak your word with all boldness”; what the Sanhedrin feared was the miracles spreading further, so they asked that “signs and wonders be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus.” Their prayer was exactly the opposite of the Sanhedrin’s ban.

Note also two titles. They called themselves “your servants,” a word meaning “bond-slaves” in the original; they called Jesus “your holy Servant,” a word meaning “child, servant,” the word for “the Lord’s servant” in Isaiah. What a bond-servant asks is that the Master’s work be done, not that he himself be comfortable.
What a person asks for shows where his focus is. Self-denial in prayer looks like this: in what is asked there is no personal safety, only the Lord’s word.
• What is asked shows the focus: asking for peace, the focus is on self; asking for boldness to preach, the focus is on the Lord.
• A bond-servant’s prayer: if the Master’s work is accomplished, that is enough; whether I am comfortable is not first.
V. “The place was shaken … they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness”—He Answered with Action
Verse 31: “When they had prayed, the place was shaken where they were gathered together. They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the word of God with boldness.”

The place shook. This was not a performance but a response. In the Old Testament, when God came down upon Sinai, “the whole mountain quaked greatly” (Exod. 19:18); when Isaiah saw the vision, “the foundations of the thresholds shook” (Isa. 6:4). Shaking is a sign of God’s own presence—He is saying: I have heard, I am here.

Then “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.” They had been filled on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:4), and here again. Being filled with the Holy Spirit is not once for all but again and again—every new need, every new battle, calls for a new filling. And what was the result of the filling? “They spoke the word of God with boldness.” In verse 29 they asked to “speak your word with all boldness,” and in verse 31 God gave them “spoke the word of God with boldness.” What they asked is what they received, word for word.
• The shaking is His response: God does not only hear; He is present.
• Filling is not a one-time matter: every battle calls for being filled afresh.
• What they asked is what they received: they did not ask for their own peace, so what they received was the Lord’s power.
The Light of the 321 Principles: A Prayer That Lets Jesus Be King
This prayer, from beginning to end, is a prayer of “letting Jesus be King.”

First it calls God Sovereign—You made heaven, earth, sea, and all that is in them; everything is in Your hand. Then it places the opposing powers within Scripture—Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, the people of Israel, all accomplished Your foreordained plan. Finally what it asks for is that the Lord’s word be spoken and the Lord’s name work miracles. In the whole prayer, “self” is nearly absent: no asking for self’s peace, no asking that opponents be punished, no asking that the ban be withdrawn.

A prayer of self asks God to come and solve my problem; a prayer emptied of self places oneself within God’s plan. The center of the former is me, with God as helper; the center of the latter is Him, with me as servant. The words of these two prayers may be much alike, but their directions are completely opposite.

And God’s response tells us which prayer He accepts: the place shaken, the Spirit’s filling, bold preaching. They gave the throne to Jesus, and Jesus worked among them. This is exactly the road of service: spirit, understanding, life, service, God—first led by the Holy Spirit back to the community, using Scripture to see the situation clearly, praying for the Lord’s matters in the likeness of Jesus, letting Him be King, and finally giving all power and glory to Him.
a: Return to Your Brothers and Sisters First
When trouble comes, don’t carry it alone; first lay it open and pray together.
Begin Prayer from God
First see how great He is, and the trouble shows its true size.
Place What Is Before You Within Scripture
First ask “What does God’s word say?”, not “What do I do?”
Check What You Ask For
Is it your own peace, or that the Lord’s word be spoken?
Ask for a New Filling
Yesterday’s filling is not enough for today; come before Him afresh for every battle.
q: Think of the last time you prayed about a difficulty: did the first sentence begin from God or from the problem? If you prayed again, how would you begin?

Honestly list the three things you ask for most often right now. How many are about your own peace and smoothness, and how many about the Lord’s word being spoken and His name receiving glory? What does that ratio say?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, You are the Sovereign who made the heaven, the earth, the sea, and all that is in them. Thank You that after leaving the Sanhedrin, the first thing the early church did was return to the brothers and sisters, and the first words were to call You Lord. Thank You for letting us see that even the opposition of kings and rulers accomplished Your foreordained plan, and that no trouble upon us today is beyond Your hand.
Lord Jesus, we confess that too often our prayers ask You to come and solve our problems, with ourselves still at the center. Forgive us, and teach us, like that group, to see first how great You are and then how small the trouble is; to ask first what Your word says and then what we should do. Look into what we ask, and change “asking for peace” into “asking for boldness to speak Your word,” and “asking that opponents be punished” into “asking that Your name do Your work.” Fill us again with the Holy Spirit today, so that we speak Your word with boldness; may You be King among us and King in our prayers. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul. Not one of them claimed that anything of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common.
With great power, the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace was on them all.
For neither was there among them any who lacked, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the proceeds of the things that were sold,
and laid them at the apostles’ feet, and distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need.
Joses, who by the apostles was also called Barnabas (which is, being interpreted, Son of Encouragement), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race,
having a field, sold it and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
b: In the last devotion, after prayer the place shook, and all were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with boldness. So how did a group filled with the Holy Spirit live their days?

Here Luke pulls the camera back, no longer filming a trial or a sermon but the whole community. This is the second time Acts describes the life of the early church (the first was in 2:42–47), and this time the focus is on something very practical—money and property. The evidence of being filled with the Spirit is not only in the mouth, boldly preaching, but also in the hand, how it holds things.
I. “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul”—One Heart, One Soul
First half of verse 32: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and soul.”

“Multitude”—by this time the men alone numbered five thousand, and with women and children it was a great crowd. “One heart and soul” in the original is “one heart, one soul,” which does not mean their opinions were all the same or their temperaments all alike, but that the direction within them was the same. So many people from such different backgrounds—Galilean fishermen, Jerusalem priests, Jews returned from the Dispersion—yet of one heart.

Unity is not negotiated into being. Before an orchestra performs, each instrument does not tune to the others but each tunes to the same tuning fork; once tuned to that one, they are naturally in harmony with each other. The early church did not reach one heart and soul by meetings and negotiation; each person tuned to the same Lord. Unity is the result of self-denial—each person’s “self” gave way, Jesus reigned in each, and this group naturally became one heart. Conversely, disunity in the church, traced to the root, always has some “self” unwilling to give way.
• Unity is tuning to the same One: not wearing each other down to fit, but each tuning to the Lord.
• The root of disunity is self: traced to the bottom, there is always an “I” still reigning.
II. “Not one of them said that anything of the things which he possessed was his own”—What Changed Was the Mindset, Not a System
Second half of verse 32: “Not one of them said that anything of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common.”

First be clear about what this sentence says. It does not say “no one owned anything”; it says no one “said” his things were his own. The things were still in each one’s hands—verse 34 says “as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them,” which shows they had held property individually; in chapter 5 Peter said to Ananias, “While it remained, didn’t it remain yours? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power?” (Acts 5:4), which shows that selling or not, and how much to give, was entirely voluntary. This was not a system abolishing private property but a change of mindset in a group of people: the things were in my hand, but I no longer called them “mine.”

The very core word of the old self’s life of self is “mine”—my money, my time, my house, my rights. This “mine” is not necessarily greedy; it just very naturally draws a line: what is within the line is mine to rule. The new self’s life emptied of self does not throw things away but wipes out that line: things are still managed, but He is the one who rules. Self-denial in money looks like this: the day the Lord asks me to give up something, there is no “But this is mine” inside me.
• Not having nothing, but not saying “mine”: property managed, sovereignty handed over.
• Wipe out the line: what is inside the line now has Him as its ruler.
III. “With great power the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus; and great grace was on them all”—Life and Witness Together
Verse 33: “With great power the apostles gave their testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus. Great grace was on them all.”

Luke sandwiched this verse between two passages on property, and it was not placed casually. The previous verse speaks of one heart and soul and all things in common, the next verse of no one lacking—both are about life within the community; yet this middle verse is about witness outward: great power, testifying to the resurrection. Life within and witness without are two sides of one thing.

“Great power”—this is a direct answer to the prayer of verses 29 and 30; they asked for boldness and miracles, and God gave power. “Testimony of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus”—the content was always that one matter: He lives. “Great grace was on them all”—“great grace” can mean God’s grace came upon them, or that they gained great favor among the people (2:47, “having favor with all the people”). The two meanings here are actually one: God’s grace flows within the community, and those outside can see it.

First life, then relationships, then ministry—this verse is “ministry,” but it is placed between “life” and “relationships,” wrapped by them. Without the one-heart-and-soul life within, the witness outside is empty; without the relationships of mutual supply in the community, great power would not last long.
• Witness grows out of life: with one heart within, there is great power without.
• Ministry wrapped by life and relationships: this is Luke’s arrangement, and it is God’s order.
IV. “Neither was there among them any who lacked … distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need”—An Old Testament Promise Came True

Verses 34 and 35: “For neither was there among them any who lacked, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, and brought the prices of the things that were sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each, according as anyone had need.”

“No one who lacked”—this sentence echoes in Jewish ears. Deuteronomy 15 says that if the people obey God’s word, “there will be no poor among you” (Deut. 15:4). This was a promise Israel had never achieved, and now it was achieved among this group. Not by a system, but by a group of people whose hearts had been changed.

One more detail: the proceeds were laid “at the apostles’ feet.” Not put in the apostles’ hands but at their feet. Put in the hand, it is given to that person; laid at the feet, it is placed under the sovereignty he represents. When these people sold their property, they were not giving the money to Peter but handing it to the Lord, with the apostles distributing according to each one’s need. Those who gave let go and no longer cared where it went; those who distributed did so by need, not by relationship or contribution.

Building God’s system is not an organizational structure but a realm formed by people who let Jesus be King. Within this realm, things naturally flow to those in need, because no one is blocking it with “mine.” This is how that purpose looks most visibly in life: not first designing a system, but first letting a group’s hearts be changed, and the system grows by itself.
• The promise came true: what Deuteronomy could not achieve, people with changed hearts did.
• At the feet, not in the hand: given to the Lord, not to a person; once let go, no longer clutched.
V. “The apostles named Barnabas … he owned a field, and sold it”—One Name, One Field, a Lifetime’s Road

In verses 36 and 37, Luke singled one person out of the group: “Joseph, who by the apostles was surnamed Barnabas (which means ‘Son of Encouragement’), a Levite, a man of Cyprus by race, having a field, sold it, and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.”

Luke gives us four pieces of information. He was a Levite—by Moses’ law, Levites were not to own property, since “Yahweh is their inheritance” (Num. 18:20), but by this age that rule had long loosened, so he had a field. He was born in Cyprus—the large island in the eastern Mediterranean, a Jew of the Dispersion. His given name was Joseph, but the apostles gave him another name: Barnabas, meaning “Son of Encouragement,” a man who constantly encouraged and supported others. The apostles gave a person a name because they saw that quality in him.

Then what he did: “having a field, sold it, and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.” Exactly the same as those before, with only the word “also” added. Why does Luke single him out? On one hand, to prepare a contrast for Ananias in chapter 5—the same selling of land, the same laying at the apostles’ feet, with hearts worlds apart. On the other hand, because this man later became so important: it was he who, when everyone feared Saul, brought Saul to the apostles (Acts 9:27); it was he who was sent to Antioch and personally went to Tarsus to find Saul (Acts 11:25–26); it was he who, when Paul would not take Mark again, took Mark and went (Acts 15:39). This man spent his whole life doing one thing: lifting others up.

Selling a field was the first step of wiping out “mine.” A person who lays his property at the feet can later lay down reputation, position, and coworkers at the feet too. For Jesus, for others, not for himself—Barnabas’ whole life began with this one field.
• A name is seen by others: “Son of Encouragement” was not self-chosen but what others saw in him.
• A field is the starting point: one who can let go of property can later let go of reputation and position.
The Light of the 321 Principles: God’s System Is a Group of People Emptied of Self

Chapter 4 begins with an arrest and ends with a field. In between came the trial, the ban, release, prayer, shaking, filling—and it finally lands here: a group of one heart and soul, no one saying things were his own, no one lacking.

This is God’s system. It is not a set of rules or an organization chart but a realm naturally formed by people who let Jesus be King. Within this realm, because each person’s “self” has given way, unity needs no negotiation, supply needs no compulsion, witness needs no packaging. Changing concepts changes life, changing life changes living—their concept changed from “mine” to “His,” their life became one heart and one soul, their living became having no one lacking.

We often want to do it the other way around: first design a good system, hoping hearts will change to follow. But the early church’s order was first life, then relationships, then ministry. If “mine” is still in the heart, even the best system will be cut apart by that line; if there is no “mine” in the heart, the simplest way—lay it at the feet, distribute by need—is enough.

Barnabas sold the field and laid it at the feet. This was not a financial decision but a decision of “who is King.” Building God’s system always begins with this kind of decision—one person, one field, one letting go.
a: Tune to the Same Tuning Fork
Unity is not worn out of each other but each tuning to the Lord.
Wipe Out the Line of “Mine”
Manage things as before, but He becomes the ruler.
Let Witness Grow from Life
With one heart within, there is great power without.
At the Feet, Not in the Hand
What is given goes to the Lord; once let go, don’t clutch it.
Begin with One Field
Is there something today the Lord wants you to lay at His feet?
q: Is there something in your life that, the moment you think of “maybe having to give it up,” the thought “But this is mine” pops up at once? Who is ruling that thing right now?

The apostles saw “Son of Encouragement” in Joseph and called him that. If brothers and sisters were to name you after the quality they see in you, what do you think it would be? What do you hope it would be?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that a group filled with the Holy Spirit not only preached boldly with their mouths but also loosened their hands. Thank You that the promise in Deuteronomy, “there will be no poor among you,” came true among people whose hearts were changed. Thank You for giving us Barnabas, a Son of Encouragement who began with one field and spent his life lifting others up.
Lord Jesus, we confess that the “This is mine” within us is still loud—my money, my time, my reputation, my position. We often want to design a good system first, yet are unwilling to let our own hearts change first. Forgive us, wipe out that line of “mine,” so that our things are managed as before but You are the One who rules. Make each of us tune to You, so that we become one heart and one soul, with no one among us lacking. And show us what, today, You want us to lay at Your feet—may we let go, no longer clutching, and let You be King over our money, our relationships, and everything. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira, his wife, sold a possession,
and kept back part of the price, his wife also being aware of it, then brought a certain part and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land?
While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.”
Ananias, hearing these words, fell down and died. Great fear came on all who heard these things.
The young men arose and wrapped him up, and they carried him out and buried him.
About three hours later, his wife, not knowing what had happened, came in.
Peter answered her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” She said, “Yes, for so much.”
But Peter asked her, “How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.”
She fell down immediately at his feet and died. The young men came in and found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her by her husband.
Great fear came on the whole assembly, and on all who heard these things.
b: In the last devotion, Luke fixed the camera on Barnabas: he sold his field and laid the money at the apostles’ feet, and chapter 4 ended in a blaze of light.

At the first line of chapter 5 the camera did not change: “A certain man … sold a possession … and laid it at the apostles’ feet.” The same selling of a field, the same laying at the feet. Luke deliberately placed the two side by side to make us see: the outward action can be exactly the same while the heart within is worlds apart. The last devotion was a “Son of Encouragement”; this one is the first funeral in church history.
I. “Kept back part of the price”—The Problem Is Not Keeping Back, but Pretending Not To
In verses 1 and 2, Ananias and Sapphira sold a possession and “kept back part of the price,” and brought the rest to lay at the apostles’ feet.

Both names are beautiful: Ananias means “Yahweh is gracious,” and Sapphira means “beautiful.” A couple with such good names did something inconsistent within and without. The phrase “kept back” in the Greek Old Testament is exactly the word used of Achan in Joshua 7—Achan “took” the devoted things and hid them in his tent (Josh. 7:1). Luke wants us to hear the echo: as soon as Israel entered Canaan, there was Achan; as soon as the church was born, there was Ananias. The new Israel met the old problem from the very start.

Be clear: their sin was not “keeping back part.” Peter made it plain in verse 4: the land was yours, the money yours to decide, whether to sell and how much to give was entirely voluntary. Their sin was that they kept back part while letting people think what they brought was the whole. What they wanted was not money but the kind of regard Barnabas received—wanting to buy the reputation of the whole with the cost of a part.
• What is voluntary needs no pressure: the Lord never forces people to sell fields; He wants only honesty.
• What they wanted was regard, not money: those who keep back money are often those who cannot bear to lose reputation.
II. “You have not lied to men, but to God”—The Wrong Audience
In verses 3 and 4, Peter spoke. He did not say, “How could you be so stingy?”; he said: “Why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit?” and then, “You haven’t lied to men, but to God.”

Note two things. First, the previous chapter had just said “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit,” yet here it says “Satan filled your heart.” The human heart is never left empty; if it is not filled with the Holy Spirit, something else fills it. Second, verse 3 says “lie to the Holy Spirit” and verse 4 says “lied to God,” speaking of the same thing—the Holy Spirit is God, one of the most direct passages in the New Testament.

Ananias thought he was dealing with Peter and a group of people: as long as they did not know, the matter would pass. He forgot that the money was laid “at the apostles’ feet”—laid at the feet, placed under the sovereignty the apostles represented. He had handed the money to God and then lied to God. We too easily do the same today: thinking giving is for people to see, service is done for people to see; when we think “as long as people don’t know, it’s fine,” we have already removed God from the audience—this is the deepest sickness of the self-centered: eyes only on people, none on God.
• The audience is Him: what is laid at the feet is watched by God, not by people.
III. “Fell down and died”—When a New System Begins, God Himself Draws the Line
In verses 5 and 6, Ananias heard these words, fell down, and died; the young men wrapped him, carried him out, and buried him. Many who read this ask: isn’t that too severe? Why him?

Note a pattern in the Bible: at the start of every new stage, God Himself draws a line. When the tabernacle had just been set up, Nadab and Abihu offered strange fire and were consumed on the spot (Lev. 10:1–2); when Israel had just entered Canaan, Achan hid something and his whole household was put to death (Josh. 7). It was not that that generation’s sin was greater than later ones, but that at the beginning God wanted everyone to see clearly: this system is holy, and who reigns within it. When the church had just been born and the first counterfeit appeared, God dealt with it Himself, so that the church for the next two thousand years would remember.

God resists the proud (James 4:6). Ananias’ pride was not showy; he only wanted a little more glory before people. But God’s system is not a group of people who do good; it is a group who let Jesus be King. One who lies at the feet is lying before the throne.
• The line is clearest at the beginning: not that this generation’s sin was worst, but God wanted those after to see.
• A little is fatal: before the throne there is no “small” dishonesty.
IV. “Why is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord?”—Three Hours, One Chance to Turn Back
Verses 7 to 10. Three hours later Sapphira came in, not knowing what had happened. Peter asked her: “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” She said, “Yes, for so much.”

This question was a door. Peter did not accuse first; he first gave her a chance to tell the truth. She could have said, “No, we kept back some”; but she said, “Yes, for so much,” and the door closed.

“Agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord”—the previous chapter said the believers were “of one heart and soul,” yet here husband and wife “agreed together” to lie. Two people agreeing together to do wrong is not called unity but conspiracy. Then Luke records an extremely sharp detail: “She fell down immediately at his feet.” They laid the money at the apostles’ feet, hoping to gain glory there; she herself fell at Peter’s feet and was judged there. What you lay at the feet, at the feet you receive back.

Phones have filters; touch up a photo, post it, and everyone likes it; but when meeting the person, the gap shows. Ananias and Sapphira put a filter on their giving—retouching out the part kept back, posting only the look of “all.” Peter’s question was meant to make her take off the filter and let the real person come out. She chose to keep the filter.
• God always opens a door first: before judgment there is always a chance to tell the truth.
• Agreeing together is not unity: two people doing wrong together is conspiracy.
V. “Great fear came on the whole assembly, and on all who heard these things”—Reverence Is the Church’s First Lesson

In verse 11, the word “church” appears in Acts for the first time. Luke called this group by this name for the first time not on the day three thousand were baptized, not on the day the place was shaken, but after two bodies had been carried out. The church’s first lesson was not power or numbers but reverence.

“Fear” is not fear that God might strike anyone at any moment but a sudden realization: He is really here, and He sees all we do. This fear does not drive people away from God but makes them unwilling to be careless with God: to speak more slowly, give more honestly, perform less in service.
• Reverence keeps people from being careless: knowing He is watching, we stop performing.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Letting Jesus Receive All the Glory—Not Even a Little Kept

Barnabas and Ananias both sold fields and laid it at the feet. The difference is that Barnabas laid down even the glory, while Ananias wanted to keep a little for himself. What he kept was not only part of the price but part of the light he wanted for himself.

Letting Jesus receive all the glory—the word “all” is the sharpest point of this passage. The old self’s life of self does not necessarily refuse to glorify God, but is used to keeping a little for itself while glorifying God: giving should be known, service should be seen, even humility should be praised. This little is “kept back part.” The focus is on Jesus, not on self or others—Ananias’ focus was on how others saw him; this was the root of the sickness.

Self-denial is not about not doing but about not keeping after doing. Barnabas did and kept nothing; Ananias also did but kept a little. Luke recorded both names, one an example, one a warning. Everything we do today chooses between these two names.
a: Don’t Use a Filter
Say as much as you gave, be as much as you do; let the real person come out.
See the Audience Clearly
What is laid at the feet is watched by God; whether people know is not the point.
Let the Right Thing Fill the Heart
The heart is never empty; if not filled with the Spirit, something else will fill it.
Take Hold of the Door of Telling the Truth
God always asks a question before holding to account; don’t say “Yes, for so much.”
Keep Not Even a Little
When glorifying Him, check whether you have kept a part for yourself.
q: Think of a service or gift you made recently that people praised. Ask yourself honestly: was there any “kept back part”—doing less than people thought, or with motives more mixed than people thought? Are you willing to bring that part out before the Lord too?
Peter first asked Sapphira one question, giving her a chance to tell the truth. Is there something right now that God is also asking you, “Is that all?” How will you answer?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for letting us see Ananias beside Barnabas, so that we know the same outward action can come from two completely different hearts. Thank You for drawing this line Yourself when the church had just been born, so that we still remember: You are holy, You are truly here, and You see everything we do.
Lord Jesus, we confess that when we glorify You, we often keep a little for ourselves—giving that people should know, service that people should see, even humility that we want praised; we think that as long as people don’t know it’s fine, yet forget that the audience has always been You. Forgive us, find that “kept back” part of light in our hearts and lay it at Your feet too. Fill our hearts with the Holy Spirit, leaving no room for Satan; and give us a heart of reverence, so that before You we speak more slowly, act more honestly, and perform less in service. May You receive all the glory, not even a little kept for ourselves. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people. They were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.
None of the rest dared to join them, however the people honored them.
More believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women.
They even carried out the sick into the streets, and laid them on cots and mattresses, so that as Peter came by, at the least his shadow might overshadow some of them.
The multitude also came together from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick people and those who were tormented by unclean spirits: and they were all healed.
b: In the last devotion, two bodies were carried out, and the whole church feared greatly. So what happens next to a fearful church? By human thinking, probably everyone looking out for himself and slowly drifting away.

What Luke wrote is the opposite. This is the third “panorama” Acts takes of the early church (the first two were in 2:42–47 and 4:32–35), and this time the scene is of miracles, of esteem, of growth beyond measure, and of people hoping even for a shadow. It turns out reverence does not make the church shrink; reverence makes the church healthy.
I. “Through the hands of the apostles”—The Subject Is the Lord; the Hands Are Human
First half of verse 12: “By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people.”

Look first at the subject. Not “the apostles did many signs and wonders” but “by the hands of the apostles”—done through them. Luke writes carefully: the One who acts is the Lord, and the apostles are only hands. At the end of chapter 4 they prayed, “while you stretch out your hand to heal, and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy Servant Jesus” (Acts 4:30); here is the answer to that prayer—God stretched out His hand, using the apostles’ hands.

When water comes out of a pipe, no one says, “What a good pipe for producing water.” A pipe does not produce water; it only lets water pass through. The apostles’ hands were like this: the hands had no power; the power came from the Lord, and the hands only had to not block it. Jesus is my example—even on earth He said, “The Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19); if even the Son of God was only a hand in the Father’s hand, we have even less reason to count ourselves the source.

The self loves to take away the word “through,” turning “the Lord did through me” into “I did.” But once that word is removed, the hand becomes the source; and a hand that becomes the source soon runs dry.
• The subject is the Lord: power was never in the hands; the hands only have to not block it.
• Don’t remove the word “through”: remove it and you become the source, and soon run dry.
II. “All with one accord in Solomon’s porch”—Returning to Where Jesus Walked

Second half of verse 12 to verse 13. Solomon’s porch was a covered colonnade on the east side of the temple’s outer court, where the Lord Jesus walked and taught in the temple in winter (John 10:23), and where, after the lame man’s healing in chapter 3, he held on to Peter and John and the people ran together to look (Acts 3:11). The early church had no house of its own and gathered in the porch where the Lord had walked. “With one accord”—this word has appeared several times (1:14, 2:46, 4:24), Luke’s favorite for describing this group. The matter of Ananias did not tear them apart; it drew them closer.

Then comes a curious statement: “None of the rest dared to join them; however, the people honored them.” Not daring to join, yet honoring—this was the direct result of the Ananias incident. Those who still wanted to keep back a part suddenly found that this group was not a place one could casually slip into; and for that very reason the people came to honor them. A group with too low a threshold lets everyone in, and so no one esteems it; a truly holy group, people dare not approach casually, but they respect it sincerely.
The church’s attraction is not in lowering the standard so everyone feels comfortable; it is in God truly being within, and people can see this is not a casual place.
• Return to where the Lord walked: they had no house of their own, but they had the Lord’s footsteps.
• Not daring to join, yet honoring: holiness does not drive people away; holiness makes people esteem.
III. “Believers were added all the more to the Lord”—Growth Comes After the Fear, Not Before
Verse 14: “Believers were added all the more to the Lord, multitudes both of men and women.”

The position of this verse matters. It follows right after “none of the rest dared to join them.” People dared not casually join, yet believers were added all the more—these two do not contradict but are two sides of one thing. True growth does not come from lowering the threshold but from letting people see God is truly here. Those drawn were not there to watch a show but “believers … added to the Lord”—Luke specially adds “to the Lord,” showing that what they turned to was that Lord, not the apostles, not a lively movement.

“Both of men and women”—Luke again mentions women. In that age numbers usually counted only men; Luke repeatedly writes women in. God’s system is not a circle of people of standing but a realm formed by everyone who lets Jesus be King, male or female, of whatever standing.
• Growth after reverence: first let God truly be here, and people will naturally come.
• What they turned to was the Lord: not the apostles, not a movement.
IV. “That at the least his shadow might overshadow some of them”—Even the Shadow Is Not His Own

Verses 15 and 16 are the most moving picture of the passage. People carried the sick into the streets, laid them on cots and mats, hoping only that when Peter passed, his shadow might fall on them. Note Luke’s wording: he says people “hoped” that his shadow might overshadow some; he did not say the shadow healed anyone; he only summarizes in verse 16 that “they were all healed.” The healer was the Lord, not the shadow. Luke does not let us make an idol of Peter or his shadow.

Still, this picture tells us something profound. What is a shadow? A person standing in light has a shadow; the shadow is not something he makes, he cannot control where it falls, and often he is not even aware of it. A truly self-denied person is like this: he just walks past, and what the Lord does through him often even he himself does not know. Peter did not stop to pray over his shadow; he just walked by. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me (Gal. 2:20)—lived to the point that even the shadow was used by the Lord.

Verse 16 has another turn: the sick came “from the cities around Jerusalem.” This is the first time Acts records the gospel’s influence crossing Jerusalem’s walls. The “Jerusalem, and in all Judea” the Lord spoke of (Acts 1:8) begins here to seep outward. And Luke closes with “they were all healed”—not some, but all.
• The healer is the Lord, not the shadow: Luke does not let people worship Peter, or Peter’s shadow.
• Self-denied to the point that even the shadow is used: he just walks past, and what the Lord does behind him he may not know.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Self-Denial Is Not Having Nothing but Entering the Limitless

In this passage the apostles hardly did anything. They did not preach a sermon, did not perform one clearly recorded miracle; Luke says only that they were “with one accord in Solomon’s porch,” and Peter “passed by.” Yet in just such “doing nothing,” the Lord did many signs and wonders through their hands, believers were added all the more, and people from the surrounding cities were all healed.

This is the secret of self-denial. Self-denial is not having nothing but entering the limitless. A person who clings to himself can do at most the little he can do; a person who hands himself over completely, the Lord can use his hands, his words, even the shadow of his passing, to do what he could never do in a lifetime. Peter’s hands were only hands, Peter’s shadow only a shadow, but because the One reigning within was the Lord, hands and shadow both became places where the Lord worked.

Use the heart and rely on the Spirit, not the head relying on self. The one using the head calculates: how should I act to get such results? The one using the heart asks only one thing: have I let Him reign today? If He reigns, passing by is enough; if self reigns, however hard one tries, it is only a pipe trying to produce water by itself.
a: Remember the Subject Is the Lord
Whatever you do today, add back that word “through” in your heart.
Return to Where the Lord Walked
You need no house of your own; you need His footsteps.
Don’t Lower the Threshold; Have God
What makes people esteem the church is not comfort but holiness.
What They Turn to Is the Lord
Bring people before the Lord, not before yourself.
Let Even the Shadow Be Used
You just walk past; leave what the Lord does behind you to Him.
q: Think of the last time someone praised you. In your heart, was the subject of that matter “I” or “the Lord through me”? If you added back the word “through,” how would your feeling differ?

Peter walked by, his shadow fell on people, and he himself may not have known. Are you willing to accept the Lord using you in places you “don’t know”? What challenge would this be to a “self” that wants to control all the results?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that after two bodies were carried out, Your church did not shrink but grew healthy in reverence. Thank You for letting us see that You are the One who works miracles, that the apostles were only hands in Your hand, and that even the shadow of Peter’s passing You can use.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often turn “the Lord did through me” into “I did,” counting ourselves the source, and soon run dry. Forgive us, put that word “through” back in our hearts, so that we are willing to be only a pair of hands, a pipe, a shadow. Give us a heart of one accord, to gather where You have walked; and let our church draw people not by lowering the threshold but because You are truly here and people esteem it. May we be self-denied to the point that we just walk past, while You do behind us what we could never do in a lifetime. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: But the high priest rose up, and all those who were with him (which is the sect of the Sadducees), and they were filled with jealousy
and laid hands on the apostles, then put them in public custody.
But an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, and brought them out and said,
“Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.”

When they heard this, they entered into the temple about daybreak and taught. But the high priest came, and those who were with him, and called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
But the officers who came didn’t find them in the prison. They returned and reported,
“We found the prison shut and locked, and the guards standing before the doors, but when we opened them, we found no one inside!”
Now when the high priest, the captain of the temple, and the chief priests heard these words, they were very perplexed about them and what might become of this.
One came and told them, “Behold, the men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching the people.”
Then the captain went with the officers, and brought them without violence, for they were afraid that the people might stone them.
b: In the last devotion, the sick were carried into the streets, hoping only for Peter’s shadow to sweep over them; people came from the surrounding cities and were all healed. Believers were added all the more.

Growth does not come without a cost. In chapter 4 the Sanhedrin arrested Peter and John once, threatened them, and let them go; this time they arrested all the apostles. But as you read this passage, you will find: the most flustered were not those imprisoned but those who imprisoned them. The apostles, locked in prison, could sleep; the Sanhedrin, seated in the great hall, was “greatly perplexed about them and what might become of this.”
I. “Filled with jealousy”—What Pride Fears Most Is Its Seat Being Threatened

In verses 17 and 18, Luke takes care to note that this group was “the sect of the Sadducees.” The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy of the time, in charge of the temple, on good terms with Rome, accepting only the five books of Moses, believing neither in resurrection nor in angels (Acts 23:8). The apostles were teaching the resurrection of Jesus in the temple every day, which was to teach daily, on their territory, what they most disbelieved—and the people were listening more and more.

“Jealousy” in the original is actually “zeal,” the same word that can mean zeal for God or envy of people. The Sadducees’ problem was that their zeal had the wrong object: they were zealous for their own position, their own territory, their own authority. Pride is leaving one’s place and grasping power, wanting to take God’s place. Priests were meant to be those who stand between God and people in service, but now they stood before God blocking the way. Today life often shows the same: hearing that someone else has done better than oneself, the first reaction is not thanks but a tightening in the heart. That tightening is the seed of jealousy.
• Zeal with the wrong object becomes jealousy: zealous for your own position, you cannot tolerate God’s work.
• The first reaction shows who is reigning: hearing someone else is blessed, is it thanks or a tightening?
II. “An angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night”—God Brings Them Out So That They May Be Sent Back In

Verses 19 and 20. “But”—Luke’s favorite turn. People did one thing, and God followed with another. The Sadducees did not believe in angels, and God sent an angel to open the prison doors; a quiet humor.

But note what the angel said. He did not say, “Run, hide in Galilee for a while”; he said, “Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.” The temple was exactly where they had been seized the day before; to stand in the temple was exactly what they had been forbidden to do. God opened the prison doors not to make them safe but to send them back to the most dangerous place to preach. “All the words of this life”—not a set of doctrines but a way that makes people come alive, all the words about the Lord who rose from the dead.
When we ask God to open a door, we mostly ask for a door to “leave here”; the door God opens is often a door to “go back there.” He rescues us from difficulty so that we may return with a testimony.
• God opens the door not for escape: but to send people back to their place to speak.
• “All the words of this life”: not teaching, but the way that makes people live.
III. “They entered into the temple about daybreak, and taught”—Hear and Do, Without Waiting for Daylight
First half of verse 21: “When they heard it, they entered into the temple about daybreak, and taught.”

What the angel said at midnight, the apostles did at first light. No meeting to discuss, no risk assessment, no “let’s watch for a while.” The Holy Spirit is my guide—the key to guidance is not how clearly you hear but how quickly you move after hearing. The self hears guidance and first runs it through its own head: Is it safe? Is it worth it? What will others think? By the time the head has finished, the opportunity has passed. The apostles used the heart and relied on the Spirit: hearing, they entered the temple.

In the second half of the same verse, another group was also moving: the high priest “called together the council, even all the senate of the children of Israel”—the whole Sanhedrin, seventy-one, the highest council of the Jews, solemnly convened. Both sides were acting at daybreak: one going into the temple to preach, one convening a great assembly to summon them. Luke places the two scenes side by side and lets us compare who is doing the thing that really matters.
• The key to guidance is moving quickly: hear and do, without first running it through your own head.
• Both sides busy: one speaking the words of life, one holding a meeting to arrest.
IV. “The prison we found shut in all safety … no one inside”—Human Locks Cannot Stop God’s Door

Verses 22 to 24. The officers returned and reported: “We found the prison shut and locked in all safety, and the guards standing before the doors; but when we had opened, we found no one inside.” This was the limit of what people can do: doors locked, guards posted, everything secure. Yet inside the secure door, there was no one. Luke deliberately has the officers say this themselves: not one of the precautions people can take had been lacking, and God brought the men out all the same.

Children sometimes build a wall of blocks and enclose their toys, thinking no one can take them. An adult walks by, reaches over the top, and takes them out. To the child the block wall is “perfectly secure”; to the adult it does not exist. The Sadducees’ prison was just such a block wall—what they built so carefully, God did not even need to dismantle; He simply led them out over the top.

And the line that follows, “greatly perplexed about them and what might become of this,” is the most thought-provoking line of the whole passage. Those in power did not know what would become of this; those in prison clearly knew what to do today. Who truly has security is plain to see. The focus is on Jesus, not on circumstances—the apostles’ circumstances were a prison, the Sanhedrin’s a great hall, yet the one at ease was the one in prison.
• Human limits cannot stop God: however securely shut, if He wants to lead out, He leads out.
• Whoever is perplexed is not king: the one truly reigning never needs to be perplexed about the future.
V. “Without violence, for they feared the people”—The Sanhedrin Feared the People; the Apostles Did Not Fear the Sanhedrin

Verses 25 and 26. Someone came to report: “Behold, the men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching the people.” The captain and the officers went and brought the apostles, “without violence, for they were afraid that the people might stone them.”

Here is a chain of “fears.” The officers feared the people, the Sanhedrin feared the people, but the apostles did not fear the Sanhedrin. They did not flee, did not hide; when the officers came, they went along. What a person fears shows who reigns in his heart. The Sanhedrin feared the people because their position rested on the people’s support; the apostles did not fear the Sanhedrin because their position rested on the risen Lord.

Those arrested were calmer than those arresting. Using the heart brings gladness, using the head brings anxiety: the apostles followed guidance with the heart, so they were at ease; the Sanhedrin calculated the people’s hearts with the head, so fear was everywhere.
• What you fear shows who reigns: those who fear people have their position built on people.
• The arrested are calmer than the arresters: those who follow guidance need not calculate; those who calculate fear everywhere.
The Light of the 321 Principles: The Focus Is Jesus, Not Circumstances

The main characters of this passage seem to be the angel, the prison doors, the officers, and the Sanhedrin, but the real main character is only One: the Lord who opened the doors by night and sent people back to the temple.

For the apostles, the circumstances were prison, guards, the Sanhedrin, and a ban; for the Sanhedrin, the circumstances were a group of disobedient people, ever more people, and an emptied prison. Neither side’s circumstances were good. But the apostles’ focus was not on circumstances but on the Lord who opened the door, so at first light they entered the temple; the Sanhedrin’s focus was wholly on circumstances, so they were perplexed, not knowing what would become of this.

The old self’s life of self always looks at circumstances: Is the door locked? Are there many people? Is it dangerous? Good circumstances bring gladness, bad circumstances bring anxiety. The new self’s life emptied of self looks at the Lord: where He says go, go; whether the door is locked is His business. Self-denial is what lets us be led by the Holy Spirit—because guidance often leads people back to the most dangerous place, and one still making plans for himself cannot walk in.

Change from the human viewpoint to God’s viewpoint: from the human view, the prison was shut in all safety; from God’s view, no one was inside. Changing concepts changes life—from which viewpoint do you look at your circumstances today?
a: Check Your First Reaction
Hearing someone else blessed, is it thanks or a tightening in your heart?
Ask for the Door of “Going Back,” Not Only “Leaving”
God brings you out to send you back to give testimony.
Hear and Move
Guidance is not for assessing but for obeying; don’t wait for daylight.
Don’t Be Troubled by Block Walls
All that people build “in all safety” does not exist before God.
See What You Fear
