What you fear shows who reigns in your heart.
q: In your life right now, is there a door “shut in all safety” that you keep looking at and worrying about? If you turned your focus from that door back to the Lord, what would you do differently today?
God’s opening of a door is often not for people to flee but for them to go back. Is there a situation you very much want to “leave” that the Lord actually wants you to “go back” to with a testimony?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that though people shut the doors in all safety, You opened them by night and led them out. Thank You for letting us see that those imprisoned could sleep while those who imprisoned them were perplexed; true security has never been in circumstances but in You.
Lord Jesus, we confess that our eyes too often fix on circumstances: whether the door is locked, whether there are many people, whether it is dangerous; good circumstances bring gladness, bad circumstances bring anxiety. We also confess that what we ask You to open is mostly a door to “leave here,” and we seldom ask for a door to “go back there.” Forgive us, turn our focus from circumstances back to You; where You say go, we will go, and whether the door is locked we leave to You. Look also into the bit of jealousy within us—the tightening when we hear someone else is blessed—and change it into thanks. May we, like the apostles, hear and move, and at first light stand where You want us to stand, speaking the words of this life to people. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

v: When they had brought them, they set them before the council. The high priest questioned them,
saying, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us.”
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree.
God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins.
We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”
b: In the last devotion, the officers did not dare use violence and brought the apostles out of the temple. The apostles did not flee but went along. Now, for the second time, they stood before the Sanhedrin.

Last time the Sanhedrin asked, “By what power, or in what name, have you done this?”; this time they did not ask but rebuked directly. And the apostles’ reply is the shortest and most powerful sermon in the whole book of Acts: only four verses, yet it states the skeleton of the gospel completely—He died, God raised Him, God exalted Him as Prince and Savior, and we and the Holy Spirit are witnesses together.
I. “You intend to bring this man’s blood on us”—The High Priest Would Not Even Say the Name

In verses 27 and 28, the high priest rebuked them. Note his wording. He did not say “Jesus” but “this name”; he did not say “Jesus’ blood” but “this man’s blood.” He would not even let that name come out of his mouth. The more a person avoids a name, the more it shows how heavily that name weighs in his heart.

Then he unintentionally spoke two true things. First: “You have filled Jerusalem with your teaching.” This was a rebuke but also the best testimony—Jerusalem was filled. The second was sharper: “You intend to bring this man’s blood on us.” Months earlier, before Pilate, this very group had cried out, “His blood be on us, and on our children” (Matt. 27:25). They had cried it with full assurance then; now they were terrified. What people say in triumph they often dare not own when afraid.
• Avoiding a name shows how heavy it is: what one will not say is often what one cannot let go of.
• Cried out in triumph, not owned in fear: people’s words change; God’s word does not.
II. “We must obey God rather than men”—Not Rebellion, but Returning to One’s Place

Verse 29. In chapter 4 they had said something similar: “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves” (Acts 4:19). That time they still left the question for the Sanhedrin to judge; this time they did not, saying directly “we must.” “Obey” in the original means “to obey one in authority,” said toward authority. The apostles did not deny the Sanhedrin had authority—they acknowledged it; only when the Sanhedrin’s command collided with God’s command, they knew which authority was higher.

Be clear: this sentence is not a rebel’s slogan. The apostles did not incite the people, did not resist arrest, and when the officers came to take them, went along. They simply could not yield on one thing: they could not stop speaking of Jesus. This is just what humility looks like—humility is not saying yes to everyone; humility is returning to one’s place: letting God be God and man be man. The Sanhedrin left its place and tried to block God’s word with human authority; the apostles kept their place, respecting what should be respected among people and obeying what must be obeyed in God.

An employee receives an instruction from his direct supervisor that is the exact opposite of the company owner’s; he obeys the owner, not out of disrespect for the supervisor but because he knows whose company it is. Such collisions do not happen often in life, but they will happen: the boss wants you to fiddle with the books, a friend wants you to tell a lie together, family wants you to give up a principle for the sake of peace. Then “obey God rather than men” is no longer the apostles’ word but your choice.
• Obeying God is not rebellion: respect what should be respected, yielding nothing only in a collision.
• Humility is returning to one’s place: let God be God and man be man, neither overstepping.
III. “The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree”—Two Actions, Two Subjects

Verse 30 has two subjects in one verse: “you” and “God.” You killed, and God raised Him. This is the contrast in every apostolic sermon (2:23–24, 3:15, 4:10), and this time it is stated shortest and starkest.

“Hanging him on a tree”—Peter did not say “crucified,” he said “hanging on a tree.” This quotes Deuteronomy: “He who is hanged is accursed of God” (Deut. 21:23). Peter said before the priests: you did not merely kill Him; you put Him to death as one accursed. But “the God of our fathers”—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, your God is also our God—Himself overturned your verdict.

This is both comfort and reminder. People can place you in the most humiliating position, but the final verdict is not in their hands. And before that, we must first honestly stand on the side of “you”: those who nailed Him were not only that group but every life of self.
• Two subjects: man’s verdict may be very heavy, but God’s verdict is final.
• First stand on the side of “you”: those who nailed Him are every life of self.
IV. “God exalted him as Prince and Savior”—The Order Cannot Be Reversed

Verse 31. “Prince” in the original means “originator, chief,” which chapter 3 translated as “Prince of life” (3:15). “Savior” is the One who saves. Note the order: first Prince, then Savior. This was not arranged casually. We often reverse it: first we want Him as Savior, to solve my problem, forgive my sins, give me peace; as for being King, that is a later matter, to be considered as circumstances allow. But God’s order in exalting Him is: first King, then saving. One who will not let Him be King has not really let Him be Savior either—what he wants is only the benefits of salvation, not that Lord.

Look at the second half of the verse: “to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins.” That forgiveness of sins is given we understand; but even “repentance” is given. Repentance is not an emotion we squeeze out by effort but a gift He sends down from the throne. If you still grieve over sin and still want to turn today, it is not that you are good but that He has already begun to work in you.
• First Prince, then Savior: those who want only the benefits and not the Lord have neither.
• Even repentance is given: that you still want to turn is evidence He is already at work.
V. “The Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him, also testifies”—Two Witnesses

Verse 32. By the law, a matter is established by the mouth of two witnesses (Deut. 19:15). Peter produced two witnesses: we, and the Holy Spirit. “We” are those who saw with their own eyes; “the Holy Spirit” is the One who worked through their hands—everything that troubled the Sanhedrin, the emptied prison, the filled Jerusalem, the sick in the streets healed, was the Holy Spirit bearing witness.

And Peter added a qualification: the Holy Spirit is “whom God has given to those who obey him.” This line goes back to “we must obey God” in verse 29. Obedience and the Holy Spirit are joined: it is not that one has power first and then obeys, but one obeys first and the Spirit then fills. If you will not obey His guidance, He cannot bear witness through you.
• Two witnesses: we and the Holy Spirit, human mouth and God’s work.
• Obedience first: not that having the Spirit comes first and then obeying, but obeying, and then the Spirit bears witness.
The Light of the 321 Principles: Letting Jesus Be King—He Is First Prince, Then Savior
The core sentence of this four-verse sermon is “God exalted him as Prince and Savior.”

Letting Jesus be King is the first of the two core principles. But we often put it far behind: first let Him be Savior, and when life is manageable and matters settled, consider letting Him be King. God’s order is not so. He exalted Jesus first as Prince, then as Savior; salvation flows down from the throne. One who wants salvation but not the King is actually grasping only himself—he still sits on his own throne, only hoping for one more helper beside him.

The apostles’ “We must obey God rather than men” before the Sanhedrin is what letting Jesus be King looks like in life: not shouting slogans, but in a specific matter, when a human command collides with God’s, choosing God. Today you may not stand before the Sanhedrin, but you will stand in an office, at a dinner table, among friends, and meet that small collision. What you choose in that moment shows who is King in your heart.
And those who obey receive the Holy Spirit. This is not an exchange but an order: first let Him be King, and the Spirit naturally bears witness.
a: Don’t Avoid That Name
Before people, say “Jesus” out loud; don’t substitute “this man” or “this name.”
Yield Only in a Collision
Respect all authority ordinarily; only when God and man collide, obey God.
Stand First on the Side of “You”
Acknowledge that what nailed Him is my own self, then receive His resurrection.
First Prince, Then Savior
Check whether you want the benefits of salvation or that Lord.
Obey First, Then Wait to Be Filled
Don’t wait for power to obey; obey, and the Holy Spirit bears witness.
q: Think honestly: since you came to faith, did you first let Him be Savior or first let Him be King? In which area of your life is He Savior but not yet King?

Recall the most recent moment when a human request collided with God’s heart—perhaps something small, a sentence, an entry, a principle. Which side did you choose? If you could do it again, how would you choose?
pr:
Dear Heavenly Father, thank You that people hung Your Son on a tree, yet You raised Him and exalted Him with Your right hand as Prince and Savior. Thank You that even a heart of repentance is a gift from You; that we still want to turn today is evidence that You are already working in us.
Lord Jesus, we confess that we often reverse Your order: wanting You first as Savior to solve our problems, while pushing back Your being King again and again. We also confess that when human commands collide with Your command, we often choose people, because we fear them more than we revere You. Forgive us, return us to our place—letting You be God and us be human; and let us choose You when we meet that small collision in the office, at the dinner table, among friends. Give us a heart to obey, so that the Holy Spirit bears witness in us; and let us no longer avoid Your name but say “Jesus” clearly before people. May You be King first in our hearts, and then Savior. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.
